tok: Process Models as Text A guide to the language, the tools and the integrations Marek Deja Preface tok is a plain-text language for process models. A .tok file describes a BPMN 2.0 process, with its pools, lanes, events, tasks, gateways, flows and data, together with the DMN decisions the process uses, the forms people fill in and the parameters needed to simulate it. Every line of the file starts with a keyword and describes one element, so a model reads almost like a list of steps: tok 1.0 "Interlibrary loan" pool library "University library" lane reader "Reader" start need "Book needed" user request "Submit a loan request" lane librarian "Librarian" user catalogues "Search the catalogues" xor available "Is the book held locally?" user locate "Point to the local copy" user order "Order from another library" end located "Local copy located" end ordered "Order placed" flow need -> request -> catalogues -> available flow available -> locate "yes" flow available -> order "no" flow locate -> located flow order -> ordered The text is the model. The tok tools check it against the rules of BPMN 2.0.2 and turn it into everything else: a BPMN 2.0 XML file with a computed diagram layout, which Camunda Modeler and bpmn.io open like any other BPMN file; an SVG picture; DMN 1.5 decision files; Camunda 8 forms; simulation results and event logs. Existing BPMN and DMN files can be converted back to text with tok import. Nothing in the language is a coordinate: the drawing is computed whenever it is needed. The tools are built around one engine, written in Rust. You reach it from the command line (tok), from Python, R and Julia, from any program that can call a C library, from a web page through WebAssembly, from editors through a language server, and from AI agents through an MCP server. All of them give the same diagnostics, the same canonical text and the same exports, because they run the same code. This book is the guide to the language, the tools and their integrations. It explains the ideas behind tok, teaches the language from the first model to executable processes and decision models, and shows how to use tok in an editor, in a program, in a data analysis, with an AI agent and alongside Camunda 8. Who this book is for The book is written for four groups of readers. They share the first chapters and then take different routes. Reader You want to Reading path Users: analysts, process owners, consultants, people documenting procedures write and maintain process models, publish diagrams, hand models to an engine Chapters 1–7, then 8, 12; 9 and 10 when the models are to be run Students and teachers of process modelling learn BPMN through a notation that can be read, checked and compared line by line Chapters 1–7 in order, with their exercises, then 9 and 11; the appendices on symbols and the cheat sheet as references Developers call the engine from code, build tok into a pipeline, a service or a tool Chapters 1, 2 and 3 for the language, then 13, 10, 15 and the command reference Agent users: people who let an AI agent write or review models give an agent the language and the tools, and check what it produces Chapters 1–3 to read models yourself, then 7 and 14 No programming knowledge is needed for the language itself. Familiarity with BPMN helps but is not required: each construct is introduced with its meaning in BPMN 2.0.2, and the glossary collects the terms. How the book is organised The first two chapters explain the idea of models as text and get the tools running. Chapters 3 to 6 teach the language of process models: the basic elements, collaboration between participants, events and exceptions, data and artifacts. Chapters 7 and 8 cover checking models and moving them between text, diagrams and other tools. Chapters 9 to 11 add the layers above the process structure: DMN decisions, executable models for Camunda 8, and simulation. Chapters 12 to 15 are about the tools around the engine: editors and the playground, programming interfaces, AI agents and integrations with other software. The appendices are references to keep at hand: the symbol catalogue, the cheat sheet, the commands, the diagnostic codes, conformance with BPMN, DMN and Camunda, a glossary and the references. Conventions Models are printed in code blocks. They are complete documents that pass tok check, unless the text says that a model contains deliberate errors (the names of such files end in -error.tok): tok 1.0 "Short example" start s "Request received" user check "Check the request" end e "Request handled" flow s -> check -> e Commands you type in a terminal, and what the tools print, appear in plain blocks: tok check model.tok model.tok: 0 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) Below the diagrams of the longer examples you will find two links: one to the .tok file and one to the BPMN file that tok bpmn writes from it. Every example of the book is in the folder examples of the book’s repository. Four kinds of boxes appear in the text: In this chapter you will find a box like this at the start of every chapter, listing what the chapter teaches. A tip gives practical advice: a shortcut, a habit that saves time, a way to avoid a common mistake. A note marks something you must not overlook: a rule that differs from what you might expect, a limit, a difference between tools. Exercise 0.1 An exercise box holds a task to do with the tools. Each chapter ends with a set of exercises. Keywords, identifiers, attributes, file names and commands are set in monospace. Labels, the human-readable names of elements, are in “quotes”. BPMN element names follow the specification (userTask, exclusiveGateway); in the text they are written as words (user task, exclusive gateway). Versions This book describes language 1.0 and tools 1.0.3. Language 1.0 is the stable language: every release 1.x of the tools reads it with the same meaning and the same outputs, and documents of the earlier versions 0.1 to 0.7 stay valid and keep their meaning. Release 1.0.1 of the tools changes nothing in the language: the project has its home on GitHub (the organisation tok-lang-bpm), issues are reported there, the Python package starts the MCP server with tok mcp, and the engine draws the catalogue of BPMN symbols in the appendix. Check your version with: tok --version tok 1.0.3 The examples use the header tok 1.0. Models written for earlier versions of the language still work; Chapter 3 explains the header line and the version it declares. Licence tok and this book are free software. The tools, the examples and the text are released under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or (at your option) any later version (GPL-3.0-or-later). The full text of the licence is in the file LICENSE of the tok repository and of the book’s repository. Reporting issues The source code of tok is at https://github.com/tok-lang-bpm/tok. If a tool gives a wrong result, a message is unclear, an export does not open in another program, or something in this book is wrong or missing, please open an issue at https://github.com/tok-lang-bpm/tok/issues. A good report includes the version (tok --version), the smallest model that shows the problem, the command you ran and what it printed. How to cite If you use tok in research or teaching, please cite the software. The repository https://github.com/tok-lang-bpm/tok contains the file CITATION.cff with the citation metadata; GitHub shows it as Cite this repository and offers it in APA and BibTeX form, and reference managers can import it. A citation in text form: Deja, M. (2026). tok: a plain-text language for information-process models (Version 1.0.3) [Computer software]. https://github.com/tok-lang-bpm/tok

Chapter 1 Models as text In this chapter you will see what a BPMN file contains and which part of it a tok model keeps · read a tok model line by line · learn the principle that the text is the model and every file is a view of it · weigh what text gives you over a drawing · place tok among other text notations for processes · see how tok rests on the BPMN 2.0.2 metamodel and how tok import brings existing diagrams back to text 1.1 Two layers of a BPMN file A process diagram drawn in Camunda Modeler, bpmn.io or any other BPMN tool is saved as a .bpmn file. The file is XML in the format defined by the BPMN 2.0.2 specification of the Object Management Group (OMG), and it holds two different kinds of information. The first layer is the semantics of the model: which participants take part, which processes they run, which events, tasks and gateways each process contains, and how sequence flows and message flows connect them. This is the part a process engine reads, the part a validator checks and the part a reader of the diagram cares about. In the XML it lives in elements such as bpmn:process, bpmn:userTask and bpmn:sequenceFlow. The second layer is the layout, called diagram interchange (BPMN DI). It records where every shape lies and how large it is, and through which points every arrow runs. In the XML it lives in elements such as bpmndi:BPMNShape with dc:Bounds, and bpmndi:BPMNEdge with di:waypoint. The layout matters to people looking at the picture, but it does not change what the process does: move a task fifty pixels to the right and the process is the same process. Here is an excerpt of a small BPMN file. The first lines belong to the semantic layer, the last ones to the layout: <bpmn:process id="library-process" name="Interlibrary loan" isExecutable="false"> <bpmn:startEvent id="need" name="Book needed" /> <bpmn:userTask id="request" name="Submit a loan request" /> <bpmn:sequenceFlow id="f-need-request" sourceRef="need" targetRef="request" /> ... </bpmn:process> <bpmndi:BPMNDiagram id="BPMNDiagram_1"> <bpmndi:BPMNPlane id="BPMNPlane_1" bpmnElement="collaboration"> <bpmndi:BPMNShape id="request_di" bpmnElement="request"> <dc:Bounds x="176" y="30" width="100" height="80" /> </bpmndi:BPMNShape> ... The whole file of this example has 122 lines. Thirty-six of them describe the process; the other 85 are coordinates. In models drawn by hand the proportion is similar, and the coordinates are what make BPMN files hard to read, hard to compare and hard to write without a graphical editor. A tok model keeps only the first layer. The same process as tok text: tok 1.0 "Interlibrary loan" pool library "University library" lane reader "Reader" start need "Book needed" user request "Submit a loan request" lane librarian "Librarian" user catalogues "Search the catalogues" xor available "Is the book held locally?" user locate "Point to the local copy" user order "Order from another library" end located "Local copy located" end ordered "Order placed" flow need -> request -> catalogues -> available flow available -> locate "yes" flow available -> order "no" flow locate -> located flow order -> ordered Figure 1.1: The interlibrary loan, drawn by tok svg from the text above. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) The text has 19 lines, two of them empty. There are no coordinates: when a picture or a BPMN file is needed, the tools compute the layout from the structure of the model. Processes are drawn from left to right, pools are stacked one under another, and lanes are rows inside their pool, as most people draw BPMN by hand. 1.2 Reading a model line by line You can read the model above without knowing the language, because every line follows the same pattern: a keyword that says what the line describes, an identifier that names the element for the tools, a label in quotes that names it for people, and sometimes attributes that add details. Line Meaning BPMN element tok 1.0 "Interlibrary loan" the header: language version and title of the model definitions pool library "University library" a participant whose process is modelled, with the identifier library participant and its process lane reader "Reader" a lane in the pool; the lines indented under it belong to it lane start need "Book needed" a start event startEvent user request "Submit a loan request" a user task: a person working with a system userTask xor available "Is the book held locally?" an exclusive gateway, labelled with a question exclusiveGateway end located "Local copy located" an end event endEvent flow need -> request -> catalogues -> available three sequence flows written as one chain three sequenceFlow elements flow available -> locate "yes" one sequence flow with a label sequenceFlow with name="yes" Three rules are enough to read any tok model: Every line starts with a keyword. The keywords are short forms of the names of BPMN elements: start, end, user, service, xor, and, pool, lane, flow, message. After the keyword comes the identifier, then the label. The identifier (catalogues) is used to refer to the element elsewhere in the text, for example in flows; it becomes the id in the BPMN file. The label ("Search the catalogues") is what the diagram shows; it may be in any language and contain any characters. Indentation means belonging. A lane is indented under its pool, and the elements of a lane are indented under the lane. Flows usually stand at the end, without indentation, because they connect elements across lanes. The order of the lines is free: a flow may name an element declared further down. By convention, and in the canonical form that tok fmt prints, the elements come first and the flows below them. 1.3 The text is the model Working with tok follows one principle: the text is the model, and everything else is a view of it. The BPMN file for Camunda Modeler, the SVG picture for a report, the DMN files of the decisions, the forms, the simulation results: each of them is produced from the text by a command, and none of them is edited by hand. When the process changes, you change the text and produce the views again. model.tok ──► tok check is the model correct? (diagnostics with line numbers) ──► tok fmt the canonical form of the text ──► tok bpmn model.bpmn: BPMN 2.0 XML with diagram layout ──► tok svg model.svg: a picture of the diagram ──► tok export every file an engine needs: BPMN, SVG, DMN, forms ──► tok sim simulation: cycle times, waiting, utilisation, event log ──► tok eval the value of a decision for given inputs Command View Used for tok check a list of diagnostics, each with a line, a code and a message finding mistakes before anyone else sees them tok fmt the same text in its one canonical form stable layout of the text, clean diffs tok bpmn BPMN 2.0 XML with a computed diagram Camunda Modeler, bpmn.io, other BPMN tools tok svg an SVG picture documents, web pages, slides tok export the BPMN file, the picture, DMN files, Camunda forms deployment to Camunda 8 tok sim indicators and an event log estimating cycle times and workloads, process mining tok eval the value of a decision as JSON testing decision tables and decision models Several consequences follow from the principle. The views are always in step. Because the picture and the BPMN file are produced from the same text by the same engine, they cannot contradict each other or the text. A diagram pasted into a report a month ago may be out of date, but running tok svg again gives the current one. The layout is not your concern while you model. You never drag shapes or route arrows. The price is that you cannot place an element exactly where you want it; the gain is that adding a task never means rearranging half of the diagram. When a drawing made in another tool must be kept, the tools keep it beside the text in a separate file, as Chapter 8 explains. The text has one canonical form. tok fmt prints any valid model in exactly one way: two spaces of indentation, one space between words, attributes in a fixed order, flows joined into chains where they form a single path, comments kept where they were. Two people who write the same model and format it get the same text, so differences between versions are differences in the process, not in style. Layers stay apart. The structure of the process, the decisions, the forms, the details that a process engine needs and the parameters of a simulation are separate statements or separate attributes. A descriptive model never has to mention any of them, and a tool that does not need a layer can ignore it. You add the layers when you need them, as Chapters 9, 10 and 11 show. 1.4 Why text Graphical editors for BPMN are mature and pleasant to use. Writing models as text is not meant to replace them for every purpose; it brings advantages that a drawing stored as XML does not have. 1.4.1 Version control A process model is a document that changes: a regulation is amended, a step is automated, a role is moved to another department. Text can be kept in a version control system such as Git next to the procedures it describes, and every change is recorded with its author, date and reason. The decisive property is the size of the difference between two versions. Suppose the library decides that the reader must be notified after an order to another library. In tok the change is one new line and one changed line: @@ -9,6 +9,7 @@ xor available "Is the book held locally?" user locate "Point to the local copy" user order "Order from another library" + user notify "Notify the reader" end located "Local copy located" end ordered "Order placed" @@ -16,4 +17,4 @@ flow available -> locate "yes" flow available -> order "no" flow locate -> located -flow order -> ordered +flow order -> notify -> ordered The BPMN files written before and after the change differ in 30 lines, most of them coordinates of shapes that moved to make room for the new task. Nobody reviews such a difference line by line; everybody can review the two lines above. 1.4.2 Review Because each line describes one element, a model can be reviewed like any other text: in a pull request, in a document with comments, on paper. A reviewer can point to a line (“line 12: this should be a manual task, the librarian does not use the system here”), and the author can find it at once. The diagnostics of tok check use the same line numbers. 1.4.3 Collaboration Two people can work on the same model at the same time, each on a copy, and combine their changes with the ordinary tools for merging text. When they change different parts of the process, the merge is automatic. When they change the same line, the conflict is a conflict between two lines of text, which a person can resolve by reading them. Merging two XML files with diagram coordinates is, in practice, impossible without a graphical tool. 1.4.4 Agents A language model working as an agent handles short, regular text well and XML with coordinates poorly. In tok an agent writes the model as text, runs tok check (or calls the check tool of the MCP server), reads diagnostics that name a line and a code, corrects the lines, and never has to produce XML or place shapes. The whole language fits on one page, which tok cheatsheet prints and which can be given to an agent as context. Chapter 14 describes the tools for agents in detail. 1.4.5 Text tools Finally, text works with every tool that handles text: search across hundreds of models for every task in a given lane, generate models from a spreadsheet of steps, compare a model with the procedure it documents, read it with a screen reader. None of this needs a BPMN editor. A model that passes tok check without errors is correct BPMN. It is not necessarily a correct description of the real process: whether the steps, roles and decisions are the right ones is the responsibility of whoever models the process, exactly as in a graphical editor. 1.5 tok among other text notations tok is not the first language that describes processes in text. Three notations are often mentioned in the same breath. Mermaid is a language for diagrams in documentation, rendered in many wikis and code-hosting platforms. Its flowcharts can look like process diagrams, but they are pictures: Mermaid has no BPMN elements and writes no BPMN file. PlantUML draws UML diagrams, among them activity diagrams with swimlanes, from text. Like Mermaid, its result is an image. The notation is UML, not BPMN, and there is no BPMN 2.0 model behind the picture. BPMN Sketch Miner turns a story written as short sentences (“Reader: request the book”) into a BPMN-style diagram. It is designed for sketching a process quickly, for example in a workshop. Its text covers the visible outline of a process, with actors, activities and simple branches, but not the BPMN metamodel as a whole: messages and their flows, data, the kinds of events and their triggers, decisions and execution details are outside its scope. These tools are good at what they were made for: putting a picture next to a text. tok starts from the other end. Its aim is the model, and the picture is one of its views. A tok document is an exact description of a BPMN 2.0 model, and from it the tools write: a standard BPMN 2.0 XML file with diagram interchange, so that Camunda Modeler, bpmn.io and other BPMN tools open it as if it had been drawn in them; for executable models, a file that Camunda 8 deploys and runs, together with its decisions and forms; DMN 1.5 files for the decisions, which Camunda and other DMN engines evaluate. The same document is checked against the rules of BPMN 2.0.2, can be simulated, and can be produced from an existing BPMN file by tok import. A Mermaid or PlantUML diagram can be drawn from a description of a process; a tok model can take the place of the BPMN file itself. 1.6 The metamodel underneath The design of tok follows the metamodel of BPMN 2.0.2, the class model that the OMG specification defines and that every BPMN file instantiates. Every construct of the language corresponds to an element of that metamodel, and every element of a BPMN file that tok understands has exactly one way of being written in tok. tok BPMN 2.0.2 the header tok 1.0 "Title" definitions with its name pool with a block participant with its process pool without a block participant without a process (a black-box pool) lane lane in the laneSet of the process start, end, catch, throw, boundary startEvent, endEvent, intermediateCatchEvent, intermediateThrowEvent, boundaryEvent task, user, service, manual, script, rule, send, receive, call task, userTask, serviceTask, manualTask, scriptTask, businessRuleTask, sendTask, receiveTask, callActivity xor, and, or, eventgw, complex exclusiveGateway, parallelGateway, inclusiveGateway, eventBasedGateway, complexGateway flow sequenceFlow message messageFlow with its message message="Name", signal="Name", error="Name" message, signal, error declared by name and referenced by event definitions decision a DMN 1.5 decision with its decision logic Identifiers become the id attributes of the XML, which is why they are restricted to ASCII letters, digits, _ and -. Labels become the name attributes. Messages, signals, errors and escalations are declared implicitly: two events that name the same message refer to one message element in the file. Because the language rests on the metamodel, the checker can apply the rules of the specification. tok check reports, among others, a message flow inside one pool, a default flow on a parallel gateway, or a start event with an incoming flow, each with a stable code; the diagnostics appendix lists every code with its meaning. The checker also knows the conformance classes that the specification defines for process modelling (Descriptive, Analytic, Common Executable and Full) and tells you the smallest class your model fits: tok check 01-interlibrary-loan.tok --json { "file": "01-interlibrary-loan.tok", "errors": 0, "bpmn_class": "descriptive", "diagnostics": [] } The interlibrary loan uses only the elements of the Descriptive class, the visible core of BPMN that every modelling tool supports. Chapter 7 shows how to check a model against a class you choose. The same holds for decisions. A decision in tok is a DMN 1.5 decision: a decision table, a literal expression in FEEL, a context, a list, a relation or an invocation, with the decision requirements graph that connects decisions to their input data, business knowledge models and knowledge sources. Chapter 9 covers them. Not every element of the BPMN metamodel has a place in tok. A few rarely used ones (for example imports of external definitions and end points) are outside the language, and the extensions that other vendors write into their files are not kept. When tok import meets such an element, it says so; nothing disappears silently. The conformance appendix lists every element of BPMN 2.0.2 and DMN 1.5 with its tok construct, or the fact that tok does not express it. 1.7 Round trip: from BPMN back to text Since tok writes BPMN, it can also read it. tok import converts a BPMN 2.0 XML file, whether drawn in Camunda Modeler, in bpmn.io or in another tool, into tok text. Importing the file that tok bpmn wrote for the interlibrary loan gives back the model: tok import 01-interlibrary-loan.bpmn tok 0.1 "Interlibrary loan" pool library "University library" lane reader "Reader" start need "Book needed" user request "Submit a loan request" ... Only the header differs from the original. The import writes the oldest version of the language that expresses everything it read, here 0.1, because the model uses nothing that was added later. A document with that header means the same under every 1.x release, and you may change the header to tok 1.0 if you prefer. For files written by tok, the round trip is exact: text, then XML, then text again gives the same model, apart from the coordinates of the diagram. Files from other tools keep their structure, names, identifiers and documentation; everything the language cannot express is reported, element by element, on the standard error stream. The coordinates are not lost either. tok import diagram.bpmn -o model.tok writes, next to the model, a small text file model.tok.layout with the positions of the shapes and the routes of the edges of the original diagram. When you later run tok bpmn or tok svg on the model, the tools draw it as it was drawn, and place only the elements you have added since. The model stays pure text; the drawing travels beside it. Chapter 8 explains the layout file and the details of import, including DMN files. Import makes tok useful for models that already exist. An organisation with a library of BPMN diagrams can convert them to text, keep them under version control, check them all with one command, and still open them in its usual editor, because the BPMN files are only a command away. Exercises Exercise 1.1 Two layers. Run tok bpmn on 01-interlibrary-loan.tok (or download its BPMN export above) and open the .bpmn file in a text editor. Find the element that describes the exclusive gateway available, then the shape that places it in the diagram. Which attributes of the shape would change if you moved the gateway in Camunda Modeler? Which element of the semantic layer would change if you renamed it? Reading a model. Without looking at the diagram, answer from the text: how many end events does the interlibrary loan have, and in which lane is each? Which task does the reader perform? How many sequence flows does the model contain? Then check your answers against the diagram. A small change. Add the user task “Notify the reader” between “Order from another library” and the end event “Order placed”, as in the section on version control. Run tok check, then tok svg, and compare the new picture with the old one. If you keep the model in Git, look at git diff before you commit. Views. For each of these needs, name the command that produces the right view of a model: (a) a picture for an annual report; (b) a file a colleague can open in Camunda Modeler; (c) the files to deploy to Camunda 8; (d) the average time a case spends waiting; (e) the answer a decision table gives for a given input. Other notations. Write the interlibrary loan as a Mermaid flowchart or a PlantUML activity diagram (from their documentation). List three things the tok model expresses that your diagram does not, and say for each who would need it: a reader of the diagram, a BPMN tool, or a process engine. Round trip. Draw a small process with three tasks and one exclusive gateway in Camunda Modeler or on bpmn.io and save it as a .bpmn file. Import it with tok import diagram.bpmn -o diagram.tok. Compare the text with your drawing: which identifiers did the editor generate, and what did the import report, if anything? Then run tok svg diagram.tok and check that the picture keeps your drawing.

Chapter 2 Getting started In this chapter you will install the tok command on Windows, macOS or Linux · learn the other ways to reach the engine: R, Julia, VS Code, the browser playground and the bundle for AI agents · write your first model and take it through tok check, tok fmt, tok bpmn and tok svg · open the result in Camunda Modeler or bpmn.io · set up your editor for tok files 2.1 Ways to use tok All the tools of tok run the same engine, so you may start with whichever suits you and add others later. A model written in the browser gives the same diagnostics and the same BPMN file as the same model checked on the command line or in R. Way What you get Install Python package tok-lang the tok command, the Python module tok.api, the MCP server (tok mcp) pip install tok-lang Rust crate tok-cli the tok command alone cargo install tok-cli R package tokr functions for R, diagrams in the viewer, a knitr engine for R Markdown and Quarto install.packages("tokr") Julia package Tok the engine in Julia, a native simulator, calibration on event logs Pkg.add(["Tok", "tok_jll"]) VS Code extension tok highlighting, live diagnostics, formatting, a diagram beside the editor, export from the Visual Studio Marketplace or Open VSX Playground the engine in a web page: editor, diagnostics, diagram, simulation, downloads nothing: https://tok-lang-bpm.github.io/playground/ Agent bundle the skills that teach an agent to model in tok and in BPMN XML, with the MCP server see Chapter 14 For this book you need the tok command. The rest of this section shows how to install it; the other ways are described afterwards. 2.2 Installing the command line 2.2.1 With Python The simplest way to get tok on any common system is the Python package tok-lang. It needs Python 3.8 or newer. The packages on PyPI (called wheels) contain the compiled Rust engine for Windows x64, Linux x86_64 and aarch64, and macOS on Intel and Apple silicon, so installing them needs nothing else. On Windows, open PowerShell or the Command Prompt and run: py -m pip install tok-lang On macOS and Linux, open a terminal and run: python3 -m pip install tok-lang If pip is on your path, pip install tok-lang does the same on every system. To upgrade later, add --upgrade. If you prefer to keep command-line tools apart from your Python projects, pipx install tok-lang installs the command in an environment of its own. Then check that the command works: tok --version tok 1.0.3 If the system answers that it does not know the command tok, the folder where pip puts commands is not on your path. You can always run the same program through Python instead: py -m tok --version on Windows, python3 -m tok --version elsewhere. Every command in this book works in that form. On a platform without a ready wheel, pip builds the engine from the source archive. That needs the Rust toolchain, version 1.99 or newer, from https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install. The build takes a few minutes; the result is the same program. The Python package also carries the MCP server, the program through which AI agents call the engine: tok mcp starts it. You do not need it now; Chapter 14 explains when and how to use it. 2.2.2 With Cargo If you work with Rust, or want the command without Python, install it from crates.io: cargo install tok-cli This compiles the program tok (Rust 1.99 or newer) and puts it in Cargo’s folder of commands, which the Rust installer adds to your path. The language server and the MCP server are separate programs from the same source: cargo install tok-lsp tok-mcp. Chapters 12 and 14 describe them. 2.2.3 Checking the installation Three commands confirm that everything is in place: tok --version # prints the version: tok 1.0.3 tok --help # lists the commands tok cheatsheet # prints the whole language on one page Every command has its own help: tok check --help, tok bpmn --help and so on. The command reference in the appendix lists all of them with their options. 2.3 Other ways to reach the engine 2.3.1 R The R package tokr gives the engine to R: diagnostics as data frames, diagrams in the RStudio viewer, simulation results as tables, and a knitr engine that draws tok models in R Markdown and Quarto documents. Install it from CRAN: install.packages("tokr") or from R-universe, where new releases appear first: install.packages("tokr", repos = c("https://tok-lang-bpm.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org")) When R installs a binary package for your system, nothing else is needed. When it builds the package from source, as on Linux, it compiles the engine, which requires Rust 1.99 or newer and, on Windows, Rtools for your version of R. A first test: library(tokr) tok_version() tok_check("model.tok") 2.3.2 Julia The Julia package Tok (Julia 1.10 or newer) gives the whole engine to Julia and adds a native simulator for large experiments and the calibration of simulation parameters on event logs: using Pkg Pkg.add(["Tok", "tok_jll"]) # tok_jll is the engine library, built for every platform using Tok Tok.Engine.available() # true when the engine library was found Tok.Engine.check(read("model.tok", String)) # the diagnostics Chapter 13 describes the Python, R, Julia and C interfaces in detail, including where the Julia package looks for the engine library. 2.3.3 Visual Studio Code The extension tok for Visual Studio Code, published by tok-lang-bpm, turns the editor into a modelling environment. Open the Extensions view, search for tok, and install the extension from that publisher. It is published both on the Visual Studio Marketplace and on Open VSX, the registry used by VSCodium and other editors built on the same code. The packages for Windows, Linux and macOS carry the language server, so no other installation is needed. With the extension, the editor colours keywords, identifiers, labels and attributes; shows the diagnostics of tok check as you type; formats the document to the canonical form; jumps from an identifier to its declaration; and opens the diagram beside the text (tok: Show diagram), redrawing it as you edit. tok: Export BPMN writes the BPMN file next to the model. Chapter 12 covers the extension and other editors. 2.3.4 The playground The playground at https://tok-lang-bpm.github.io/playground/ is the engine compiled to WebAssembly and running in your browser. You type a model on the left; the diagnostics, the diagram, the BPMN file in the bpmn-js viewer, the simulation and the decisions appear in tabs. Every file tok export would write can be downloaded. Nothing is sent to a server: the page computes everything locally. The playground is the quickest way to try tok, to show a model to someone who has nothing installed, or to share a model as a link (Copy link puts the whole text into the address). 2.3.5 The agent bundle If you work with an AI agent, the bundle at https://github.com/tok-lang-bpm/tok-agent contains the skill that teaches an agent the workflow of modelling in tok, together with the configuration of the MCP server. Chapter 14 explains how to give it to an agent and how to check the agent’s work. 2.4 Your first model This section takes you through the whole cycle of work with tok on one small model: write, check, format, export, look at the result. The process is a request to see records in the reading room of an archive. A reader submits a request; the archivist checks the reference code; if the records are available, they are issued at the desk, otherwise the reader is informed. 2.4.1 Step 1: write the text Create a folder for your models, open your editor, and save a new file as reading-room.tok. Type the model below. You do not need to copy the spacing exactly; the next steps will tidy it up. # Access to records in an archive reading room tok 1.0 "Reading room request" start submitted "Request submitted" # the archivist checks the reference code first user check "Check the reference code" xor available "Are the records available?" manual issue "Issue the records" # at the reading room desk user inform "Inform the reader" end issued "Records issued" end informed "Reader informed" flow submitted -> check flow check -> available flow available -> issue "yes" flow available -> inform "no" flow issue -> issued flow inform -> informed Look at what each line does. The first line is a comment: everything after # is a note for people, which the tools ignore. The second line is the header, which every document must start with: tok, the version of the language (1.0) and the title of the model. Then come the elements, one per line: a start event, a user task (the archivist works in the archive’s system), an exclusive gateway with a question, a manual task (handing over records needs no system), another user task and two end events. The flow lines connect them by their identifiers; a label after the arrow names a branch of the gateway. 2.4.2 Step 2: check the model In a terminal, go to the folder of the model and run: tok check reading-room.tok reading-room.tok: 0 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) No errors, no warnings, no notes: the model is valid BPMN. When the model has problems, tok check lists them, one per line, before the summary. Here is what it prints for a version of the model with two mistakes, a duplicated identifier and a misspelled one (the file 02-reading-room-error.tok among the examples): tok check 02-reading-room-error.tok 02-reading-room-error.tok:9: error R001: identifier 'issued' is already used on line 8 02-reading-room-error.tok: 1 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) Each diagnostic has the same parts: the file, the line number, the severity, a code and a message. The line number tells you where to look. The severity is one of three: Severity Meaning Effect error the document is not a valid model the exports refuse to run until it is fixed warning the model is valid but probably not what you meant the exports run; read the warning and decide note a matter of style, such as a gateway whose label is not a question the exports run The code is stable across versions and languages, so you can look it up in the diagnostics appendix. R001 belongs to the group of reference errors: two elements declared with the same identifier. Notice that only one error is reported, although the file has two mistakes. The checker works in stages: first the lines and statements, then the identifiers and references, then the rules of BPMN. A later stage runs only when the earlier ones found no errors, because an error in the structure would make its results misleading. After you rename the second end event to informed, the next stage reports the misspelled identifier in a flow: 02-reading-room-error.tok:14: error R002: unknown flow node 'isued' Fix the errors from the top, run tok check again, and repeat until the summary shows zero errors. tok check --lang pl prints the messages in Polish; the codes stay the same. For programs and scripts, tok check --json prints the diagnostics as JSON. Every command ends with exit code 0 on success, 1 when the document has errors and 2 when the command line itself is wrong, so tok check can stop a build or a continuous-integration job. 2.4.3 Step 3: format the text The text you typed works, but its spacing is irregular and the flows take six lines. Run: tok fmt reading-room.tok The command prints the canonical form of the model. When you are happy with it, write it back into the file: tok fmt reading-room.tok -w The file now reads: # Access to records in an archive reading room tok 1.0 "Reading room request" start submitted "Request submitted" # the archivist checks the reference code first user check "Check the reference code" xor available "Are the records available?" manual issue "Issue the records" # at the reading room desk user inform "Inform the reader" end issued "Records issued" end informed "Reader informed" flow submitted -> check -> available flow available -> issue "yes" flow available -> inform "no" flow issue -> issued flow inform -> informed tok fmt changed the spacing, added a blank line between the elements and the flows, joined the first two flows into a chain (submitted -> check -> available, because they form one path without labels), and kept both comments: the comment above a statement stays above it, the comment at the end of a line stays at the end of that line. It never changes what the model means. tok fmt --check only reports whether a file is already in canonical form, which is useful in scripts. Formatting is optional, but it is a good habit. When every model in a repository is in canonical form, the difference between two versions shows only real changes. 2.4.4 Step 4: export BPMN Now produce the BPMN file: tok bpmn reading-room.tok BPMN: reading-room.bpmn The file reading-room.bpmn is BPMN 2.0 XML with the diagram layout computed by tok. By default it gets the name of the model with the extension .bpmn; -o chooses another file name (tok bpmn reading-room.tok -o request.bpmn), in an existing folder. 2.4.5 Step 5: draw the picture tok svg reading-room.tok SVG: reading-room.svg The SVG picture opens in any web browser and can be inserted in documents and web pages. It is the same drawing as in the BPMN file: Figure 2.1: The reading room request, drawn by tok svg. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) 2.4.6 Step 6: open the model in a BPMN tool The BPMN file is the bridge to every other BPMN tool. Two are worth trying at once: Camunda Modeler, the desktop editor from https://camunda.com/download/modeler/: choose File › Open File… and select reading-room.bpmn. The diagram appears as tok laid it out. Click an element and the properties panel shows its type and name; the identifiers are those of your text. bpmn.io, the web modeller at https://demo.bpmn.io/: drag the file from your folder onto the page. Both tools let you move shapes and edit the model. Remember the principle of Chapter 1: the text is the model. If you change the process in a graphical editor, bring the change back with tok import (Chapter 8); otherwise the next tok bpmn overwrites the file with the text’s version. 2.4.7 Step 7: change and repeat Real work is a loop: change the text, check, format, export. Try it once now. Add a user task “Register the visit” between “Issue the records” and the end event “Records issued”: one new line among the elements, and the flow issue -> issued replaced by issue -> register -> issued. Choose an identifier that is not taken yet, run tok check, tok fmt -w, tok svg, and look at the new picture. The layout makes room for the new task by itself. tok export reading-room.tok -o out/ writes the BPMN file and the picture in one step, into the folder out (created when needed), together with any decision and form files the model has. For a descriptive model like this one, tok bpmn and tok svg are all you need. 2.5 Setting up your editor A tok model is plain text, so any text editor will do. A few settings make the work smoother. Encoding. Save files as UTF-8, which is the default of every modern editor. Labels may then contain any characters: accents, other alphabets, typographic quotes. A byte order mark at the start of the file is accepted and ignored. Identifiers are restricted to ASCII on purpose, as the next chapter explains; the restriction does not apply to labels and comments. Indentation with spaces. Blocks (lanes in pools, elements in lanes) are made by indentation, and the indentation must be spaces. A tab character in the indentation is an error: model.tok:4: error T002: tab character in indentation; use spaces Set your editor to insert spaces when you press the Tab key. In VS Code, the status bar at the bottom right shows Spaces: 2 when this is so; click it to change. Two spaces per level is the canonical form, and tok fmt will convert any consistent indentation to it. Line endings. Windows, macOS and Linux line endings are all accepted; tok fmt -w writes the file with Unix line endings. Line numbers. Keep them visible. Every diagnostic names a line, and every review comment will too. File extension. Save models with the extension .tok. The VS Code extension recognises it, and so do the language server and the other tools. In VS Code with the tok extension, the settings "editor.insertSpaces": true and "editor.tabSize": 2 for tok files match the canonical form, and Format Document (or format on save) runs the same formatter as tok fmt. Other editors (Neovim, Helix, Emacs and others that speak the Language Server Protocol) get the same help from the language server tok-lsp, as Chapter 12 shows. Exercises Exercise 2.1 Install. Install tok in one of the ways of this chapter and run tok --version. If the command is not found, run it through Python (py -m tok --version or python3 -m tok --version) and find out which folder you would add to your path. First model. Type the reading room request from Step 1 into reading-room.tok, then run tok check, tok fmt -w, tok bpmn and tok svg. Compare the formatted file with the one printed in Step 3: are they identical? Fix a model. Download 02-reading-room-error.tok from the examples. Run tok check, fix the first error, run tok check again, and continue until no errors remain. Write down every code you saw and what it meant. Download the model with errors (.tok) Into a BPMN tool. Open your reading-room.bpmn in Camunda Modeler or on demo.bpmn.io. Click the gateway and the manual task and note the type the properties panel shows. Then rename a task in the graphical tool, save the file, and run tok import reading-room.bpmn: where does your change appear in the text? Playground. Paste your model into the playground. Introduce a tab character before one line, and then an unknown keyword (taks instead of task). Watch the diagnostics change as you type, and use Copy link to share the broken model with a colleague. Editor. Configure your editor to insert two spaces for the Tab key and to save in UTF-8. If you use VS Code, install the tok extension, open your model, and open the diagram beside it with tok: Show diagram. Change a label and watch the diagram follow.
