Chapter 3 Process basics 3.1 The header line 3.2 Statements 3.3 Identifiers and labels 3.4 Tasks 3.5 Events 3.6 Gateways 3.7 Sequence flows 3.8 Indentation and blocks 3.9 Comments 3.10 Levels of the language 3.11 Typical mistakes Exercises

Chapter 3 Process basics In this chapter you will learn the header line and the structure of a statement · tell identifiers from labels and write both correctly · choose among the nine kinds of task · use start, intermediate and end events · split and join paths with exclusive, parallel, inclusive and event-based gateways · write sequence flows, chains, labels, conditions and default flows · use indentation and comments · restrict a model to a level of the language with --level 3.1 The header line Every tok document begins with a header. It is the first statement of the file; only comments and blank lines may stand above it. tok 1.0 "Digital copy request" The header has three parts. The keyword tok says that this is a tok document. The number 1.0 is the version of the language the document is written in; it is required and has a minor part (1.0, not 1). The label "Digital copy request" is the title of the model: it becomes the name of the definitions element of the BPMN file and, in a document without pools, the name of the process. The tools accept the versions 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7 and 1.0. A document written for an earlier version means exactly the same under the current tools, so models from earlier years need no change. Write tok 1.0 for new models: it gives you every construct of the language. A version number the tools do not know is a warning (P006), and the document is then read as language 1.0; a header whose version is not a number at all is the error P005, and a second header further down the file is the error P010. The header may also carry attributes. You will meet them in later chapters: Attribute Meaning Chapter doc="Text" documentation of the model, exported to the BPMN file this chapter process=ID the identifier of the process of a document without pools (default process) this chapter process-name="Name" the name of that process, when it should differ from the title this chapter executable, target=camunda, version-tag="v1" the model is meant for a process engine 10 A document without pools, like all the examples of this chapter, describes one process. Its elements stand at the top level of the file, without indentation, and the BPMN export puts them into a single process element. Documents with pools and lanes describe collaborations between participants; they are the subject of Chapter 4. 3.2 Statements After the header comes a sequence of statements, one per line. A statement cannot continue on the next line, and two statements cannot share a line. Every statement starts with a lowercase keyword; keywords are case-sensitive, so Start or USER is not a keyword. The statements that declare flow nodes (events, tasks and gateways) all have the same shape: KIND IDENTIFIER "Label" attributes tok 1.0 "Statement parts" start received "Request received" message="Copy request" send deliver "Send the copy" message="Digital copy" end sent "Copy sent" flow received -> deliver -> sent In send deliver "Send the copy" message="Digital copy", send is the kind (a send task), deliver is the identifier, "Send the copy" is the label, and message="Digital copy" is an attribute that names the message the task sends. Attributes come in two forms. A key=value pair has a value that is a word (P14D), a number (3, 0.25) or a quoted string ("Digital copy"). A flag is a bare word that switches something on, such as parallel on a task or default on a flow. Attributes may be written in any order; tok fmt prints them in a fixed order, so they always appear the same way. The checker treats mistakes in attributes differently. An unknown keyword is an error, because the tools cannot know what the line means. An unknown key of an attribute is only a warning, because the rest of the line still makes sense. An unknown flag is an error: model.tok:4: warning R010: unknown attribute 'colour' on user model.tok:5: error R011: unknown flag 'urgent' on user model.tok:6: error P001: unknown keyword 'taks' Each key is written once per line. In language 1.0, giving the same key or flag twice on one line is a deprecation warning (R090): only the last value ever counted, and tok fmt keeps only that one. (Events with several triggers, described in Chapter 5, are the exception.) One attribute is allowed on almost every statement: doc="Text" gives the element its documentation, which the BPMN export writes as the documentation of the element and which BPMN tools show in their properties panel. Use \n inside the text for a line break. tok 1.0 "Documented task" start s "Request received" user check "Check the copyright status" doc="Works by authors who died less than 70 years ago need the rights holder's consent." end e "Request checked" flow s -> check -> e 3.3 Identifiers and labels Every element has an identifier, written right after its keyword. The identifier is how the rest of the document refers to the element: flows connect identifiers, boundary events name the activity they are attached to by its identifier, and so on. It also becomes the id attribute of the element in the BPMN XML, and the name under which a process engine reports the element. An identifier must satisfy three conditions: Condition Correct Wrong starts with a letter or _ scan2, _draft 2scan contains only ASCII letters, digits, _ and - register, check-rights, fee_total prüfen, check rights, fee.total is unique in the whole document end-ok, end-rejected end twice Identifiers are ASCII because they end up in XML identifiers, file names, logs and the code of programs that work with the process; many of these systems handle only plain Latin letters reliably. The checker enforces both rules: model.tok:4: error R004: identifier 'prüfen' must use only ASCII letters, digits, '_' and '-' model.tok:5: error R001: identifier 's' is already used on line 3 The label is the name for people. It is written in double quotes after the identifier and appears in the diagram. A label can be in any language and contain any character. Inside a label, \" stands for a double quote, \\ for a backslash and \n for a line break in the diagram. A label is optional: a joining gateway, for example, usually needs no name on the diagram, so and results is a complete statement. Good identifiers are short but readable: register, fee, sent. They should describe the element, so that a flow line such as flow fee -> deliver -> sent reads like a sentence. Avoid numbering (t1, t2, t3): it makes the flows unreadable and breaks down as soon as a step is inserted. Labels follow the conventions of BPMN: a task is named with a verb and an object (“Scan the item”), an event with a state that has been reached (“Copy sent”), a splitting gateway with a question (“Is the query complete?”). 3.4 Tasks A task is a unit of work that the process model does not break down further. BPMN distinguishes kinds of task by who or what does the work, and tok has a keyword for each: Keyword BPMN element Use it when task task the kind of work is not known or does not matter user user task a person does the work with the help of an information system: a form, a records system, a library catalogue manual manual task a person does the work without a system: a conversation, carrying files, a phone call service service task a system does the work by itself, without a person script script task a calculation by a fixed formula, executed by the process engine rule business rule task the result follows from a set of rules, typically a decision table (Chapter 9) send send task the work is sending a message to someone outside the process receive receive task the work is waiting for a message from outside call call activity the work is another process, described on its own The words of a description usually point to the right kind. “Enters into the system”, “checks in the catalogue” or “fills in the form” mean a user task. “Carries”, “hands over”, “phones” mean a manual task. “Automatically”, “the system assigns” mean a service task. “Sends” and “receives” in contact with another organisation mean send and receive tasks. The following model of a request for a digital copy uses seven kinds of task: # Digital copy request in a library tok 1.0 "Digital copy request" start received "Request received" message="Copy request" service register "Register the request" user review "Check the copyright status" manual fetch "Fetch the original from the stacks" user scan "Scan the item" script fee "Calculate the fee" send deliver "Send the copy" message="Digital copy" end sent "Copy sent" flow received -> register -> review -> fetch -> scan -> fee -> deliver -> sent Figure 3.1: A digital copy request: a sequence of tasks of different kinds. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) The library system registers the request without human help (service). A librarian checks the copyright status in the catalogue (user) and fetches the original from the stacks by hand (manual). The scan is made at a scanning station that records the job (user). The fee is calculated by a fixed tariff (script), and the copy is sent to the reader (send). The diagram shows each kind with its marker in the top left corner of the task. send and receive tasks name their message with message="Name". Messages are declared by their names: every element that names the same message refers to one message in the BPMN file. A call activity names the process it calls with process=ID; the called process is usually modelled in a file of its own. 3.4.1 Markers of repetition Three flags mark a task that is performed more than once. They apply to every kind of task: Flag BPMN Meaning loop standard loop the task repeats until a condition is met parallel parallel multi-instance several instances run at the same time, for example one per reviewer sequential sequential multi-instance several instances run one after another tok 1.0 "Task markers" start s "Manuscript accepted" user review "Review the manuscript" parallel user proofs "Correct the proofs" loop manual sheets "Check each printed sheet" sequential call print "Print the book" process=printing end e "Book printed" flow s -> review -> proofs -> sheets -> print -> e The diagram shows a loop as a circular arrow and multi-instance as three bars, vertical for parallel and horizontal for sequential. The condition of a loop and the collection a multi-instance task works through are details for the executable layer and for the more precise models of later chapters; the flag alone already makes the diagram say what it should. The flag compensation, which marks a task that undoes the effect of another, belongs with the exceptions of Chapter 5. The attributes that make tasks executable, such as forms of user tasks or job types of service tasks, are the subject of Chapter 10. 3.5 Events An event is something that happens: a request arrives, a deadline passes, a state is reached. BPMN distinguishes events by their position in the process: Keyword BPMN element Position start start event where the process begins; no incoming flow end end event where a path of the process ends; no outgoing flow throw intermediate throw event on a path, signalling that something has happened catch intermediate catch event on a path, waiting for something to happen boundary boundary event attached to an activity, interrupting or accompanying it An event without attributes has no trigger: it is a plain (none) event. A plain start event simply marks where the process begins, a plain end event where a path ends, and a plain intermediate throw event marks a milestone, a state the process has reached that is worth showing on the diagram. Most of the events in the examples of this chapter are plain events. A trigger says what causes or is caused by the event, and is given as an attribute. Two triggers are useful from the start: message="Name" on a start event: the process starts when a message arrives (a request, an application, a letter). timer=... on a start event: the process starts at a given time or regularly. The time of a timer follows ISO 8601, the same notation BPMN tools and Camunda use: Value Meaning P3D a duration of 3 days PT2H 2 hours (T separates the days from the hours) PT30M 30 minutes P1DT12H a day and a half 2027-01-15T09:00 a date and time R/2027-01-04T08:00/P1M a cycle: from 4 January 2027, 8:00, every month R3/PT1H a cycle: three times, every hour On end events, the flag terminate makes a terminate end event: when the process reaches it, the whole process instance ends at once, even if other paths are still active. The monthly report of a library’s acquisitions department shows these events together: tok 1.0 "Monthly acquisitions report" start month "First working day of the month" timer=R/2027-01-04T08:00/P1M service figures "Collect the acquisition figures" user draft "Write the report" throw drafted "Report drafted" user approve "Approve the report" xor approved "Is the report approved?" service publish "Publish the report on the intranet" end published "Report published" end withdrawn "Report withdrawn" terminate flow month -> figures -> draft -> drafted -> approve -> approved flow approved -> publish "yes" default flow approved -> withdrawn "no" when="approved = false" flow publish -> published Figure 3.2: A process started by a timer, with a milestone and a terminate end event. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) The process starts on the first working day of every month (timer=). The plain intermediate throw event “Report drafted” marks a milestone between writing and approval. If the report is not approved, the terminate end event “Report withdrawn” ends the process instance. Intermediate catch events always need a trigger, because they wait for something; a catch line without one is the error E010. The full set of triggers (messages, timers, signals, errors, escalations, conditions, links, compensation and cancellation), boundary events and event sub-processes are the subject of Chapter 5. 3.6 Gateways A gateway splits the flow of a process into several paths or joins several paths into one. tok has a keyword for each kind of gateway in BPMN: Keyword BPMN element As a split As a join xor exclusive gateway exactly one path is taken lets through every token that arrives and parallel gateway all paths are taken at once waits for all paths or inclusive gateway one or more paths, by their conditions; the default path if no condition holds waits for the paths that were actually taken eventgw event-based gateway the path of the event that happens first (not used as a join) complex complex gateway paths by conditions, like or fires when its activation condition holds Two naming conventions from BPMN apply. A splitting gateway is labelled with a question: xor complete "Is the query complete?". A joining gateway usually has no label: and results. A splitting gateway whose label is not a question gets a style note (L020) from the checker. Every split of an and or or gateway should be joined by a gateway of the same kind. An and split joined by an xor gateway lets every parallel path continue on its own, so everything after the join runs several times, which is rarely what you want; the checker warns about it (W051). 3.6.1 Exclusive, parallel and inclusive gateways The following model of a query to an archive uses three kinds of gateway. The exclusive gateway checks whether the query is complete; the “no” branch asks for the missing details and returns to the assessment, which forms a loop. The parallel gateway starts two searches at once. The inclusive gateway chooses how to send the answer: by e-mail, by post or both, and if neither applies, the answer is handed over in person. tok 1.0 "Archive query" start arrived "Query received" user assess "Assess the query" xor complete "Is the query complete?" user ask "Ask for missing details" and search user finding-aids "Search the finding aids" user register "Search the query register" and results user answer "Draft the answer" or channel "How should the answer be sent?" send email "Send the answer by e-mail" message="Answer" send post "Send the answer by post" message="Answer" manual desk "Hand the answer over at the desk" or delivered end closed "Query closed" flow arrived -> assess -> complete flow complete -> search "yes" when="complete = true" flow complete -> ask "no" default flow ask -> assess flow search -> finding-aids -> results flow search -> register -> results -> answer -> channel flow channel -> email "e-mail" when="email != null" flow channel -> post "post" when="address != null and paper = true" flow channel -> desk "in person" default flow email -> delivered flow post -> delivered flow desk -> delivered -> closed Figure 3.3: An archive query: exclusive gateway with a loop, parallel split and join, inclusive split and join with a default flow. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) Notice three details. A loop needs no extra gateway. The flow ask -> assess returns to a task that already has an incoming flow. A task with two incoming flows behaves like an exclusive join. If you prefer to show the join explicitly, put an xor gateway before the assessment and direct both flows into it; the meaning is the same. Splits and joins match. The paths from and search meet in and results, those from or channel in or delivered. A chain is not an order of work. The canonical form writes search -> register -> results -> answer -> channel as one chain, but that does not mean the register is searched after the finding aids. The flows describe connections only; that both searches run at once follows from the parallel gateway. 3.6.2 The event-based gateway An event-based gateway checks no conditions. The process stops at the gateway and waits; whichever of the following events happens first decides the path. The elements directly after the gateway must therefore be intermediate catch events (with a message, timer, signal or conditional trigger) or receive tasks. tok 1.0 "Waiting for missing details" start asked "Request for details sent" eventgw wait "What happens first?" catch details "Details received" message="Missing details" catch deadline "14 days passed" timer=P14D user reassess "Reassess the query" user shelve "Close the query without action" end reassessed "Query reassessed" end shelved "Query closed without action" flow asked -> wait flow wait -> details flow wait -> deadline flow details -> reassess -> reassessed flow deadline -> shelve -> shelved Figure 3.4: Waiting for missing details: a message or a deadline, whichever comes first. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) The flows leaving an event-based gateway have no labels or conditions: the labels of the events (“Details received”, “14 days passed”) carry the answer. If anything other than a catch event or a receive task follows the gateway, the checker reports the error E016. 3.6.3 The complex gateway The complex gateway covers the cases the other gateways cannot express. Its typical use is a join that continues as soon as enough paths have arrived: for example, when a decision can be taken after two of three reviews. The condition is given with activation=, in which _activationCount is the number of paths that have arrived: tok 1.0 "Two of three reviews" start s "Manuscript sent out" and invite user r1 "First review" user r2 "Second review" user r3 "Third review" complex enough "Two reviews in?" activation="_activationCount >= 2" user decide "Decide on the manuscript" end e "Decision made" flow s -> invite flow invite -> r1 -> enough flow invite -> r2 -> enough flow invite -> r3 -> enough -> decide -> e The complex gateway is part of BPMN 2.0.2 and of the analyses and simulations of tok, but Camunda 8 does not execute it; Chapter 10 lists what that means for executable models. 3.7 Sequence flows Sequence flows connect the flow nodes of a process and give the order in which the work is done. In tok they are written with the keyword flow and arrows between identifiers: tok 1.0 "Flows" start received "Request received" user register "Register the request" user review "Check the copyright status" end done "Request checked" flow received -> register flow register -> review -> done A line with two arrows or more is a chain: flow register -> review -> done creates two sequence flows, one from register to review and one from review to done. Chains make linear parts of a model short and readable. Each sequence flow gets an identifier derived from its ends: f-register-review, f-review-done. When two flows connect the same pair of nodes, the second one gets -2, the third -3. You will see these identifiers in some diagnostics and in the BPMN file. To choose an identifier yourself, write id= on the flow. Flow lines may stand anywhere in the document, and a flow may name a node that is declared further down. By convention they come after the elements, and the canonical form prints them there. 3.7.1 Labels and attributes A flow can have a label, written in quotes after the target, and attributes. Because a label or an attribute must describe one particular flow, a line with a label or attributes contains exactly one arrow. The line flow g -> a -> e "yes" is ambiguous (which of the two flows says “yes”?) and is rejected: model.tok:10: error R020: a flow line with a label or attributes must contain exactly one arrow Write it as two lines instead: flow g -> a "yes" and flow a -> e. Attribute Meaning "Label" the name of the flow, shown next to it; for the branches of a gateway, the answer to its question when="FEEL" the condition of the flow, evaluated on the data of the case default the default flow, taken when no condition of the other flows holds id=ID an explicit identifier doc="Text" documentation p=0.3 the probability of the branch in a simulation (Chapter 11) 3.7.2 Conditions A label such as “yes” is enough for a person reading the diagram. A process engine, a simulation or a careful reviewer needs a condition that can be evaluated on the data of the case. Conditions are written with when= in FEEL, the Friendly Enough Expression Language defined by DMN, which is also the expression language of Camunda 8. Here are four branches of a gateway that sorts readers into categories: tok 1.0 "Reader categories" start s "Registration requested" xor kind "Which reader category?" user student "Register a student" user senior "Register a senior reader" user staff "Register a staff member" user other "Register an external reader" xor merged end e "Reader registered" flow s -> kind flow kind -> student "student" when="type = \"student\" and age >= 18" flow kind -> senior "senior" when="age between 65 and 120" flow kind -> staff "staff" when="employee = true or email != null" flow kind -> other "other" default flow student -> merged flow senior -> merged flow staff -> merged flow other -> merged -> e The basic forms of FEEL cover most conditions: Expression Meaning age >= 18, price < 150, days != 0 comparisons: =, !=, <, <=, >, >=; a single = compares, it does not assign complete = true, urgent a boolean value; urgent alone means “urgent is true” type = "student" text in double quotes a and b, a or b, not(a) combining conditions email != null the value exists age between 18 and 26 a range, both ends included Mind the quotes. The whole condition is already the quoted value of when=, so a text inside it is written with escaped quotes: when="type = \"student\"" is the condition type = "student". Conditions are written without the leading = that Camunda Modeler shows in executable models. The exporter adds it where Camunda expects it. tok check checks the syntax of every condition. A mistake is the error F002, with an explanation: model.tok:9: error F002: FEEL syntax error: expected ')', found end of expression Documents of language 1.0 use the full FEEL of DMN 1.5 (conformance level 3): dates and durations, lists, contexts, functions and more. Chapter 9 introduces the rest of the language. While a model is still descriptive, labels alone are fine. Add conditions when the model is to be simulated or executed, or when the labels leave room for doubt. A condition you have not worked out yet can be written as when="": the BPMN file then has a condition without an expression, as BPMN tools draw it. 3.7.3 Default flows One outgoing flow of an xor, or or complex gateway may be marked as the default flow with the flag default. It is taken when none of the conditions of the other flows holds. The diagram shows it with a short slash at its start. A default flow has no condition; the checker rejects a flow that is both (E015), and a default flow or a condition on a flow leaving a parallel gateway (E017), because a parallel gateway takes every path anyway. An inclusive gateway without a default flow gets the warning W050: if no condition holds, the process would be stuck. Each branch of an exclusive or inclusive split should have a label, a condition or the default status; a branch without any of them gets the warning W021. Conditional flows can also leave a task directly, without a gateway. In that case default marks the flow taken when no condition holds: tok 1.0 "Conditional flows from a task" start s "Order received" user check "Check the order" user urgent "Handle as urgent" user normal "Handle as normal" end e1 "Urgent order handled" end e2 "Order handled" flow s -> check flow check -> urgent "urgent" when="total > 1000" flow check -> normal default flow urgent -> e1 flow normal -> e2 Most modellers prefer an explicit gateway, which makes the decision visible; both forms are valid BPMN. 3.8 Indentation and blocks Indentation in tok has a meaning: a line indented deeper than the statement above it belongs to the block of that statement. A block ends at the first line that is indented as much as its parent statement or less. Only some statements have blocks: pools and lanes, which hold flow nodes (Chapter 4); sub-processes, which hold a process of their own; choreographies; decisions, which hold tables or boxed expressions (Chapter 9); forms, which hold fields (Chapter 10). In a document without pools and sub-processes, like those of this chapter, every statement starts at the beginning of its line. Three rules keep indentation unambiguous: Indentation is made of spaces. A tab character in the indentation is the error T002. A line indented under a statement without a block is an error. Indenting a task under another task gives P003 (the statement cannot have an indented block). When a block ends, the next line returns to an earlier level. A line indented to a depth that matches no open block is T003. The canonical form uses two spaces per level. You may indent with any consistent number of spaces; tok fmt converts it. 3.9 Comments A comment starts with # and runs to the end of the line. It is a note for people, and the tools ignore it when they build the model. A comment can take a whole line or stand at the end of a statement: # Digital copy request, as agreed with the reading room on 12 March tok 1.0 "Digital copy request" start received "Request received" # the fee follows the tariff of the current year script fee "Calculate the fee" send deliver "Send the copy" message="Digital copy" # by e-mail or download link end sent "Copy sent" flow received -> fee -> deliver -> sent A # inside a quoted label or attribute value is ordinary text, not a comment. tok fmt keeps every comment. A comment line belongs to the statement that follows it and is printed above it, even if the formatter moves the statement; a comment at the end of a line stays at the end of that statement’s line; comments at the end of the file are printed last. Comments are therefore a safe place for the source of a requirement, the person to ask about a step, or a reminder of a decision taken in a meeting. 3.10 Levels of the language tok covers the whole of BPMN 2.0.2 and much of DMN 1.5. A beginner, or the reader of a high-level model, needs much less. The option --level of tok check restricts the language to one of three levels, and reports everything beyond it: Level Accepts basic plain start and end events; the tasks task, user, service and manual; the gateways xor and and; pools, lanes and message flows; data and notes; no attributes of the executable layer analytic all of BPMN except the executable layer, forms and decisions, and without the advanced elements added in languages 0.5 and 0.6 (transactions, complex gateways, multiple events, conversations, choreographies and others) full (default) everything tok check 03-copy-request.tok --level basic 03-copy-request.tok:4: error R040: 'start' is not available at level basic 03-copy-request.tok:9: error R040: 'script' is not available at level basic 03-copy-request.tok:10: error R040: 'send' is not available at level basic 03-copy-request.tok: 3 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) The start event is allowed at the level basic, but not with a message trigger; script and send tasks belong to analytic models. The interlibrary loan of Chapter 1 and the reading room request of Chapter 2 pass at the level basic. Levels are a teaching and communication device. A course can require models at the level basic in its first weeks; a team can agree that models for management stay at the level basic or analytic, so that they remain readable to people who know only the core of BPMN. In VS Code the setting tok.level applies a level to the live diagnostics. The levels are not the conformance classes of the BPMN specification, which tok check --class checks; Chapter 7 explains the classes. 3.11 Typical mistakes The following model of preparing an exhibition contains four mistakes that are common in models with gateways. Try to find them by reading the text before you look at the diagnostics. tok 1.0 "Preparing an exhibition (with errors)" start decided "Exhibition decided" and prepare user select "Select the objects" user captions "Write the captions" xor ready xor accepted "Did the director approve?" user install "Install the exhibition" user revise "Revise the script" end opened "Exhibition opened" flow decided -> prepare flow prepare -> select "objects" when="objects = true" flow prepare -> captions flow select -> ready flow captions -> ready flow ready -> accepted flow accepted -> install "yes" flow accepted -> revise flow install -> opened tok check 03-exhibition-error.tok 03-exhibition-error.tok:7: warning W051: join of a different type than the split (e.g. AND split joined by XOR) (ready) 03-exhibition-error.tok:10: warning W042: path without an end event (element without outgoing flow) (revise) 03-exhibition-error.tok:14: error E017: condition or default flow on a parallel gateway (f-prepare-select) 03-exhibition-error.tok:20: warning W021: branch of an XOR/OR split without label, condition or default status (f-accepted-revise) 03-exhibition-error.tok: 1 error(s), 3 warning(s), 0 note(s) The identifier in parentheses at the end of each message names the element or flow concerned; note the derived identifiers of flows such as f-prepare-select. Code Problem Correction E017 a condition on a flow leaving a parallel gateway remove when=; a parallel gateway always takes every path W051 an and split joined by an xor gateway change xor ready to and ready W021 a branch of an exclusive split with neither label, condition nor default status add the label "no" and, if the other branch has a condition, default W042 a path that ends at a task add a flow from “Revise the script”, back to the approval or to an end event Warnings do not stop the exports, but they almost always point to a real mistake in the model. Treat a model as finished when it has no errors and every remaining warning has a reason you can state. Exercises Exercise 3.1 Task kinds. For each step, choose the keyword of the task and write the statement with an identifier and a label: (a) the reading room attendant brings the boxes from the stacks; (b) the repository system assigns a DOI to a deposited article; (c) an editor fills in the review form in the journal system; (d) the library sends an overdue notice to a reader; (e) the loan fee is computed from a tariff; (f) the whole cataloguing procedure, modelled in another file, is carried out. A linear process. Write a model of the registration of an incoming letter in a university registry: the letter arrives by post; a clerk registers it in the records system; the system assigns a case number by itself; the clerk scans the letter; the head of the registry assigns it to a unit in the system; the clerk carries the original to the archive; the system notifies the unit automatically; the process ends. Check the model, format it and draw it. Gateways. Extend the archive query: after the answer is drafted, the head of the department approves it; if it is not approved, it goes back to the archivist for correction. Add the gateway, the flows and conditions on both branches (approved = true and a default), and check that no warning appears. Fix the exhibition. Download 03-exhibition-error.tok and correct it until tok check reports no errors and no warnings. Compare your corrected diagram with the original. Download the model with errors (.tok) Waiting for a reply. A library asks a publisher for a licence. If the licence arrives within 30 days, the e-book is added to the catalogue; if not, the request is closed; if the publisher refuses in that time, the refusal is recorded. Model the waiting with an event-based gateway and three events, one of them a timer. Levels. Check each model of this chapter with --level basic and --level analytic. For each element rejected at the level basic, write a version of the model that stays at that level and say what information the simpler model loses.

Chapter 4 Pools, lanes and messages 4.1 From one process to a collaboration 4.2 Pools 4.3 Lanes and nested lanes 4.4 Message flows 4.5 Structural rules 4.6 Conversations 4.7 Choreographies 4.8 Participant multiplicity 4.9 Collaborations, levels and Camunda 4.10 The canonical form of a collaboration Exercises

Chapter 4 Pools, lanes and messages In this chapter you will model collaborations between participants with pools · divide a pool into lanes, nested where needed · use black-box pools for participants whose work you do not model · connect pools with message flows and name their messages · read and correct the structural errors R030, R031, R021 and R022 · describe interactions at a higher level with conversations and choreographies · give a participant a multiplicity 4.1 From one process to a collaboration The models of Chapter 3 describe one process. Their elements stand at the top level of the document, and the BPMN export puts them into a single process. Real processes rarely end at the door of one organisation. A library orders a book from another library; an archive answers a request from a citizen; a journal waits for reports from external reviewers. BPMN models such situations as a collaboration: several participants, each with its own process, which communicate only by exchanging messages. In a BPMN diagram, each participant is a pool. Inside a pool, lanes show who does what: roles, departments or systems of that participant. Between pools, message flows (dashed arrows) show the messages; sequence flows never cross the border of a pool. tok writes all of this with the same kind of one-line statements as the rest of the language. tok BPMN 2.0.2 Diagram pool with a block participant with its process a pool with content pool without a block participant without a process an empty (black-box) pool lane lane a row of a pool message A -> B "Label" messageFlow and its message a dashed arrow with a circle at its start As soon as a document contains a pool, the export writes a collaboration element with one participant per pool, and the diagram shows the pools stacked one under another. 4.2 Pools A pool is declared with the keyword pool, an identifier and a label. What the pool means depends on whether it has a block, that is, indented lines below it. tok 1.0 "Two pools" pool library "University library" start need "Book needed" send order "Send the loan request" message="Loan request" end sent "Request sent" pool lender "Lending library" flow need -> order -> sent message order -> lender "Loan request" A pool with a block is a participant whose process you model. The export writes two elements for it: the participant and its process. The identifier of the process is the identifier of the pool followed by -process (library-process); the attribute process=ID chooses another one. This matters for executable models, where a process engine shows and starts processes by their identifiers (Chapter 10). The process is named after the title of the document when the document has only one pool with a block, and after the label of its pool otherwise; process-name="Name" sets the name explicitly. A pool without a block is a black-box pool: a participant whose inner work you do not know or do not need to show. The export writes a participant without a process. In the example, the lending library is a black box; the model shows only that it receives a request. Pool attribute Meaning process=ID the identifier of the pool’s process (default: the pool identifier followed by -process) process-name="Name" the name of the pool’s process executable the pool’s process is meant for a process engine (Chapter 10) min=N, max=N the multiplicity of the participant (see Participant multiplicity) doc="Text" documentation of the participant A black-box pool must have no block at all. If you accidentally indent a line below it, the pool gets a process, and the line becomes part of it. Keep a blank line after a black-box pool, as the canonical form does, so that the absence of a block is visible. Once a document has a pool, every event, task and gateway must be inside a pool. An element left at the top level is the error R031: the tools would not know which participant does the work. 4.3 Lanes and nested lanes A lane is declared with the keyword lane inside the block of a pool. Every flow node indented under a lane belongs to that lane. Lanes may themselves contain lanes, to any depth: a faculty can be divided into its dean’s office and its dean, a department into its teams. tok 1.0 "Routing an incoming letter" pool university "University" process=letter-routing lane registry "Central registry" start received "Letter received" user register "Register the letter in the records system" lane faculty "Faculty" lane office "Dean's office" user assign "Assign the letter to a unit" user reply "Draft the reply" lane dean "Dean" user sign "Sign the reply" end replied "Reply sent" flow received -> register -> assign -> reply -> sign -> replied Figure 4.1: Routing an incoming letter: a pool with nested lanes. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) Read the indentation as a path. The task “Assign the letter to a unit” is indented six spaces: it is in the lane “Dean’s office”, which is in the lane “Faculty”, which is in the pool “University”. In the BPMN export, the task is listed in the deepest lane that contains it, and the lanes are nested in the laneSet of the process as the text nests them. The pool has the attribute process=letter-routing, so its process has that identifier instead of university-process. The flows stand at the end of the document, without indentation, although they connect tasks in different lanes. Inside one pool, steps in different lanes are connected by sequence flows, exactly as in a diagram: a lane is a role within one participant, not a separate participant. Where a flow line stands in the document does not matter; the tools find the process of each flow from its two ends. Two rules apply to lanes: If a pool has lanes, every flow node of its process must be in a lane. A node that stands directly in the pool next to the lanes is the error R030. A pool does not need lanes. A participant with one role, or one you do not want to divide, has its flow nodes directly in its block. 4.4 Message flows A message flow is written with the keyword message, the sender, an arrow, the receiver and a label: tok 1.0 "Message flows" pool library "University library" start need "Book needed" send order "Send the loan request" message="Loan request" receive parcel "Receive the parcel" message="Parcel with the book" end received "Book received" pool lender "Lending library" flow need -> order -> parcel -> received message order -> lender "Loan request" message lender -> parcel "Parcel with the book" The sender and the receiver are flow nodes or whole pools, and they must be in different pools: a message flow between two elements of the same pool is the error R022. A black-box pool has no inner elements, so a message to or from it always names the pool itself. Each message flow is a line of its own; there are no chains of message flows, because each has its own sender, receiver and message. The label names the message flow and, unless you say otherwise, the message it carries. Messages in tok are declared by their names: the send task order with message="Loan request" and the message flow labelled “Loan request” refer to one message element in the BPMN file. When the label of the flow should differ from the name of the message, give the name with message=: tok 1.0 "Message names" pool library "Library" start s "Need" send order "Send the order" message="Purchase order" end e "Order sent" pool supplier "Supplier" flow s -> order -> e message order -> supplier "Order for 12 titles" message="Purchase order" The identifier of a message flow is derived from its ends, m-order-supplier, unless you give one with id=. You will need explicit identifiers when conversations refer to message flows, later in this chapter. Not every element can send or receive messages. Tasks can (send and receive tasks are made for it, but a user or manual task can receive a letter too), and so can events with a message trigger and pools. A message flow that ends at a gateway, a data object or an event without a message trigger is the error E009. Conversely, in a model with several pools, a send or receive task or a message event without any message flow gets the warning W054: the diagram promises a message but does not show where it goes. 4.4.1 A collaboration with a black-box pool The interlibrary loan of Chapter 1 becomes a collaboration when the other library appears as a participant: tok 1.0 "Interlibrary loan: collaboration" pool library "University library" lane reader "Reader" start need "Book needed" user request "Submit a loan request" user collect "Collect the book" end borrowed "Book borrowed" lane ill "Interlibrary loan desk" user catalogues "Search the union catalogue" send order "Send the loan request" message="Loan request" receive parcel "Receive the parcel" message="Parcel with the book" lane system "Library system" service record "Record the loan" pool lender "Lending library" flow need -> request -> catalogues -> order -> parcel -> record -> collect -> borrowed message order -> lender "Loan request" message lender -> parcel "Parcel with the book" Figure 4.2: The interlibrary loan as a collaboration with a black-box pool. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) The university library has three lanes: the reader, the interlibrary loan desk and the library system. The desk sends the request to the lending library with a send task and waits for the parcel with a receive task. The lending library is a black box: the model says what it receives and what it sends, not how it handles the request. 4.4.2 Two processes that talk to each other When both participants’ processes matter, both pools have blocks. In the next model an applicant sends a query to a state archive and waits for the answer; the archive’s process starts when the query arrives and ends by sending the answer. tok 1.0 "Archive query: two participants" pool applicant "Applicant" start need "Information needed" send submit "Submit the query" message="Query" catch answer "Answer received" message="Answer" manual read "Read the answer" end done "Information obtained" pool archive "State archive" lane registry "Registry" start received "Query received" message="Query" user register "Register the query" end sent "Answer sent" message="Answer" lane archivist "Archivist" user search "Search the holdings" user draft "Draft the answer" flow need -> submit -> answer -> read -> done flow received -> register -> search -> draft -> sent message submit -> received "Query" message sent -> answer "Answer" Figure 4.3: An archive query between two participants, each with its own process. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) Here the messages connect events and tasks inside the pools. The archive’s process begins with a message start event: it is started by the arrival of the query. The applicant’s process waits at an intermediate catch event with a message trigger, and the archive’s process ends with a message end event that sends the answer. The names "Query" and "Answer" tie each message flow to the events and the task that send and receive it. The applicant’s pool has no lanes; the archive’s pool has two. Each pool has its own sequence flows, from its own start event to its own end event, and the two processes are connected only by the two messages. Since the document has two pools with blocks, their processes are named after the pools: “Applicant” and “State archive”. 4.4.3 Correlation keys When many instances of the same processes run at once, an engine must know which answer belongs to which query. BPMN describes this with correlation keys: properties of the messages, such as a query number, that identify the conversation. tok writes them with key and one prop line per message: tok 1.0 "Correlation" pool applicant "Applicant" start need "Information needed" send submit "Submit the query" message="Query" catch answer "Answer received" message="Answer" end done "Information obtained" pool archive "State archive" start received "Query received" message="Query" user search "Search the holdings" end sent "Answer sent" message="Answer" flow need -> submit -> answer -> done flow received -> search -> sent message submit -> received "Query" message sent -> answer "Answer" key query-number "Query number" prop number message="Query" path="query.number" prop number message="Answer" path="answer.reference" Each prop line says where the property is found in one message. A correlation key belongs to a collaboration, so a document with key needs pools. Correlation keys describe the model; Camunda 8 correlates messages differently, with the attribute correlation= of executable models (Chapter 10). 4.5 Structural rules Pools bring four rules about where elements may stand and what flows may connect. They are checked before the rules of BPMN, and their codes start with R: Code Rule R031 when a document has a pool, events, tasks and gateways stand inside pools, not at the top level R030 when a pool has lanes, every flow node of its process is in a lane R021 a sequence flow connects two nodes of the same process (or sub-process); it never leaves its pool R022 a message flow connects two different pools The following model breaks all four: tok 1.0 "Routing a letter (with errors)" start received "Letter received" pool university "University" user register "Register the letter" lane office "Dean's office" user assign "Assign the letter to a unit" end assigned "Letter assigned" flow received -> register -> assign -> assigned message register -> assign "Letter" tok check 04-lanes-error.tok 04-lanes-error.tok:3: error R031: 'received' is declared at top level, but the document has pools; move it into a pool 04-lanes-error.tok:6: error R030: 'register' is in a pool with lanes but outside every lane 04-lanes-error.tok:11: error R021: sequence flow received -> register crosses a process or sub-process boundary 04-lanes-error.tok:12: error R022: message flow register -> assign must connect two different pools 04-lanes-error.tok: 4 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) The first error causes the third. The start event received stands outside the pool, so it does not belong to the university’s process, and the flow from it to register crosses the border of that process. Moving the start event into a lane removes both errors. This is common: one mistake in the structure produces several messages. Correct the diagnostics from the top and check again after each correction. The fourth error is the most frequent misunderstanding in collaboration models. Registering a letter and assigning it are two steps of the same university; they are connected by a sequence flow, even though different people do them. Messages pass only between participants. When you are unsure whether two parties are lanes of one pool or two pools, ask whether one of them can give the other an instruction. Departments of one organisation work in one process, under one control: they are lanes. Independent organisations, and people outside the organisation such as customers and readers, only send each other messages: they are pools. 4.6 Conversations A collaboration diagram with many participants and many messages can become crowded. BPMN offers a more abstract view, the conversation diagram: it shows the participants and the logical exchanges between them, each exchange grouping the message flows that belong together. A conversation is drawn as a hexagon connected to its participants by double lines. A conversation is declared with the keyword conversation, the pools it links (pools=, at least two) and, optionally, the message flows it groups (messages=, by their identifiers): tok 1.0 "Peer review: conversations" pool author "Author" pool journal "Journal editorial office" pool reviewer "Reviewer" min=2 max=3 message author -> journal "Manuscript" id=m-manuscript message journal -> author "Decision" id=m-decision message journal -> reviewer "Review invitation" id=m-invitation message reviewer -> journal "Review report" id=m-report conversation submission "Submission" pools="author journal" messages="m-manuscript m-decision" conversation review "Review" pools="journal reviewer" messages="m-invitation m-report" Figure 4.4: Peer review: two conversations between three participants; the reviewer pool has a multiplicity. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) All three pools are black boxes here: the view is about who talks to whom, not about the work inside. The message flows have explicit identifiers (id=m-manuscript and so on), because the conversations name them. The conversation “Submission” groups the manuscript and the decision exchanged between the author and the editorial office; “Review” groups the invitation and the report exchanged with the reviewers. Conversations can be grouped and reused: Statement BPMN Meaning conversation ID "Label" pools="P Q" [messages="M1 M2"] conversation an exchange between the pools, with the message flows it groups subconversation ID "Label" pools="P Q" with a block of conversations subConversation a group of related conversations, drawn with a + callconversation ID "Label" pools="P Q" collaboration=ID [map="inner:outer; …"] callConversation a conversation defined in another collaboration, drawn with a thick border tok 1.0 "Sub-conversations" pool reader "Reader" pool library "Library" pool supplier "Book supplier" message reader -> library "Loan request" id=m-request message library -> reader "Pick-up notice" id=m-notice conversation loan "Loan" pools="reader library" messages="m-request m-notice" subconversation acquisition "Acquisition" pools="library supplier" conversation offer "Offer" pools="library supplier" conversation purchase "Purchase order" pools="library supplier" callconversation complaint "Complaint" pools="library supplier" collaboration=complaints The checker makes sure the parts fit together. A conversation must link at least two different pools, and a conversation inside a sub-conversation only pools of that sub-conversation (R070); every message flow named in messages= must connect two of the conversation’s pools (R071). Conversations stand only at the top level or in the block of a sub-conversation, and the canonical form prints them after the message flows. Conversations do not replace message flows; they are a view on top of them. The same document can contain the pools with their processes, the message flows and the conversations that group them. The BPMN file then holds all of it, and BPMN tools that support conversation diagrams show them. 4.7 Choreographies A choreography describes a collaboration from yet another angle: not the work of each participant, but the order of the message exchanges between them, as an observer would see it. Each step is a choreography task, an exchange of a message between two participants, possibly with a reply. The steps are connected by sequence flows and gateways, like the tasks of a process. A choreography is a top-level block. Its participants are pools of the document, usually black boxes: tok 1.0 "Book purchase: choreography" pool library "Library" pool supplier "Book supplier" choreography purchase "Book purchase" start need "Purchase approved" choreo order "Place the order" from=library to=supplier message="Order" reply="Order confirmation" xor stock "Is the book in stock?" choreo ship "Ship the book" from=supplier to=library message="Parcel and invoice" choreo decline "Decline the order" from=supplier to=library message="Out of stock notice" end delivered "Book delivered" end declined "Order declined" flow need -> order -> stock flow stock -> ship "yes" default flow stock -> decline "no" when="in_stock = false" flow ship -> delivered flow decline -> declined Figure 4.5: A book purchase as a choreography, drawn below the pools of the collaboration. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) A choreography task is written with choreo, the initiating participant from=, the other participant to=, the message with message= and, optionally, the reply with reply=. The diagram draws it as a rounded rectangle with a band for each participant: the initiator on top, white; the other at the bottom, shaded. The messages appear as envelopes next to the band of their sender, white for the initiating message and shaded for the reply. The choreography is drawn in a diagram of its own, below the collaboration. The gateway stock decides on the basis of the order’s content, which both participants know; its branches have labels and a default flow as in a process. The block of a choreography may contain: choreography activities: choreo (a task), subchoreo (a sub-choreography with a block of its own) and callchoreo (a call of another choreography); the gateways xor, and, or, eventgw and complex; events, restricted by BPMN to those that make sense without a participant’s process: a start event without a trigger or with a timer, conditional or signal trigger; intermediate events with a timer, conditional, signal or link trigger; end events without a trigger or with terminate; sequence flows between them. Other elements, such as tasks of a process or data, are the error R073 inside a choreography. A sub-choreography groups several exchanges among several participants: tok 1.0 "Sub-choreography" pool reader "Reader" pool library "Library" pool courier "Courier" choreography delivery "Home delivery" start s choreo order "Order a book" from=reader to=library message="Order" subchoreo ship "Ship the book" pools="library courier reader" from=library start s2 choreo handover "Hand over the parcel" from=library to=courier message="Parcel" choreo deliver "Deliver the parcel" from=courier to=reader message="Parcel" end e2 end e flow s2 -> handover -> deliver -> e2 flow s -> order -> ship -> e The participants of a sub-choreography are listed with pools= and its initiator with from=; the activities inside it may only involve those participants (R072). A callchoreo names the choreography it calls with choreography=ID, and map="inner:outer" pairs the participants of the called choreography with its own. The flags loop, parallel and sequential mark choreography activities that repeat, as they mark tasks. Choreographies are useful in the early design of an interaction between organisations, when the parties agree on the order of messages before each designs its own process, and in describing standard exchanges such as a purchase or an interlibrary loan protocol. 4.8 Participant multiplicity Sometimes several participants of the same kind take part in one collaboration: three reviewers of one manuscript, several suppliers asked for an offer. BPMN expresses this with the multiplicity of a participant, written in tok with min= and max= on the pool: tok 1.0 "Multiplicity" pool journal "Journal" start s "Manuscript received" send invite "Invite the reviewers" message="Invitation" end e "Reviewers invited" pool reviewer "Reviewer" max=3 flow s -> invite -> e message invite -> reviewer "Invitation" The pool is then drawn with the multi-instance marker, three vertical bars at the bottom, as in the reviewer pool of the peer review conversation above. When only max= is given, the minimum is 2; when only min= is given, the maximum is 1, the default of BPMN. Both are whole numbers with 0 <= min <= max and max >= 1; anything else is the error R074. 4.9 Collaborations, levels and Camunda Pools, lanes and message flows belong to the core of BPMN. They are accepted at every level of the language, including basic, and every BPMN tool supports them. Correlation keys, conversations, choreographies and participant multiplicity are advanced elements: the levels basic and analytic reject them with R040. tok check 04-peer-review-conversation.tok --level analytic 04-peer-review-conversation.tok:7: error R040: 'min' is not available at level analytic 04-peer-review-conversation.tok:14: error R040: 'conversation' is not available at level analytic 04-peer-review-conversation.tok:15: error R040: 'conversation' is not available at level analytic 04-peer-review-conversation.tok: 3 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) In executable models for Camunda 8, a collaboration is deployed as the processes of its pools; Camunda Modeler shows the pools and lanes, and the engine runs each executable process. The descriptive elements of this chapter are reported where Camunda would ignore or reject them: conversations and participant multiplicity are warnings (Camunda ignores them), choreographies are errors (Camunda does not execute them). Chapter 10 lists these codes, C110 and C120 to C123, and the conformance appendix the coverage of each element. 4.10 The canonical form of a collaboration tok fmt prints a collaboration in a fixed order that follows the way a reader takes in the model: first who takes part and what each does, then how the work flows, then how the participants communicate. The header. The pools, each followed by a blank line, with their lanes and flow nodes in the order you declared them. The choreographies, each with its nodes and, at the end of its block, its sequence flows. The other sequence flows, as chains where possible. The message flows, then the conversations. The correlation keys. Data, artifacts, decisions, forms and simulation statements follow, as later chapters show. Whatever order you write a collaboration in, the formatted text of the same model is the same. Exercises Exercise 4.1 Lanes or pools? For each pair, decide whether the two parties are lanes of one pool or two pools, and give the reason: (a) the registry and the dean’s office of a faculty; (b) a library and its reader; (c) a publisher and an external reviewer; (d) the cataloguing team and the library system; (e) an archive and a ministry that supervises it. Fix the structure. Download 04-lanes-error.tok and correct it so that tok check reports no errors. Keep the meaning: the letter is received and registered by the registry, and assigned by the dean’s office. Download the model with errors (.tok) An archive query with a black box. Model an archive that handles a query from an applicant who is a black-box pool. The archive has three lanes (registry, archivist, head of department). The query arrives as a message; the archivist may ask the applicant for missing details (a send task) and wait for them (a receive task); the head approves the answer; the registry sends it. Write the message flows for the four messages and check the model at the level full and the level basic. Open the box. Take the interlibrary loan collaboration and give the lending library a process: it receives the request, checks whether the book can be lent, and either sends the parcel or sends a refusal. Connect the two processes with message flows, and add to the university library an event-based gateway that waits for the parcel or the refusal. A conversation view. Draw the conversation diagram of exercise 4: keep the pools and message flows, give the message flows identifiers, and group them into one conversation “Interlibrary loan”. Then add a black-box pool “Courier” and a second conversation “Delivery” between the lending library, the courier and the university library. A choreography. Write the exchange of exercise 4 as a choreography between two black-box pools: the request (with an acknowledgement as its reply), a gateway on whether the book can be lent, and the parcel or the refusal. Compare the length of the choreography with the length of the two processes. Which view would you show to the two libraries when they negotiate the procedure, and which to the staff who carry it out?
