Chapter 5 Events, sub-processes and exceptions In this chapter you will tell catching events from throwing events and know where each trigger may stand · write message, timer, conditional, signal, error, escalation, compensation, cancel, link, terminate, multiple and parallel multiple events · attach interrupting and non-interrupting boundary events to activities · group work in embedded sub-processes, event sub-processes, transactions and ad-hoc sub-processes · call other processes and global tasks · mark loops and multi-instance activities · undo completed work with compensation handlers A process description written by the people who do the work usually covers the normal case: the request comes in, it is checked, it is answered. The interesting questions come afterwards. What happens if the reader never collects the book? If the registration system is down? If the applicant withdraws the request while the archivist is still searching? In BPMN these questions are answered with events: things that happen and either start, interrupt or redirect the work. This chapter covers every kind of event of BPMN 2.0.2 as tok writes it, and the containers that give events a scope: sub-processes, event sub-processes, transactions and ad-hoc sub-processes. Chapter 3 introduced the five event keywords and the plain (none) events. Here they receive their triggers. 5.1 Catching and throwing Every event either catches something or throws something. A catching event waits until its trigger happens: a message arrives, a time passes, a condition becomes true. A throwing event makes its trigger happen: it sends a message, raises an error, broadcasts a signal. In the diagram a catching event has a white symbol and a throwing event a black one. The position of the event decides which of the two it is: Keyword BPMN element Catches or throws start start event catches: the trigger starts the process (or the sub-process) catch intermediate catch event catches: the token waits on the path until the trigger happens boundary boundary event catches: the trigger happens while the activity it is attached to is running throw intermediate throw event throws: the token passes through and the trigger happens end end event throws: the path ends and the trigger happens A trigger is an attribute of the event. message="Order" on a catch line waits for the message “Order”; the same attribute on a throw line sends it. Messages, signals, errors and escalations are declared implicitly by their name: two events that write signal="Order closed" refer to the same signal, and the BPMN export writes one signal element for both. 5.2 Triggers The table lists every trigger and the positions where BPMN allows it. A trigger in a position the table does not allow is the error E010 (for example a timer on an end event, or any trigger on the start event of an embedded sub-process). Trigger tok Catching positions Throwing positions message message="Name" start, catch, boundary throw, end timer timer=VALUE start, catch, boundary none conditional condition="FEEL" start, catch, boundary none signal signal="Name" start, catch, boundary throw, end error error="Name" boundary, start of an event sub-process end escalation escalation="Name" boundary, start of an event sub-process throw, end compensation compensate (flag) boundary throw, end cancel cancel (flag) boundary of a transaction end inside a transaction link link="Name" catch throw terminate terminate (flag) none end Message. A message is sent from one participant to another: a request, a letter, an e-mail, a reply from a supplier. A message event usually has a message flow from or to another pool (Chapter 4); in a model with several pools, a message event without a message flow is the warning W054. Timer. A timer is a duration (P14D, PT2H), a date and time (2027-01-15T09:00) or a cycle (R3/PT1H, three times every hour). Chapter 3 has the table of ISO 8601 values. A value that contains a space must be quoted. Conditional. condition="FEEL" waits until a condition over the data of the process becomes true: condition="status = \"withdrawn\"". The condition is written in FEEL without a leading = (Chapter 9 describes FEEL). Signal. A signal is broadcast: every process that catches a signal of that name reacts to it, and the thrower does not know who listens. Use a signal for announcements (“the reading room is closed today”) and a message for communication with a known partner. Error. An error ends the work of an activity because it cannot be completed: a record cannot be saved, a payment is refused. An error is thrown by an end event inside a sub-process and caught by a boundary event of that sub-process or by an event sub-process. A boundary error event on a task stands for a failure of the task itself. Both error= and escalation= accept a code="…", the code a process engine matches. Escalation. An escalation tells someone higher up that something needs their attention, without necessarily stopping the work: a search is taking too long, a request needs the director’s decision. It can be thrown by an intermediate event, so the work continues after it. Compensation, cancel. Compensation undoes completed work; cancellation ends a transaction. Both are described in their own sections below. Link. A pair of link events is a “go to” inside one process: the throwing link event jumps to the catching link event with the same name. Links help to break a long diagram into parts, or to avoid long crossing lines. They have no meaning beyond the drawing. Terminate. A terminate end event ends the whole process instance at once, including every other path that is still active. 5.2.1 Events on a path: waiting for a supplier A library orders a book that is out of stock. After sending the order, it waits for whichever happens first: the book arrives, the supplier refuses, the publisher withdraws the title, or fourteen days pass. tok 1.0 "Waiting for a supplier" start needed "Book needed" send order "Send the order" message="Order" eventgw first "What happens first?" catch delivered "Book delivered" message="Delivery" catch refused "Refusal received" message="Refusal" catch timeout "14 days passed" timer=P14D catch withdrawn "Title withdrawn by the publisher" condition="status = \"withdrawn\"" user receive-book "Receive the book" end done "Book received" throw closed "Order closed" signal="Order closed" end not-delivered "Order not fulfilled" throw to-reminder "To reminder" link="Reminder" catch reminder "Reminder" link="Reminder" user send-reminder "Send a reminder" end reminded "Reminder sent" flow needed -> order -> first flow first -> delivered flow first -> refused flow first -> timeout flow first -> withdrawn flow delivered -> receive-book -> done flow refused -> closed -> not-delivered flow withdrawn -> closed flow timeout -> to-reminder flow reminder -> send-reminder -> reminded Figure 5.1: Catching events after an event-based gateway, a signal throw event and a pair of link events. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) The event-based gateway first is followed by four catching events: two message events, a conditional event and a timer event. The first of them to happen decides the path, and the others are no longer awaited. Both negative outcomes pass the signal throw event “Order closed”, which announces the closure to anyone who listens (for example the acquisitions statistics). The timeout does not draw a long line back across the diagram: it jumps through the link events “To reminder” and “Reminder” to a separate part of the diagram. The catching link event has no incoming sequence flow; the link is its incoming path. 5.2.2 Triggers without a value In an early draft you may know that a step waits for a message without knowing which one. The trigger keys message, timer, signal, condition, error and escalation may be written as flags without a value: catch reply "Reply or timeout" message timer. The event gets the event definition without a reference, as graphical BPMN tools draw it when the details are not filled in yet. Such an event is valid; a message event without a message is the note L010, a reminder to complete the model. On boundary events and on the start events of event sub-processes the flags error and escalation have a precise meaning: they catch every error or escalation, whatever its name. 5.3 Boundary events Many exceptions happen during an activity: while the reader has not yet collected the book, the deadline passes; while the system records the copy, the database fails. A boundary event is attached to the activity with on=ID and catches its trigger only while that activity is running: boundary seven-days "7 days passed" on=pickup timer=P7D A boundary event is interrupting by default: when its trigger happens, the activity is cancelled and the process continues along the outgoing flow of the boundary event. With the flag noninterrupting the activity keeps running, and the boundary event starts an additional path in parallel. The diagram draws a non-interrupting boundary event with a dashed circle. Boundary trigger Interrupting Non-interrupting message, timer, conditional, signal, escalation yes yes error yes no: an error always interrupts (E012) cancel yes (only on a transaction) no: always interrupts (R060) compensation not a path: it connects the activity with its compensation handler A boundary event needs on= (R032), the activity must exist (R002) and must be an activity, not a gateway or an event (R003). A boundary event has no incoming sequence flow: its only “incoming path” is the activity. The following model shows a reader picking up a book that arrived through interlibrary loan. Three boundary events cover three exceptions. tok 1.0 "Picking up an interlibrary loan" pool library "University library" lane librarian "Interlibrary loan librarian" start arrived "Book arrived" service register "Register the copy" boundary save-failed "Saving failed" on=register error="Saving failed" user register-by-hand "Register the copy by hand" user notify "Notify the reader" user send-back "Send the book back" end returned "Book returned to the lending library" lane reader "Reader" user pickup "Pick up the book" boundary three-days "3 days passed" noninterrupting on=pickup timer=P3D boundary seven-days "7 days passed" on=pickup timer=P7D end picked-up "Book picked up" lane system "Library system" service remind "Send a reminder" end reminded "Reminder sent" flow arrived -> register -> notify -> pickup -> picked-up flow save-failed -> register-by-hand -> notify flow three-days -> remind -> reminded flow seven-days -> send-back -> returned Figure 5.2: An error boundary event and two timer boundary events, one of them non-interrupting. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) save-failed is an error boundary event on the service task “Register the copy”. If the system cannot save the record, the task is abandoned and the librarian registers the copy by hand; both paths meet again at “Notify the reader”. three-days is a non-interrupting timer. After three days the system sends a reminder, but the reader can still pick up the book: the task “Pick up the book” continues. seven-days is an interrupting timer. After seven days the pick-up is cancelled and the book is sent back to the lending library. Two timers on one task, one non-interrupting and one interrupting, are a common pattern: a reminder first, a deadline later. Note what the model says precisely: the reminder is sent once, after three days. A reminder every three days would be the cycle timer=R/P3D. 5.4 Embedded sub-processes A sub-process (sub) groups activities that belong together into one activity of the parent process. It has its own block, with its own start event, end events and sequence flows: sub search "Search the holdings" start search-start user finding-aids "Review the finding aids" ... The block of a sub-process is a separate scope for sequence flows. A flow cannot cross its border: a flow from a node inside the sub-process to a node outside it is the error R021. The parent process enters the sub-process through its incoming flow, the inner start event begins, and when every inner path has reached an end event the sub-process completes and the parent continues along its outgoing flow. The start event of an embedded sub-process has no trigger (E010); the sub-process starts when the token arrives. The flows of a sub-process may be written in its block or at the top level; the canonical form prints them with the other sequence flows after the pools, because the identifiers alone say where each flow belongs. A sub-process is useful for three reasons. It gives the diagram a level of detail that can be read separately from the whole. It is a scope for boundary events: a timer on the sub-process limits the duration of all its work together, and an error thrown anywhere inside it can be caught on its border. And it is a scope for event sub-processes and data. 5.4.1 Escalation from a sub-process The search of an archive for a reader’s request is a sub-process. Sometimes the archivist cannot decide alone whether the search should continue, and the head of department has to decide. The archivist does not stop working: the escalation is thrown inside the sub-process, caught by a non-interrupting boundary event on its border, and the head’s decision runs in parallel with the search. tok 1.0 "Archival search with a sub-process" pool archive "State archive" lane registry "Registry office" start request "Search request received" message="Search request" user register "Register the request" xor in-scope "Does the request concern the holdings?" end out-of-scope "Request outside the holdings" terminate eventsub withdrawal "Withdrawal of the request" start withdrawn "Request withdrawn" message="Withdrawal" user close "Close the case" end closed "Case closed" lane archivist "Archivist" sub search "Search the holdings" start search-start user finding-aids "Review the finding aids" xor found "Were the records found?" throw difficult "Head of department must decide" escalation="Difficult search" user analyse "Analyse the records" end search-end "Search finished" boundary escalated "Difficult search" noninterrupting on=search escalation="Difficult search" user answer "Prepare the answer" end answered "Answer sent" message="Search answer" lane head "Head of department" user decide "Decide on further searching" end decided "Decision recorded" pool applicant "Applicant" flow withdrawn -> close -> closed flow search-start -> finding-aids -> found flow found -> analyse "yes" flow found -> difficult "no" flow difficult -> analyse -> search-end flow request -> register -> in-scope flow in-scope -> search "yes" flow in-scope -> out-of-scope "no" flow search -> answer -> answered flow escalated -> decide -> decided message applicant -> request "Search request" message answered -> applicant "Search answer" message applicant -> withdrawn "Withdrawal" Figure 5.3: An escalation thrown inside a sub-process and caught on its border, an event sub-process and a terminate end event. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) The throw event difficult and the boundary event escalated name the same escalation, “Difficult search”. If nothing inside the sub-process throws the escalation or error that a boundary event of the sub-process catches, tok check reports the warning W052; an escalation that is thrown and caught nowhere is the warning W053. Both usually mean a typing error in the name. The model also shows a terminate end event: a request outside the holdings ends the whole case at once. 5.5 Event sub-processes An event sub-process (eventsub) is a sub-process that is not on the path of the process. It has no incoming or outgoing sequence flows, and its block begins with exactly one start event with a trigger. It runs when that trigger happens while the enclosing process (or sub-process) is active. In the archive model, the event sub-process “Withdrawal of the request” runs when the applicant withdraws the request: eventsub withdrawal "Withdrawal of the request" start withdrawn "Request withdrawn" message="Withdrawal" user close "Close the case" end closed "Case closed" The start event of an event sub-process may be interrupting (the default) or noninterrupting. An interrupting start cancels everything else in the enclosing scope: when the request is withdrawn, the search stops and only the closing of the case remains. A non-interrupting start runs the event sub-process alongside the normal work, for example a change of address that has to be recorded while the case continues. The diagram draws an event sub-process with a dotted border, and a non-interrupting start event with a dashed circle. Its start event may have a message, timer, conditional, signal, error or escalation trigger. An error start event, such as start failure "Any error" error, handles an error thrown inside the enclosing scope: it is an alternative to a boundary error event that keeps the handling inside the scope. An event sub-process with a sequence flow to or from it, or without a triggered start event, is the error E013. Construct Where it is When it runs boundary event on a sub-process on the border of the sub-process its trigger happens while the sub-process runs; the handling continues outside event sub-process inside the process or sub-process it belongs to its trigger happens while that scope runs; the handling stays inside 5.6 Compensation Some completed work cannot simply be cancelled: a reservation of funds has already been made, an order has already been sent. When the process later decides that the work must be undone, BPMN compensates it: it runs, for each completed activity, a compensation handler that reverses its effect. In tok, an activity names its handler with compensate=HANDLER, and the handler carries the flag compensation: service reserve "Reserve funds" compensate=release service release "Release the reserved funds" compensation The export attaches a compensation boundary event to reserve and connects it with release by an association. The handler has no sequence flows (R051); it is not a step of the normal path, it is called only by compensation. If you want to give the boundary event a label or documentation, declare it yourself with boundary ID "Label" on=ACTIVITY compensate; the export then uses that event. Compensation is triggered by a throwing compensation event: throw ID "Label" compensate or end ID "Label" compensate compensates every completed activity of the scope that has a handler, the latest completed first; with activity=ID it compensates only that activity. tok 1.0 "Ordering books from a supplier" start s "Order approved" service reserve "Reserve funds" compensate=release service release "Release the reserved funds" compensation user send-order "Send the order" compensate=withdraw manual withdraw "Withdraw the order" compensation xor confirmed "Did the supplier confirm the delivery?" end ordered "Books ordered" throw undo-funds "Undo the reservation" compensate activity=reserve end cancelled "Order cancelled" compensate flow s -> reserve -> send-order -> confirmed flow confirmed -> ordered "yes" flow confirmed -> undo-funds "no" flow undo-funds -> cancelled Figure 5.4: Two compensation handlers, a throw event that compensates one activity and an end event that compensates the rest. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) If the supplier does not confirm the delivery, the throw event undo-funds first compensates only reserve (activity=reserve): the funds are released. The end event cancelled then compensates whatever else has completed and has a handler, here the sending of the order, which is withdrawn by its manual handler. Compensation runs only for activities that have completed; an activity that never ran has nothing to undo. 5.7 Transactions and cancellation A transaction is a sub-process whose activities succeed or fail together. If the transaction is cancelled, its completed activities are compensated, and the process continues from the cancel boundary event of the transaction: tok BPMN transaction ID "Label" with a block a transaction: a sub-process with a double border method=compensate\|store\|image the transaction method (written only when given; compensate is the BPMN default) end ID "Label" cancel a cancel end event, only directly inside a transaction (R060) boundary ID "Label" on=TRANSACTION cancel a cancel boundary event, only on a transaction, always interrupting (R060) Booking a study trip shows the pattern. The room and the ticket are booked together; if one of them fails, both bookings are reversed. tok 1.0 "Booking a study trip" start requested "Trip requested" transaction booking "Book the room and the ticket" start booking-start service room "Book a room" compensate=release-room service release-room "Release the room" compensation service ticket "Buy a ticket" compensate=refund-ticket service refund-ticket "Refund the ticket" compensation xor booked "Was everything booked?" end booked-end "Booked" end cancel-end "Cancel the booking" cancel boundary cancelled "Booking cancelled" cancel on=booking user confirm "Confirm the trip to the traveller" user inform "Inform the traveller of the cancellation" end trip-booked "Trip booked" end trip-cancelled "Trip cancelled" flow booking-start -> room -> ticket -> booked flow booked -> booked-end "yes" flow booked -> cancel-end "no" flow requested -> booking -> confirm -> trip-booked flow cancelled -> inform -> trip-cancelled Figure 5.5: A transaction with compensation handlers, a cancel end event and a cancel boundary event. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) When the token reaches the cancel end event cancel-end, three things happen in order. The transaction stops. Its completed activities are compensated through their handlers, the latest completed first: the ticket is refunded, then the room released. Finally the process continues from the cancel boundary event cancelled, so the traveller is informed. When the transaction completes normally, through booked-end, the process continues along its ordinary outgoing flow to “Confirm the trip”. 5.8 Multiple and parallel multiple events An event may have more than one trigger. On a catching event, several triggers mean “any one of them”: the event happens when the first of them happens. On a throwing event, all triggers happen. BPMN calls such an event a multiple event and draws it with a pentagon. A trigger key may be repeated for this purpose, and different keys may be combined: tok 1.0 "Handling a service request" start request "Request by e-mail or web form" message="E-mail" message="Web form" user record "Record the request" boundary nudge "Three days passed or reminder received" noninterrupting on=record timer=P3D signal="Reminder" user chase "Chase the case owner" end chased "Case owner chased" catch confirmed "Confirmation and payment" parallel message="Confirmation" signal="Payment" throw announce "Notify the customer and the manager" message="To customer" signal="Case confirmed" end closed "Request closed" message="Closing note" signal="Request closed" flow request -> record -> confirmed -> announce -> closed flow nudge -> chase -> chased Figure 5.6: Multiple start, boundary and end events, a parallel multiple catch event and a multiple throw event. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) The start event request starts the process when an e-mail or a web form arrives. The non-interrupting boundary event nudge fires after three days or when the signal “Reminder” arrives, whichever comes first. The catch event confirmed has the flag parallel: it waits until both the confirmation and the payment have arrived. BPMN calls this a parallel multiple event and draws it with a plus sign. parallel needs a catching event with two or more triggers (R062). The throw event announce and the end event closed throw all their triggers. The triggers terminate, compensation, cancel and link cannot be combined with any other trigger (R062). Only events take several triggers: a trigger key repeated on another flow node, such as message= written twice on a send task, is also R062. Any other key or flag written twice on one line is the deprecation warning R090 in a 1.0 document, and only its last value counts. 5.9 Ad-hoc sub-processes Some work has no fixed order. Processing a bequest of papers involves describing, digitising and conserving files, but which of these is done first, and how often, is decided by the archivist case by case. An ad-hoc sub-process (adhoc) contains activities that can be performed in any order and as often as needed: adhoc processing "Process the papers" user describe "Describe the files" user digitise "Digitise the files" manual conserve "Conserve damaged files" flow describe -> digitise An ad-hoc sub-process contains at least one activity and no start or end events (R050). Flows between inner activities are allowed and express a constraint: here, a file is digitised after it is described. The flag sequential says that only one activity runs at a time (the BPMN ordering is then sequential instead of parallel). The diagram marks an ad-hoc sub-process with a tilde. The attributes that tell a process engine which activities to activate and when the sub-process is complete (active=, until=, wait) belong to the executable layer of Chapter 10. 5.10 Call activities and global tasks A call activity (call) runs something defined elsewhere, so that a procedure used in several processes is modelled once: call ID "Label" process=ID calls a process, usually defined in another file. The diagram draws it with a thick border and a + marker. call ID "Label" task=ID calls a global task, a task declared once at the top level of the document with global: global identity-check "Check the donor's identity" kind=user call check-donor "Check the donor's identity" task=identity-check kind= is task (default), user, manual, script or rule; it gives the BPMN element (globalUserTask and so on) and the icon of the call activity. A call activity has either process= or task=, not both (R065); a task= that names no global is R066. The bindings of a called process for Camunda 8 (binding=, version=, variable propagation) are described in Chapter 10. 5.11 Loops and multi-instance Chapter 3 introduced three markers of repetition. Their full form describes how the repetition works. A standard loop repeats an activity while a condition holds: service publish "Publish the finding aid" loop test-before while="not(published)" loop-max=3 tok BPMN Meaning loop standardLoopCharacteristics the activity repeats while="FEEL" loopCondition it repeats while the condition is true test-before testBefore="true" the condition is tested before each iteration, so the activity may not run at all; by default it is tested after, so the activity runs at least once loop-max=N loopMaximum at most N iterations while=, test-before and loop-max= require loop, and loop-max is a whole number (R061). A multi-instance activity runs once for each element of a collection: once per box of a bequest, once per reviewer of a manuscript. parallel runs the instances at the same time (three vertical bars), sequential one after another (three horizontal bars). Which collection the instances work through, and when the activity is complete, are attributes of the executable layer (collection=, item=, output=, until=; Chapter 10). The markers apply to tasks, sub-processes and call activities alike. The bequest process combines most of the constructs of the last three sections: tok 1.0 "Processing a bequest of papers" global identity-check "Check the donor's identity" kind=user start received "Bequest offered" call check-donor "Check the donor's identity" task=identity-check user appraise "Appraise each box" parallel adhoc processing "Process the papers" user describe "Describe the files" user digitise "Digitise the files" manual conserve "Conserve damaged files" service publish "Publish the finding aid" loop test-before while="not(published)" loop-max=3 user proofread "Proofread the finding aid" sequential call catalogue "Catalogue the collection" process=cataloguing end done "Bequest processed" flow describe -> digitise flow received -> check-donor -> appraise -> processing -> publish -> proofread -> catalogue -> done Figure 5.7: A call activity of a global user task, a parallel multi-instance task, an ad-hoc sub-process, a standard loop, a sequential multi-instance task and a call activity of a process. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) Each box of the bequest is appraised (parallel multi-instance); the papers are then processed in an ad-hoc sub-process; publishing the finding aid is attempted until it succeeds, at most three times; it is proofread section by section (sequential multi-instance); and cataloguing, a procedure of its own, is called as a separate process. 5.12 Exceptions and process engines Everything in this chapter is BPMN 2.0.2, and every BPMN tool that supports the full notation reads it. A process engine may support less. Camunda 8 does not execute transactions, cancel events, multiple and parallel multiple events, standard loops with while=, test-before or loop-max=, instantiating receive tasks and event-based gateways, or calls of global tasks. In a document marked executable for Camunda, tok check reports each of them with a code from C100 to C108, so that a model meant for execution does not rely on what the engine cannot run. Descriptive and analytic models are not affected. Chapter 10 lists the codes, and Chapter 7 explains how to check a model against the conformance classes of BPMN. The levels of tok check follow the same line: boundary events, sub-processes and the triggers of BPMN’s analytic class pass at the level analytic, while transactions, multiple events, the loop attributes and global tasks need the level full. 5.13 Typical mistakes The following model of returning a damaged book contains several mistakes with events and handlers. tok 1.0 "Returning a damaged book" start returned "Book returned" user inspect "Inspect the book" boundary too-long "2 days passed" timer=P2D service charge "Charge the reader" compensate=refund service refund "Refund the charge" eventsub dispute "Reader disputes the charge" start disputed "Dispute received" user review "Review the dispute" end reviewed "Dispute reviewed" end done "Return closed" end cancelled "Return cancelled" cancel flow returned -> inspect -> charge -> done flow too-long -> cancelled flow charge -> refund flow disputed -> review -> reviewed tok check 05-exceptions-error.tok 05-exceptions-error.tok:5: error R032: boundary event 'too-long' needs on=ACTIVITY 05-exceptions-error.tok:6: error R051: compensation handler 'refund' needs the flag compensation 05-exceptions-error.tok:13: error R060: cancel end event 'cancelled' must be inside a transaction 05-exceptions-error.tok: 3 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) Code Problem Correction R032 the boundary event does not say which activity it is attached to add on=inspect R051 the handler named by compensate= lacks the flag, and it also has a sequence flow add compensation to refund and remove the flow charge -> refund R060 a cancel end event outside a transaction a plain end event is enough here: remove cancel After these corrections, tok check reaches the BPMN rules and reports one more error, E013: the start event of the event sub-process has no trigger. Errors of the BPMN layer appear only when the tok layer is clean; Chapter 7 explains this order. Exercises Exercise 5.1 Fix the returned book. Download 05-exceptions-error.tok and correct it until tok check reports no errors and no warnings. The dispute arrives as a message from the reader: give the start event of the event sub-process the right trigger. Download the model with errors (.tok) Deadlines on a task. An editor reviews a manuscript. After 10 days the system reminds the editor (the review continues); after 30 days the manuscript goes to another editor (the review stops). Model both deadlines with boundary events and draw the diagram. Then change the reminder so that it repeats every 10 days. Error or escalation? For each situation, decide whether it is an error or an escalation, whether it interrupts, and where it is caught: (a) the digitisation scanner breaks down in the middle of a sub-process “Digitise the volume”; (b) a cataloguer finds a rare item that the head of collections must see, but cataloguing continues; (c) the payment gateway refuses a fee payment. Write the events in tok. An event sub-process. Extend the archive search of this chapter with a non-interrupting event sub-process: when the applicant sends additional information (a message), the registry office adds it to the case file while the search continues. Check that the new message has a message flow from the applicant. A transaction. A conference registration books a seat in a session and charges the fee. If the charge fails, the seat is released and the participant is told. Model it as a transaction with compensation handlers and a cancel boundary event, and check it with --level analytic and --level full. Explain the difference. Multiple triggers. A process starts when a request arrives by post, by e-mail or at the desk. Write it once with three start events and once with one multiple start event. Which version would you show to the staff, and which to a process engine that does not execute multiple events?

Chapter 6 Data, resources and artifacts In this chapter you will show the documents and records a process uses with data objects, collections and data stores · connect them to activities and events with reads and writes · model the states of a document and its state transitions · declare item definitions, process inputs and outputs and properties · name the performers of activities with resources · add text annotations, groups and documentation to any element The sequence flows of a process say in which order the work is done. They do not say what the work is done with: the application form, the catalogue, the decision letter, the case file. For an information institution this is often the more important half of the model. An archive’s process is largely a story of records that are received, registered, described, made available and destroyed; a library’s process is a story of requests, loans and catalogue records. BPMN shows this half with data: data objects for the documents of one case, data stores for the systems and registers that outlive the case, and data associations for reading and writing them. It also has artifacts that do not change the meaning of the process but explain it to the reader: text annotations and groups. This chapter covers all of them, together with the declarations of process data and resources that make a model precise enough for analysis and execution. 6.1 Data objects A data object stands for information that exists within one case of the process: the purchase proposal of this reader, the decision on this application. It is declared with data: data proposal "Purchase proposal" state=submitted Attribute Meaning label the name of the document, shown under the symbol state="…" the state of the document at this point of the process, shown in square brackets collection the data object is a list of items (an order with several lines, a set of scans); drawn with three vertical bars object="Name" the name of the data object behind the reference, when several references share it (see below) type=ITEM the item definition of the data (see Process data) doc="Text" documentation Strictly speaking, BPMN distinguishes the data object (the information itself) from a data object reference (one appearance of it in the diagram, possibly in a particular state). Each data statement in tok is one reference with its own identifier. Normally each reference has its own data object. When the same document appears several times, for example in different states, give the references the same object="…": all data statements with the same object name in one process or sub-process share one data object in the BPMN file. data proposal "Purchase proposal" state=submitted object="Purchase proposal" data proposal-checked "Purchase proposal" state=checked object="Purchase proposal" A data element belongs to the process or sub-process in whose block it is declared. A data statement at the top level of a document with pools belongs to the process of the first activity that reads or writes it. The canonical form prints data statements at the end of the block they were declared in. 6.2 Data stores A data store stands for information that persists beyond one case and is shared by many cases: a library catalogue, a records management system, a register of loans. It is declared with store: store catalogue "Library catalogue" All store statements with the same label refer to one data store in the BPMN file; each statement is one reference in the diagram. A data store takes type= and doc= like a data object, but has no state and no collection flag. The choice between a data object and a data store is a modelling decision. If the information is created for the case and ends with it (an application, a decision letter), it is a data object. If the case only consults or updates something that existed before and will exist afterwards (a catalogue, a finance system), it is a data store. 6.3 Reading and writing A data element is connected to the work by a data association: reads check proposal # the activity check reads the data object proposal writes check proposal-checked reads ACTIVITY DATA creates a data input association from the data element to the activity; writes ACTIVITY DATA creates a data output association from the activity to the data element. The diagram draws both as dotted arrows. The data element may be a data object, a data store, or one of the inputs, outputs and properties described later in this chapter. Events can carry data too. A catching event (start, catch, boundary) can write the data it receives, for example a start event that writes the incoming application; a throwing event (end, throw) can read the data it sends. Writing from an end event, or reading into a start event, is the error R003, because it would make the event a step of work it cannot do. The following model shows a reader’s proposal to buy a book for the library. tok 1.0 "Book purchase proposal" doc="How the library handles a reader's proposal to buy a book." pool library "University library" lane reader "Reader" start need "Reader needs a book" user propose "Fill in the purchase proposal" lane acquisitions "Acquisitions librarian" user check "Check the catalogue and the budget" doc="Duplicates are rejected. The budget is read from the finance system." xor accepted "Is the purchase accepted?" user order "Order the book" user refuse "Inform the reader of the refusal" end ordered "Book ordered" end refused "Proposal refused" data proposal "Purchase proposal" state=submitted object="Purchase proposal" data proposal-checked "Purchase proposal" state=checked object="Purchase proposal" data order-lines "Order lines" collection store catalogue "Library catalogue" store finance "Finance system" flow need -> propose -> check -> accepted flow accepted -> order "yes" flow accepted -> refuse "no" flow order -> ordered flow refuse -> refused writes propose proposal reads check proposal reads check catalogue reads check finance writes check proposal-checked reads order proposal-checked writes order order-lines note budget-rule "Purchases over 500 EUR need the director's approval." on=accepted group decision-stage "Acquisition decision" members="check accepted" Figure 6.1: Data objects in two states, a collection, two data stores, a text annotation and documentation. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) The reader fills in the proposal, which creates the data object in the state “submitted”. The acquisitions librarian reads it together with two data stores, the catalogue (is the book already there?) and the finance system (is there money in the budget?), and writes the proposal in the state “checked”. The ordering of the book writes the order lines, a collection. The model also uses the artifacts of the end of this chapter: a text annotation on the gateway, a group around the decision stage and documentation on the header and on one task. The reads and writes lines are printed after the flows in the canonical form, in declaration order, so that a reader of the text finds all data associations in one place. 6.3.1 States and state transitions A state transition is an activity that reads a document in one state and writes it in another. In the proposal model, check reads the proposal “submitted” and writes it “checked”. This is how a process model shows the life cycle of a record: received, registered, assessed, archived. An activity that reads and writes a data object in the same state is suspicious: either the state has not changed, and the write is unnecessary, or it has, and the new state is missing. tok check reports it as the warning R064. The check compares the labels of the data objects, so give all states of one document the same label. 6.4 Process data The data objects above describe documents for the human reader. A model meant for analysis or for a process engine often needs more: what type of information each element carries, what the process receives when it starts and returns when it ends, and which values an activity keeps for itself. BPMN describes this with item definitions, data inputs and outputs, and properties. 6.4.1 Item definitions An item definition says what kind of information a data element holds. It is declared at the top level with item: item application-type "Grant application" structure="Application" item decision-type "Decision letter" structure="xsd:string" kind=information item file-type "Paper file" kind=physical Attribute BPMN Meaning label documentation an item definition has no name in BPMN; the label is its documentation structure=NAME structureRef the type: a name without a prefix (Application), an XML Schema type (xsd:string, xsd:decimal) or a name with another prefix namespace="URI" the namespace of that prefix needed for a prefix other than xsd kind=information\|physical itemKind information (the default in BPMN) or a physical thing, such as a paper file or a box collection isCollection a list of such items A data element refers to its item definition with type=ITEM. A reference to an item that is not declared is the error R066; a structure= that is not a qualified name, or a kind= other than information and physical, is R013. An XML Schema type uses the prefix xsd, which the exporter declares itself. Any other prefix needs namespace=, a prefix has one namespace in a document, and the prefixes the exporter uses for its own purposes (bpmn, bpmndi, dc, di, xsi, zeebe, modeler, xml) cannot be used for your own types: item text-t "Text" structure="feel:string" namespace="https://www.omg.org/spec/DMN/20191111/FEEL/" In a document of language 1.0 an item can also be a DMN type: with type=, allowed= or a block of components it describes the type of the input data of a decision, not of a BPMN element. Chapter 9 describes DMN types. One item cannot be both (R081). 6.4.2 Inputs, outputs and properties Statement BPMN Meaning input ID "Label" [type=ITEM] [collection] [on=ID] dataInput data the process (or the activity named by on=) receives output ID "Label" [type=ITEM] [collection] [on=ID] dataOutput data it returns property ID "Label" [type=ITEM] [on=ID] property a value kept by the process, the activity or the event, not visible from outside Without on=, an input or output belongs to the process (or to the sub-process in whose block it stands): it is what the process needs to start and what it delivers when it ends. The diagram draws process inputs and outputs as data objects with a white or black arrow. With on=ACTIVITY, it belongs to that activity and is not drawn; it describes the interface of the activity. An input may also be declared on= an end or intermediate throw event, an output on a start, intermediate catch or boundary event, and a property on any event. Every reads and writes line in a document of language 1.0 connects the data element with a data input or data output of the activity, as BPMN 2.0.2 requires. By default tok generates them, named after the data element (identifiers ACTIVITY-in-N, ACTIVITY-out-N). To connect the association to an input or output you declared yourself, name it with input=ID or output=ID: input scan-in "Scan to assess" on=assess reads assess scan input=scan-in An input= that is not declared is R066; one that belongs to another activity is R013. The assessment of a grant application uses all of these: tok 1.0 "Assessing a grant application" item application-type "Grant application" structure="Application" item decision-type "Decision letter" structure="xsd:string" kind=information item file-type "Paper file" kind=physical start received "Application received" user assess "Assess the application" task archive "Archive the paper file" end decided "Application decided" input application "Grant application" type=application-type output decision "Decision" type=decision-type input criteria "Assessment criteria" collection on=assess input scan-in "Scan to assess" on=assess property reviews "Number of reviews" on=assess data scan "Scanned application" state=received type=application-type data scan-assessed "Scanned application" state=assessed store files "Paper files" type=file-type flow received -> assess -> archive -> decided reads assess application reads assess scan input=scan-in writes assess scan-assessed writes assess decision writes archive files Figure 6.2: A process input and output, data objects with an item definition, a data store of physical items. Inputs and properties of activities are not drawn. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) The process receives the grant application (input application) and returns the decision (output decision). The task assess has three data inputs: the criteria (a collection), the named input scan-in through which it reads the scan, and the input that tok generates for the application. It also has a property that counts the reviews. In the BPMN file the task carries its input-output specification: <bpmn:userTask id="assess" name="Assess the application"> <bpmn:ioSpecification id="assess-io"> <bpmn:dataInput id="criteria" name="Assessment criteria" isCollection="true" /> <bpmn:dataInput id="scan-in" name="Scan to assess" /> <bpmn:dataInput id="assess-in-1" name="Grant application" /> <bpmn:dataOutput id="assess-out-3" name="Scanned application" /> <bpmn:dataOutput id="assess-out-4" name="Decision" /> ... </bpmn:ioSpecification> <bpmn:property id="reviews" name="Number of reviews" /> <bpmn:dataInputAssociation id="assess-dia-1"> <bpmn:sourceRef>application</bpmn:sourceRef> <bpmn:targetRef>assess-in-1</bpmn:targetRef> </bpmn:dataInputAssociation> ... You rarely need to read this XML, but it shows why the declarations exist: a BPMN tool or engine that imports the file finds a complete, typed interface for every activity. Process data belongs to the precise end of modelling. Item definitions, inputs, outputs and collections are elements of BPMN’s Common Executable conformance class; properties and data states are outside the three sub-classes and belong only to the full language (Chapter 7). The levels basic and analytic of tok check reject item, input, output, property and type= on data. A descriptive model does not need them: data objects, stores and associations already tell the reader what the work is done with. 6.5 Resources and performers Lanes (Chapter 4) show who is responsible for the activities they contain: a department, a role, a system. BPMN has a second, more precise way to say who performs an activity: resources and performers. tok 1.0 "Lending a book at the desk" start arrived "Reader at the desk" user lend "Check the reader's account" by=librarian service record "Record the loan" by=system manual hand-over "Hand over the book" by=librarian end lent "Book lent" flow arrived -> lend -> record -> hand-over -> lent resource librarian "Librarian" count=2 resource system "Library system" Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) resource ID "Label" declares a resource; by=ID on an activity names the resource that performs it. In a document of language 1.0 the export writes a BPMN resource and, for each activity with by=, a performer that refers to it: a humanPerformer on user and manual tasks, a performer on the others. <bpmn:resource id="librarian" name="Librarian" /> <bpmn:resource id="system" name="Library system" /> <bpmn:process id="process" name="Lending a book at the desk" isExecutable="false"> <bpmn:startEvent id="arrived" name="Reader at the desk" /> <bpmn:userTask id="lend" name="Check the reader's account"> <bpmn:humanPerformer id="lend-performer"> <bpmn:resourceRef>librarian</bpmn:resourceRef> </bpmn:humanPerformer> </bpmn:userTask> <bpmn:serviceTask id="record" name="Record the loan"> <bpmn:performer id="record-performer"> <bpmn:resourceRef>system</bpmn:resourceRef> </bpmn:performer> </bpmn:serviceTask> Performers are not drawn: the diagram stays the same. The same statements serve the simulation of Chapter 11: there count=2 says that two librarians work at the desk, and an activity with by= waits until one of them is free. count= is a simulation setting only; it does not appear in the BPMN file. Lanes and resources answer different questions and can be used together. A lane is a part of the diagram: everything drawn in it is the responsibility of that role. A resource is an attribute of one activity, independent of the drawing, and it can be counted, which a lane cannot. Use lanes when the reader of the diagram should see responsibilities at a glance, and resources when the model is analysed or simulated. The executable layer has its own assignment of user tasks to people and groups (assignee=, candidate-groups=); it is described in Chapter 10 and is independent of by=. 6.6 Text annotations A text annotation (note) adds a comment to the diagram. With on=ID it is connected by a dotted line (an association) to the element it explains: note budget-rule "Purchases over 500 EUR need the director's approval." on=accepted Without on=, the note stands alone. An annotation does not change the meaning of the process, but it is part of the BPMN model and every BPMN tool shows it. Use it for information the reader of the diagram needs and the symbols cannot show: a rule behind a decision, a legal basis, a known problem. A comment (#) is different: it is part of the text only, for the people who edit the model, and it never reaches the BPMN file. 6.7 Groups A group marks elements that belong together for the reader, across lanes and pools, without affecting the flow: a stage of the process, the activities covered by one regulation, the part of a process that an IT system supports. group decision-stage "Acquisition decision" members="check accepted" members= lists the identifiers of the elements in the group. The BPMN export writes the group with its label (as a category value), but BPMN stores no list of members: a group is only a shape drawn around the elements. The automatic layout of tok does not draw groups. A group gets its shape when the model has a layout sidecar, for example after importing a drawing from a graphical editor (Chapter 8); the members are then a record, in the text, of what the group means. When you import a BPMN file with groups, tok import reports that the membership must be added by hand. 6.8 Documentation Every element that BPMN can document accepts doc="Text": flow nodes, flows, message flows, pools, lanes, data objects, stores, inputs, outputs, properties, notes, groups, global tasks, interfaces and operations, and in language 1.0 also conversations and choreographies. The text becomes the documentation of the element in the BPMN file, and BPMN tools show it in the properties panel. user check "Check the catalogue and the budget" doc="Duplicates are rejected. The budget is read from the finance system." On the header, doc= documents the process of a document without pools, or the whole model (the definitions element) of a document with pools. The text is plain; \n makes a line break. Documentation, annotations and comments have different readers: Form Reader Where it appears # comment the people who edit the text only in the .tok file note the reader of the diagram as a shape on the diagram, and in the BPMN file doc= the user of a BPMN tool or engine in the properties of the element, and in the BPMN file 6.9 Typical mistakes The following model of registering a thesis contains several mistakes with data. tok 1.0 "Registering a thesis" item thesis-type "Thesis" structure="Thesis" start submitted "Thesis submitted" user check "Check the thesis" user register "Register the thesis" end registered "Thesis registered" data thesis "Thesis" state="submitted" type=thesis-type data thesis-checked "Thesis" state="submitted" data report "Plagiarism report" type=report-type store repository "Thesis repository" flow submitted -> check -> register -> registered reads check thesis writes check thesis-checked writes check report reads register thesis-checked writes register repositry writes registered thesis-checked note check-rule "Theses are checked within 14 days." on=chek tok check 06-data-error.tok 06-data-error.tok:11: error R066: unknown item definition 'report-type'; declare it with 'item' 06-data-error.tok:16: warning R064: activity 'check' reads and writes data object 'Thesis' in the same state 'submitted'; a state transition writes another state 06-data-error.tok:20: error R002: unknown data object or store 'repositry' 06-data-error.tok:21: error R003: 'registered' is a 'end' element; required here: activity, start, intermediate catch or boundary event 06-data-error.tok:23: error R002: unknown flow node 'chek' 06-data-error.tok: 4 error(s), 1 warning(s), 0 note(s) Code Problem Correction R066 type=report-type names an item that is not declared declare item report-type "Plagiarism report", or remove type= R064 the checked thesis has the same state as the submitted one give thesis-checked the state checked R002 a typing error in an identifier (repositry, chek) write repository and check R003 an end event cannot write data; it can only read the data it sends use reads registered thesis-checked, or remove the line Exercises Exercise 6.1 Fix the thesis. Download 06-data-error.tok and correct it until tok check reports no errors and no warnings. Draw the diagram and check that the thesis appears in two states. Download the model with errors (.tok) The life cycle of a record. In a university registry an incoming letter is registered, assigned to a case, answered and archived. Model the process with one data object “Letter” in four states and a data store “Records system”, so that every activity is a state transition. Give all references of the letter the same object=, and check that tok check reports no R064. Object or store? For each of these, decide whether it is a data object or a data store and give a reason: a reader’s account, an interlibrary loan request, the union catalogue, a scan of a manuscript, the access log of a digital repository, the minutes of an appraisal committee. Process interface. Extend the reading room request of Chapter 2 (or your own model) with a process input “Request”, a process output “Answer”, item definitions for both and a property “Number of reminders” on the task that waits for the reader. Export the BPMN file and find the ioSpecification of the process in it. Performers. Add resources and by= to a process of your own with at least two roles. Compare the result with a version that uses lanes for the same roles. Which version would you give to the head of department, and which to someone who simulates the workload? Annotations and documentation. Take a model from an earlier chapter and add a text annotation with the legal basis of one decision, a group around one stage, and documentation on the header and on two tasks. Explain in two sentences what each addition tells which reader.
