Chapter 7 Checking models In this chapter you will read a diagnostic of tok check and tell its layer, severity and code · repair a model with many errors in the right order · get diagnostics in Polish and as JSON for programs · restrict a model to a level of the language and test it against the conformance classes of BPMN 2.0.2 · keep models in the canonical form with tok fmt · know what a clean check proves about a model and what it does not Writing a model in tok is a short loop: write a few lines, run tok check, read the diagnostics, correct, run it again. The checker is fast enough to run after every change, and the editors of Chapter 12 run it while you type. This chapter explains what it checks, how to read what it reports, and how far its verdict goes. 7.1 What tok check does tok check FILE reads the document, checks it, and prints one line per problem, followed by a summary: tok check 07-registry-error.tok 07-registry-error.tok:24: error R001: identifier 'unit' is already used on line 9 07-registry-error.tok: 1 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) Every line has the same parts: Part Example Meaning file and line 07-registry-error.tok:24 where to look; editors and terminals make this a link to the line severity error how serious the problem is code R001 a stable identifier of the kind of problem; the same problem always has the same code, in every language of the messages and in every release 1.x message identifier 'unit' is already used on line 9 what is wrong, with the identifiers concerned The exit code of tok check is 1 when the document has errors and 0 otherwise, so scripts and continuous integration can use it directly. Appendix D lists every code with its message. The other commands check the document too. tok fmt, tok bpmn, tok svg and tok export refuse to work on a document with errors: they print the same diagnostics and exit with code 1. Warnings and notes do not stop them. 7.1.1 Severities Severity Meaning What you do error the document breaks a rule of the language or of BPMN 2.0.2; no valid BPMN file can be made from it correct it, always warning the document is valid, but it very probably contains a mistake: an unreachable task, a branch without a condition, an escalation nobody catches correct it, or keep it deliberately and be able to say why note a convention of good style: a gateway whose name is not a question, a task without a name consider it A model is finished when it has no errors and every warning that remains has a reason you can state. 7.2 Layers and codes The first letter of a code tells which layer of the checker reported it: Letter Layer Examples T tokens and lines a tab in the indentation (T002), an unclosed string (T001) P statements an unknown keyword (P001), a malformed attribute (P007), a malformed row of a decision table (P009) R references and structure of the document an identifier used twice (R001), a reference to an unknown element (R002), a message flow inside one pool (R022) D decision tables and relations a rule with the wrong number of cells (D002), rules that overlap under the hit policy unique (D010) F FEEL expressions a syntax error (F002) M forms an unknown field type (M001) S simulation parameters an invalid distribution (S001) C the executable profile for Camunda 8 a script task without an expression (C040), an element Camunda does not execute (C100–C132) E, W, L the rules of BPMN 2.0.2: errors, warnings and style notes a message flow to a gateway (E009), a join of another type than its split (W051), a splitting gateway without a question (L020) The layers T to S work on the text: their diagnostics point to the line where the problem is written. The C layer applies only to documents marked executable (Chapter 10). The last layer works on the model itself: tok exports the document to BPMN 2.0 in memory and checks the result against the rules of the specification. Its diagnostics name the element or flow concerned in parentheses, with the identifier tok derived for it, such as f-urgent-file for the flow from urgent to file. 7.2.1 The order of the layers and cascades The layers run in order. If the text cannot be read, or an identifier is used twice, there is no point in checking references: every reference to the duplicated identifier would be ambiguous. tok then reports only the first problems. Likewise, the BPMN rules are checked only when the tok layers report no error, because the model they check is the export of the document. As a result, fixing one error can reveal others. The following model of registering incoming letters at a university contains mistakes on every layer. tok 1.0 "Registering incoming letters" pool university "University" lane registry "Registry office" start received "Letter received" message="Letter" user register "Register the letter" form=f-register rule assign "Assign the responsible unit" decision=unit xor urgent "Urgency" lane unit "Responsible unit" user file "File the letter for later" user handle "Handle the case" priority-level=high boundary deadline "14 days passed" timer=P14D user reply "Prepare the reply" end done "Case closed" pool sender "Sender" flow received -> register -> assign -> urgent flow urgent -> handle "urgent" when="urgency = = \"high\"" flow urgent -> fiel flow file -> handle -> reply -> done flow deadline -> reply message done -> register "Reply" decision unit "Responsible unit" requires="kind" hit=unique | kind: string || unit: string | | "complaint" || "Rector's office" | | "application" || "Student affairs" | inputdata kind "Kind of letter" type=string Download the model with errors (.tok) The first run reports one error, shown above: the decision table and the lane are both called unit. Identifiers are unique in the whole document, not only among elements of one kind. After renaming the decision to responsible-unit (on line 24 and in decision= on line 7), the checker gets further and reports much more: tok check 07-registry-error.tok 07-registry-error.tok:6: error R002: unknown form 'f-register' 07-registry-error.tok:11: warning R010: unknown attribute 'priority-level' on user 07-registry-error.tok:12: error R032: boundary event 'deadline' needs on=ACTIVITY 07-registry-error.tok:18: error F002: FEEL syntax error: unexpected '=' 07-registry-error.tok:19: error R002: unknown flow node 'fiel' 07-registry-error.tok:22: error R022: message flow done -> register must connect two different pools 07-registry-error.tok: 5 error(s), 1 warning(s), 0 note(s) These are independent mistakes of the text: a form that does not exist (forms are described in Chapter 10; here the attribute is simply removed), an attribute tok does not know, a boundary event without its activity, a doubled = in a condition, a typing error in an identifier and a message flow between two elements of the same pool. After correcting all of them, the document reaches the BPMN rules for the first time: tok check 07-registry-error.tok 07-registry-error.tok:8: note L020: name of a splitting gateway is not a question (urgent) 07-registry-error.tok:19: warning W021: branch of an XOR/OR split without label, condition or default status (f-urgent-file) 07-registry-error.tok:22: error E009: message flow to a gateway, data or a non-message event (m-done-sender) 07-registry-error.tok: 1 error(s), 1 warning(s), 1 note(s) The message flow now connects the two pools, but it leaves an end event that sends nothing: a message flow belongs to a message event or a task, so the end event needs message="Reply". The gateway “Urgency” is not a question, and one of its branches has neither a label nor a condition. The corrected model: tok 1.0 "Registering incoming letters" pool university "University" lane registry "Registry office" start received "Letter received" message="Letter" user register "Register the letter" rule assign "Assign the responsible unit" decision=responsible-unit xor urgent "Is the letter urgent?" lane unit "Responsible unit" user file "File the letter for later" user handle "Handle the case" boundary deadline "14 days passed" on=handle timer=P14D user reply "Prepare the reply" end done "Reply sent" message="Reply" pool sender "Sender" flow received -> register -> assign -> urgent flow urgent -> handle "yes" when="urgency = \"high\"" flow urgent -> file "no" default flow file -> handle -> reply -> done flow deadline -> reply message sender -> received "Letter" message done -> sender "Reply" inputdata kind "Kind of letter" type=string decision responsible-unit "Responsible unit" requires="kind" hit=unique | kind: string || unit: string | | "complaint" || "Rector's office" | | "application" || "Student affairs" | Figure 7.1: The registry model after all corrections. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) The cascade suggests a way of working: Start with the first error, and with the lowest layer. T and P before R, R before the rest. Run tok check again after each correction. The list can change more than you expect, in both directions. Errors first, then warnings, then notes. Read the message, not only the code. It names the element and often the correction: needs on=ACTIVITY. Do not delete an element only to silence a message. If the step exists in the real process, correct the way it is written. 7.2.2 Messages in Polish --lang pl prints the messages in Polish; the environment variable TOK_LANG=pl does the same for every command. The codes do not change: tok check 07-registry-error.tok --lang pl 07-registry-error.tok:24: błąd R001: identyfikator „unit” jest już użyty w wierszu 9 07-registry-error.tok: błędy 1, ostrzeżenia 0, uwagi 0 7.2.3 Diagnostics for programs --json prints the diagnostics as JSON, for editors, scripts and AI agents: tok check 07-registry-error.tok --json { "file": "07-registry-error.tok", "errors": 1, "bpmn_class": "full", "diagnostics": [ { "code": "R001", "severity": "error", "line": 24, "id": "unit", "message": "identifier 'unit' is already used on line 9" } ] } Each diagnostic has its code, severity (error, warning or note), line, the identifier id of the element concerned and the message. bpmn_class is the smallest conformance class of BPMN 2.0.2 the document fits (see below). A program does not have to parse the text of the messages: the code and the identifier say what is wrong and where. This is the form the agents of Chapter 14 work with. tok fmt, tok bpmn, tok svg and tok export also accept --json; for a document with errors they print an object with the file, the number of errors and the diagnostics instead of the text report. 7.3 The BPMN rules The E, W and L codes come from the BPMN 2.0.2 specification. Every rule the checker enforces is tied to a clause of the specification; Appendix E gives the clauses. Some rules are checked earlier, in the text, where tok can point to the exact line: a message flow inside one pool is R022 rather than E008, a duplicate identifier R001 rather than E003. Area What is checked Codes identifiers and references identifiers are unique, ASCII and refer to existing elements of the right kind R001–R004, E003, E004, E018 sequence flows they connect flow nodes of one process or sub-process; no flow into a start event or out of an end event; a default flow has no condition; a parallel gateway has no conditions; no flow written twice or from an element back to itself; a task or an event splits only through conditions or a gateway R021, E005, E006, E011, E015, E017, W023, W043 message flows they connect two different pools, and end at a message event, a task, a sub-process or a pool R022, E007–E009, W054 events each trigger only in the positions BPMN allows; boundary events attached to activities; error boundary events interrupting; event sub-processes without sequence flows; an event with several triggers is reported, since the bpmn.io linters reject it E010, E012, E013, R032, R060, R062, W047 activities and handlers compensation handlers without sequence flows; ad-hoc sub-processes without start and end events, every other sub-process with its own; loop attributes only on loops R050, R051, E014, R061, R063, R065, W045, W046 gateways an event-based gateway followed only by catching events or receive tasks; a split joined by a gateway of the same type; an inclusive split with a default; next to a default flow, every other branch has a condition E016, W016, W020, W021, W022, W050, W051 reachability every process has a start and an end; every element can be reached from a start and leads to an end W040–W042 lanes a node in at most one lane; in a pool with lanes, every node in a lane E030, R030, W030, W031 escalations and errors what a boundary event of a sub-process catches is thrown inside it; a thrown escalation is caught somewhere W052, W053 data associations connect data with activities or events; a state transition changes the state R003, R064 style splitting gateways ask a question; a gateway either splits or joins; tasks have names L020, L021, L030 The style notes L are conventions of good modelling, not rules of BPMN. A model with notes is valid BPMN; the notes help the reader. 7.3.1 BPMN files from other tools The same rules check a BPMN 2.0 XML file drawn in Camunda Modeler, bpmn.io or any other tool, or written by an agent: give tok check the .bpmn file. Each finding names the element and the line of the file where it is defined. tok check order.bpmn # the BPMN rules tok check order.bpmn --steps --steps-from process.md # and the step numbers of a description tok check order.bpmn --camunda # and the Camunda 8 profile of executable models tok bpmn order.bpmn # a fresh diagram layout, written into the file tok svg order.bpmn # the picture of its diagram --steps asks for element names that start with the step number of a process description (12. Request for quotation); --steps-from reads the steps from the table of the description and reports those without an element. The codes of BPMN files are in Appendix D. An agent that writes BPMN XML instead of tok uses these commands through the skill bpmn-modelling (Chapter 14). 7.4 Levels of the language --level restricts the elements tok check accepts to a level of the language. Chapter 3 introduced the three levels: basic (plain events, the core tasks and gateways, pools, lanes, data, notes), analytic (all of BPMN apart from the executable layer, forms, decisions and the advanced elements of languages 0.5 and 0.6), and full, the default. Each element beyond the level is the error R040: tok check 07-registry.tok --level analytic 07-registry.tok:7: error R040: 'rule' is not available at level analytic 07-registry.tok:27: error R040: 'inputdata' is not available at level analytic 07-registry.tok: 2 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) tok check 05-book-pickup.tok --level basic 05-book-pickup.tok:7: error R040: 'boundary' is not available at level basic 05-book-pickup.tok:14: error R040: 'boundary' is not available at level basic 05-book-pickup.tok:15: error R040: 'boundary' is not available at level basic 05-book-pickup.tok: 3 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) The registry model needs full because it contains a decision (the elements of a decision model are reported once, at the first of them); the book pick-up of Chapter 5 passes at the level analytic but not basic. Levels are an agreement about the readers of a model: a team can require that models for management stay at the level basic, and a course can introduce the language level by level. They are also a guard for an AI agent that should not use constructs beyond the task. 7.5 BPMN conformance classes The BPMN 2.0.2 specification (clause 2) defines its own sub-classes of process modelling. They say which elements a tool must support to claim conformance, and therefore which elements a model may use to be readable in tools of that class: Class Contains descriptive the visible elements of high-level modelling: tasks, sub-processes, call activities, exclusive and parallel gateways, none and message start and end events, timer start events, terminate end events, data objects and stores, pools and lanes, annotations, groups analytic descriptive and about half of the rest: conditions and default flows, intermediate events with message, timer, signal, conditional, escalation and link triggers, boundary events with message, timer, signal, conditional and error triggers, inclusive and event-based gateways, send and receive tasks, loops and multi-instance common-executable what an executable process needs: data inputs and outputs, item definitions, operations, but no pools, lanes or message flows, so it is not a superset of the other two full the whole modelling language, including transactions, compensation, script, business rule and manual tasks, event sub-processes, conversations and choreographies tok check --class CLASS reports every element outside the chosen class as the error R075, naming the BPMN element and the first class that contains it: tok check 05-book-pickup.tok --class descriptive 05-book-pickup.tok:7: error R075: 'save-failed' (boundary error event) is outside the BPMN conformance class descriptive; it belongs to the class analytic 05-book-pickup.tok:14: error R075: 'three-days' (non-interrupting boundary timer event) is outside the BPMN conformance class descriptive; it belongs to the class analytic 05-book-pickup.tok:15: error R075: 'seven-days' (boundary timer event) is outside the BPMN conformance class descriptive; it belongs to the class analytic 05-book-pickup.tok: 3 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) tok check --json always reports the smallest class the document fits as "bpmn_class". For the models of the previous chapters: Model bpmn_class Why 05-book-pickup analytic boundary events 07-unformatted analytic a non-interrupting boundary timer 05-trip-booking full a transaction 06-purchase-proposal full states of data objects 08-document-delivery full a manual task The last two rows are worth noticing. BPMN puts data states and manual tasks outside its sub-classes, so a model that uses them is in the full class, even though both are simple to draw and to read. --class analytic tells you exactly which elements are responsible: tok check 06-purchase-proposal.tok --class analytic 06-purchase-proposal.tok:14: error R075: 'proposal' (dataState) is outside the BPMN conformance class analytic; it belongs to the class full 06-purchase-proposal.tok:15: error R075: 'proposal-checked' (dataState) is outside the BPMN conformance class analytic; it belongs to the class full 06-purchase-proposal.tok:16: error R075: 'order-lines' (dataObject isCollection, itemSubjectRef) is outside the BPMN conformance class analytic; it belongs to the class common-executable 06-purchase-proposal.tok: 3 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) Levels and classes answer different questions. A level is an agreement about the language you write in: what a reader of the model is expected to understand. A class is a property of the BPMN file: which tools are guaranteed to read it. Use --class when a model has to travel to a tool that supports only part of BPMN, or when a call for tenders or a standard requires a conformance class. Appendix E lists the class of every construct of tok. 7.6 The canonical form A valid model can be written in many ways: with different indentation and spacing, attributes in any order, flows as separate lines or as chains, flows next to the nodes or at the end. tok fmt prints every valid document in exactly one way, its canonical form: the header; item definitions and global tasks, then interfaces; flow nodes in the order of declaration, then pools with their lanes and nodes; data at the end of the block it was declared in; sequence flows in the order of declaration, joined into chains where a chain is unambiguous; message flows; correlation keys; reads and writes; notes and groups; decisions; forms; simulation statements; two spaces of indentation, one space between tokens, labels always quoted, attributes in a fixed order, a blank line between sections. Comments are kept. A comment line belongs to the statement after it and moves with it; a comment at the end of a line stays at the end of that statement’s line. The following model is valid but written carelessly: flows next to the nodes, extra spaces, attributes in another order. tok 1.0 "Renewing a loan" # the reader asks online start asked "Renewal requested" flow asked -> check user check "Check reservations" xor reserved "Is the book reserved by someone else?" flow check -> reserved flow reserved -> refuse "yes" flow reserved -> renew "no" user renew "Extend the loan" # by 30 days user refuse "Refuse the renewal" end renewed "Loan extended" end refused "Renewal refused" flow renew -> renewed flow refuse -> refused boundary late "Two days passed" timer=P2D noninterrupting on=check flow late -> remind service remind "Remind the circulation desk" end reminded "Desk reminded" flow remind -> reminded Download the model (.tok) tok fmt FILE prints the canonical form without changing the file: tok fmt 07-unformatted.tok tok 1.0 "Renewing a loan" # the reader asks online start asked "Renewal requested" user check "Check reservations" xor reserved "Is the book reserved by someone else?" user renew "Extend the loan" # by 30 days user refuse "Refuse the renewal" end renewed "Loan extended" end refused "Renewal refused" boundary late "Two days passed" noninterrupting on=check timer=P2D service remind "Remind the circulation desk" end reminded "Desk reminded" flow asked -> check -> reserved flow reserved -> refuse "yes" flow reserved -> renew "no" flow renew -> renewed flow refuse -> refused flow late -> remind -> reminded Option Effect none prints the canonical form to the standard output -w, --write rewrites the file in its canonical form --check changes nothing; reports whether the file is already canonical (exit code 0) or not (exit code 1) tok fmt --check 07-unformatted.tok 07-unformatted.tok: not in canonical form The canonical form is a matter of order, not of correctness: the careless model and its canonical form are the same model and give the same BPMN file. It matters in practice because two canonical files differ only where their content differs. A change of one condition is then a change of one line in version control, and the review of a change does not drown in reformatting. tok fmt is idempotent (formatting a formatted file changes nothing), it never changes the version in the header, and it removes the deprecation warning R090 by keeping only the last of a repeated attribute. Run tok fmt -w before you commit a model or hand it over, and tok fmt --check in continuous integration (Chapter 15). 7.7 Typical errors and their corrections Code Typical cause Correction T002 a tab in the indentation, often from copying text indent with spaces; editors can convert tabs T003 a line indented deeper or shallower than any open block align it with the block it belongs to P001 a misspelt keyword (usr, gateway) use a keyword of the language; Appendix B lists them P007 a label after the attributes, or a missing quote write KIND ID "Label" attributes R001 the same identifier for two elements, often a lane and a task, or a decision and a variable rename one of them and the references to it R002 a typing error in a reference correct the identifier; the message quotes it R010 an attribute tok does not know check the spelling; it may belong to another tool R020 a chain of flows with a label or a condition split the chain: one flow per line where a flow has a label R021 a sequence flow into or out of a sub-process block connect to the sub-process itself, or use events R022 a message flow inside one pool use a sequence flow between lanes R030, R031 a node outside every lane of a pool, or outside every pool move it into a lane or a pool R032 a boundary event without on= add the activity it is attached to F002 a FEEL syntax error, often = =, a missing quote or an unclosed parenthesis correct the expression; remember that tok writes FEEL without a leading = E009 a message flow to a gateway or from a plain event connect it to a task or give the event a message trigger E010 a trigger in a position BPMN does not allow, or an intermediate catch event without a trigger see the table of triggers in Chapter 5 E015 when= and default on the same flow a default flow has no condition W021 a branch of a split without label or condition label every branch with the answer to the gateway’s question W022 a branch without a condition next to a default flow give every other branch its condition (when="…", or when="" until it is known) W023, W043 a flow written twice, or a flow from an element back to itself delete the copy; repeat an activity with loop or with a gateway W044 a task or an event with several outgoing flows and no gateway: all of them are taken split with an and gateway, or give the flows conditions behind an xor W045, W046 a sub-process without its own start or end event give the block of the sub its start and end W041, W042 an element that cannot be reached, or a path that does not end add the missing flow or end event W051 a parallel split joined by an exclusive gateway, or the reverse join with the same type of gateway 7.8 What a clean check means A clean check, 0 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s), means that the document is a valid tok document, that its BPMN export follows the rules of BPMN 2.0.2 that tok enforces, and that it avoids the common modelling mistakes that the warnings detect. It also means that every BPMN tool will open the exported file, and that its diagram will be drawn. It does not mean that the model is right about the process. The checker knows the rules of the notation, not the work of your registry office. Consider the book pick-up of Chapter 5. If the seven-day deadline is written with one more word, boundary seven-days "7 days passed" noninterrupting on=pickup timer=P7D the model is still valid, and tok check still reports no errors, no warnings and no notes. But it now says that the library sends the book back to the lending library while the reader can still pick it up. Only someone who knows the process can see that this is wrong. The same holds for every other choice the notation leaves to you: whether a step is a user task or a manual task, whether a message goes to the right participant, whether a condition uses the right variable, whether the decision table gives the answers the regulation requires, whether a step is missing altogether. To check a model against the real process: Read it with the people who do the work. Walk through the diagram case by case: the normal case, the exceptions, the case that happens once a year. Keep a mapping between the source of the model (an interview, a regulation, a table of steps) and its elements, and check that every row of the source is in the model and every element has a source. Test the decisions with tok eval and real cases (Chapter 9). Simulate the process (Chapter 11): a simulation shows where cases queue, which paths are never taken and which end events are never reached. A clean check is the beginning of a review, not its end. Exercises Exercise 7.1 The registry, step by step. Download 07-registry-error.tok and repair it yourself, running tok check after every change. Write down how many diagnostics each run reports and from which layer. Compare your result with 07-registry.tok. Download the model with errors (.tok) A study room. The model 07-study-room-error.tok has mistakes on the layers T, P, R and E, and style problems. Correct it until the check is clean, and explain for each code what was wrong. Download the model with errors (.tok) JSON for a script. Run tok check --json on a model with errors and write a short script (in any language) that prints only the codes and lines of the errors, sorted by line. Levels and classes. Check three models of the previous chapters with --level basic, --level analytic, --class descriptive and --class analytic, and record the bpmn_class of each. For one model in the class full, write a version in the class analytic and say what information the change removes. Canonical form. Rewrite one of your models by hand in a careless way (different spacing, attributes in another order, flows next to the nodes) and check that tok fmt --check rejects it. Format it with tok fmt -w and compare the result with the original using diff or your version control. Valid but wrong. Take a clean model of your own and make three changes that keep it valid but make it wrong about the process (for example, a timer that should interrupt but does not, a message sent to the wrong pool, two branch labels swapped). Give the model to a colleague and ask them to find the changes by reading the diagram.

Chapter 8 Layout, export and import In this chapter you will draw a model with the automatic layout of tok · write BPMN 2.0 XML with and without diagram information, SVG pictures and the complete set of files of a model · open the exported files in Camunda Modeler and bpmn.io · import BPMN and DMN files drawn in other tools and read what the import reports · keep the drawing of an imported model in the layout sidecar and change the model without losing it · keep models and sidecars in version control A tok document contains no coordinates. It says that “Check the copyright limits” comes after “Request received”, not that it stands 120 units to the right of it. This is a deliberate choice: the text is the model, and every picture and every file is a projection of it, produced by the tools. A model that has no coordinates cannot have a crooked line, an overlapping label or a shape that someone forgot to move. Two people who change the same model do not fight over the positions of boxes. And an AI agent that writes a model does not have to compute a drawing. The other side of the choice is that tok has to draw the model itself, and that a drawing made in a graphical editor has to be kept somewhere when such a model comes into tok. This chapter covers both directions. 8.1 The automatic layout Every command that produces a picture or a BPMN file computes a layout from the structure of the model: The process flows from left to right. Each element is placed in a column after the elements before it, and parallel branches take separate rows. Pools are stacked from top to bottom in the order of the document, and lanes inside a pool likewise; a black-box pool is drawn as a band without content. A sub-process is drawn expanded, with its content inside its border; an event sub-process inside its parent, with a dotted border. Boundary events sit on the lower border of their activity. Their paths leave downwards. Data objects and data stores are placed below the activities that read or write them; process inputs below the start of the process. Message flows are dashed lines between pools, routed through the gaps between the pools, with the name of the message. Text annotations are placed near the element they explain. The layout is deterministic: the same document always gives the same drawing, so a picture in a report can be produced again at any time. The layout does not draw groups, because their members do not form a rectangle in general; a group gets its shape from a layout sidecar (below). The following model of a document delivery service is drawn entirely by the automatic layout. tok 1.0 "Document delivery" pool reader "Reader" start need "Article needed" send request "Request a scan" message="Scan request" eventgw reply "What comes back?" catch scan "Scan received" message="Scan" catch refusal "Refusal received" message="Refusal" manual read "Read the article" end done "Article read" end gave-up "Article not obtained" pool library "University library" lane desk "Document delivery desk" start received "Request received" message="Scan request" user check "Check the copyright limits" xor allowed "Is copying allowed?" send deliver "Send the scan" message="Scan" end delivered "Scan delivered" end refused "Request refused" message="Refusal" lane stacks "Stacks staff" user fetch "Fetch the volume" user digitise "Scan the pages" flow need -> request -> reply flow reply -> scan flow reply -> refusal flow scan -> read -> done flow refusal -> gave-up flow received -> check -> allowed flow allowed -> fetch "yes" flow allowed -> refused "no" flow fetch -> digitise -> deliver -> delivered message request -> received "Scan request" message deliver -> scan "Scan" message refused -> refusal "Refusal" Figure 8.1: The automatic layout: two pools, two lanes, an event-based gateway and three message flows. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) If you do not like how the automatic layout draws a model, the first thing to change is usually the model. The order of the statements can change the order of parallel rows; a long chain of elements in one lane may be clearer split into a sub-process; a path that crosses the whole diagram may be shorter with a pair of link events (Chapter 5). 8.2 Pictures: tok svg tok svg FILE writes a picture of the diagram as SVG, a vector format that every web browser shows and every word processor and presentation program can insert. Without -o the picture is written next to the model, with the same name: tok svg 08-document-delivery.tok SVG: 08-document-delivery.svg -o OUT.svg (or --output) names the file. The picture uses the symbols of BPMN 2.0, as Appendix A shows them. Every diagram in this book was made with tok svg. A model with errors has no picture: tok svg prints the diagnostics and exits with code 1. Warnings do not prevent the picture. 8.3 BPMN files: tok bpmn tok bpmn FILE writes the model as BPMN 2.0 XML, with a diagram (the BPMN DI part of the file) computed by the automatic layout: tok bpmn 08-document-delivery.tok BPMN: 08-document-delivery.bpmn The file begins like this: <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <bpmn:definitions xmlns:bpmn="http://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/20100524/MODEL" ... id="definitions" name="Document delivery" targetNamespace="http://bpmn.io/schema/bpmn" exporter="tok" exporterVersion="1.0"> <bpmn:message id="Message_Scan_request" name="Scan request" /> <bpmn:message id="Message_Scan" name="Scan" /> <bpmn:message id="Message_Refusal" name="Refusal" /> <bpmn:collaboration id="collaboration"> <bpmn:participant id="reader" name="Reader" processRef="reader-process" /> <bpmn:participant id="library" name="University library" processRef="library-process" /> <bpmn:messageFlow id="m-request-received" name="Scan request" sourceRef="request" targetRef="received" messageRef="Message_Scan_request" /> ... A few things are worth knowing about this file: The identifiers of the elements are the identifiers of the document. A pool reader is the participant reader and its process reader-process (or the identifier given with process=). Sequence flows get the identifiers f-SOURCE-TARGET, message flows m-SOURCE-TARGET, unless id= gives another. Because the identifiers are stable, a process engine, a report or a mining tool can refer to an element by the same name across versions of the model. Messages, signals, errors and escalations, which tok declares implicitly by name, are written as separate declarations, as BPMN requires. exporterVersion is the language version of the document, here 1.0. In a document marked executable, the file carries the extension attributes of Camunda 8 (Chapter 10). --no-layout writes the semantic model only, without the diagram. Such a file is smaller and is what a process engine or an analysis tool needs; most modelling tools draw a file without a diagram poorly or not at all, so keep the layout for files that people will open. 8.4 Everything at once: tok export tok export FILE writes every file the model produces: the BPMN file, its SVG picture, the decision files (Chapter 9) and one Camunda form file per form (Chapter 10). -o FOLDER names the output folder; without it, the files go next to the model. The command lists what it wrote: tok export 09-purchase-approval.tok -o out out\09-purchase-approval.bpmn out\09-purchase-approval.svg out\approval-mode.dmn out\approval-mode.drd.svg (The paths are printed with the separator of your system; this listing comes from Windows.) The process of Chapter 9 gives four files: the BPMN process, its picture, the DMN file of its decision model and the picture of the decision requirements diagram. A document of language 1.0 that has only decisions writes only the DMN files and their pictures. Command Writes tok svg FILE [-o OUT.svg] the picture tok bpmn FILE [-o OUT.bpmn] [--no-layout] the BPMN file, with or without diagram tok export FILE [-o FOLDER] BPMN, SVG, DMN files with their pictures, form files All three read the layout sidecar of the document when there is one, and accept --no-sidecar to ignore it. All three refuse a document with errors. 8.5 Opening the files in BPMN tools The BPMN files of tok open in the common BPMN tools. Two are worth knowing: bpmn.io is the open-source modeller in the browser, at https://demo.bpmn.io. Drag the .bpmn file onto the page. It is the quickest way to show a model to someone who has no tools installed. Camunda Modeler is the desktop application built on bpmn.io, with the properties panels of Camunda 8. Open the .bpmn file with File → Open File; the .dmn and .form files written by tok export open the same way. Both show the diagram computed by tok and let you inspect every element: its identifier, its name, its documentation (doc=), and in Camunda Modeler the execution properties of an executable model. You can also edit the model there. If you do, the drawing is the tool’s and the text is not updated: to bring the change back into the tok document, import the edited file (next section). Decide in a team which side is the source of a model. Most teams that use tok keep the text as the source and use the graphical tools to show and to inspect. 8.6 Importing BPMN files tok import FILE.bpmn reads a BPMN 2.0 XML file and prints the same model as tok text. It is the way to bring existing models into tok: a collection of diagrams drawn over the years in Camunda Modeler, a model received from a consultant, a reference model of a standard. Suppose a colleague has drawn the booking of a reading room seat in a graphical editor and sent you the file 08-drawn-elsewhere.bpmn (Download the drawn file (.bpmn)). Without -o, the text is printed on the standard output and the import’s remarks on the standard error: tok import 08-drawn-elsewhere.bpmn 08-drawn-elsewhere.bpmn: Group_0alloc7: group membership is not stored in BPMN; add members="…" by hand 08-drawn-elsewhere.bpmn: Activity_1check3: attribute {http://camunda.org/schema/1.0/bpmn}assignee was skipped tok 0.1 "Booking a reading room seat" id=Definitions_0r7k2m1 collaboration=Collaboration_1x4d9qa pool Participant_0lib8rr "City library" process=Process_1seat42 lane Lane_0reader1 "Reader" start Event_0asked1 "Seat needed" user Activity_0ask1ab "Ask for a seat" lane Lane_1staff22 "Reading room staff" user Activity_1check3 "Check free seats" xor Gateway_0free5k "Is a seat free?" user Activity_0assign "Assign a seat" user Activity_1offer9 "Offer another day" end Event_1booked7 "Seat booked" end Event_0other88 "Other day offered" flow Event_0asked1 -> Activity_0ask1ab id=Flow_0s1t2a3 flow Activity_0ask1ab -> Activity_1check3 id=Flow_1a2b3c4 flow Activity_1check3 -> Gateway_0free5k id=Flow_0c4d5e6 flow Gateway_0free5k -> Activity_0assign "yes" id=Flow_1yes123 flow Gateway_0free5k -> Activity_1offer9 "no" id=Flow_0no4567 flow Activity_0assign -> Event_1booked7 id=Flow_1e2n3d4 flow Activity_1offer9 -> Event_0other88 id=Flow_0o9t8h7 note TextAnnotation_0note1x "Seats can be booked up to 7 days ahead" on=Gateway_0free5k group Group_0alloc7 "Seat allocation" 8.6.1 What is kept The import keeps the structure of the model, the names, the documentation and the identifiers. Identifiers matter beyond tok: under them the model may already be known to a process engine, a report or another system. Graphical editors generate identifiers such as Activity_0ask1ab, and the import keeps them as they are. An identifier that is not a valid tok identifier (with spaces or non-ASCII letters, or starting with a digit) is converted, every reference to it is rewritten, and each conversion is reported. The header carries what tok needs to write the same file back: id= and collaboration= give the identifiers of the definitions and collaboration elements when they differ from the defaults, and the pool keeps the identifier of its process with process=. The import writes the oldest language version that expresses what it read: tok 0.1 for this model, 0.3 for a model with Camunda execution attributes, 0.5 or 0.6 for the elements added in those versions. Each of these headers is a valid document of every release 1.x with the same meaning; change the header to tok 1.0 when you start to extend the model. A sequence flow keeps its identifier with id= when it differs from the identifier tok would derive. Drawn models usually have identifiers like Flow_0s1t2a3, so every flow gets its own line. --no-flow-ids drops these identifiers, and the flows print as compact chains: flow Event_0asked1 -> Activity_0ask1ab -> Activity_1check3 -> Gateway_0free5k flow Gateway_0free5k -> Activity_0assign "yes" flow Gateway_0free5k -> Activity_1offer9 "no" flow Activity_0assign -> Event_1booked7 flow Activity_1offer9 -> Event_0other88 Use it when nothing outside the model refers to the flows. Default flows are kept either way, because tok records them with the flag default. 8.6.2 What is reported Everything the import does not keep is reported: each element, attribute, extension or piece of documentation that tok cannot express is named on the standard error, an extension attribute of another tool once per document. In the example, the group lost its members (BPMN does not store them) and an attribute of Camunda 7 was skipped. Other things commonly reported are: Reported Why extension elements and attributes of other tools (Camunda 7, Signavio, Trisotech, …) tok keeps only the extensions of Camunda 8 isImmediate, implementation, startQuantity, completionQuantity and other attributes without a tok equivalent they have no tok attribute documentation of elements that have no doc= in tok, further documentation elements, formats other than plain text tok keeps one plain text per element lanes inside a sub-process the nodes stay in the sub-process messages, signals, errors and data stores that no element uses tok declares them through their use line breaks in names a label is one line; they become spaces Read the report: it tells you exactly what the text does not contain. Then run tok check on the result. An imported model may break rules that its editor did not enforce (a node in a pool with lanes but in no lane is kept in the pool and reported by tok check as R030), and the check is the moment to correct them. The import reads a file with several collaborations by merging them into one, takes a process that no participant references into a new pool, and refuses files nested more than 64 levels deep, far beyond what modelling tools write. 8.7 The layout sidecar With -o, the import writes the text into a file and the drawing of the original file into a second file next to it, the layout sidecar FILE.tok.layout: tok import 08-drawn-elsewhere.bpmn -o 08-imported.tok --no-flow-ids 08-drawn-elsewhere.bpmn: Group_0alloc7: group membership is not stored in BPMN; add members="…" by hand 08-drawn-elsewhere.bpmn: Activity_1check3: attribute {http://camunda.org/schema/1.0/bpmn}assignee was skipped tok: 08-imported.tok layout: 08-imported.tok.layout The sidecar is a plain text file. Its first line is tok-layout 1; each further line names an element by its tok identifier and gives its geometry in the units of the BPMN file: tok-layout 1 Participant_0lib8rr 160 80 840 350 Lane_0reader1 190 80 810 120 Lane_1staff22 190 200 810 230 Event_0asked1 232 122 36 36 Event_0asked1/label 220 165 60 14 Activity_0ask1ab 320 100 100 80 ... Group_0alloc7 740 195 140 225 f-Event_0asked1-Activity_0ask1ab 268 140 320 140 f-Activity_0ask1ab-Activity_1check3 420 140 450 140 450 290 480 290 ... Line Meaning ID x y w h the bounds of a shape: position of the upper left corner, width, height ID x1 y1 x2 y2 … the waypoints of an edge (a flow or an association) ID/label x y w h the bounds of the label of a shape or an edge Empty lines and lines starting with # are ignored. The flows in this sidecar are named by the identifiers tok derives (f-SOURCE-TARGET), because the import dropped the original identifiers; elements without an identifier of their own, such as the associations of notes, are matched by what they connect. tok bpmn, tok svg and tok export read the sidecar when it exists next to the document, and draw the model as it was drawn: Figure 8.2: The imported model drawn with its layout sidecar: the geometry of the original drawing, including the group. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) The sidecar never changes the meaning of the model. Deleting it gives the automatic layout again; --no-sidecar ignores it for one command; tok import --no-layout does not write it at all. 8.7.1 Changing a model that has a sidecar The point of the sidecar is that the text can be changed while the drawing stays. When the model changes: a shape whose identifier is still in the model keeps its bounds and its label; an edge keeps its waypoints when both of its ends kept their geometry and it still touches them; other edges are routed again; a new shape is placed next to a neighbour that kept its place, at the distance the automatic layout would use, moved aside from other shapes; pools, lanes and sub-processes grow to hold the new content; lines of the sidecar that name elements no longer in the model are ignored. Suppose the library adds a confirmation e-mail after a seat is assigned, and records which elements the group contains: tok 0.1 "Booking a reading room seat" id=Definitions_0r7k2m1 collaboration=Collaboration_1x4d9qa pool Participant_0lib8rr "City library" process=Process_1seat42 lane Lane_0reader1 "Reader" start Event_0asked1 "Seat needed" user Activity_0ask1ab "Ask for a seat" lane Lane_1staff22 "Reading room staff" user Activity_1check3 "Check free seats" xor Gateway_0free5k "Is a seat free?" user Activity_0assign "Assign a seat" service confirm "Send a confirmation e-mail" user Activity_1offer9 "Offer another day" end Event_1booked7 "Seat booked" end Event_0other88 "Other day offered" flow Event_0asked1 -> Activity_0ask1ab -> Activity_1check3 -> Gateway_0free5k flow Gateway_0free5k -> Activity_0assign "yes" flow Gateway_0free5k -> Activity_1offer9 "no" flow Activity_0assign -> confirm -> Event_1booked7 flow Activity_1offer9 -> Event_0other88 note TextAnnotation_0note1x "Seats can be booked up to 7 days ahead" on=Gateway_0free5k group Group_0alloc7 "Seat allocation" members="Activity_0assign Activity_1offer9" If the sidecar is copied unchanged, the end event “Seat booked” keeps its place, and the new task is placed next to it, beyond the end event: the drawing is valid but awkward, because the new step belongs before the end. The remedy is to delete the lines of the end event from the sidecar (Event_1booked7 and Event_1booked7/label). Without a geometry of its own, the end event is placed anew, after the new task: Figure 8.3: The imported model with a new task. The end event was removed from the sidecar and placed again; every other shape keeps the geometry of the original drawing. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) This is the general technique: the sidecar is text, and deleting a line hands one element back to the automatic layout. Deleting the whole file hands back the whole diagram. 8.7.2 The round trip Import is the inverse of export. A document written by tok survives the round trip tok → BPMN → tok unchanged, apart from the header version, which the import sets to the oldest version that expresses the model: tok bpmn 08-document-delivery.tok tok import 08-document-delivery.bpmn -o back.tok back.tok is the text of 08-document-delivery.tok with the header tok 0.1 "Document delivery". A model from another tool keeps its structure, names, identifiers and documentation, and everything else is reported. The evidence for this promise is public. The BPMN Model Interchange Working Group (MIWG) of the OMG maintains a set of reference models that BPMN tools use to test their import and export. tok imports, prints and exports all 22 of them; of their 3770 semantic facts (elements, attributes, references, documentation), 3533 survive the round trip (93.7 %), and every fact that does not survive is reported by the import. Appendix E gives the details per model. 8.8 Importing DMN files tok import FILE.dmn reads a DMN file of version 1.1 to 1.5 and prints a document of language 0.7 (valid in every release 1.x), with its decisions, input data, knowledge sources, business knowledge models, decision logic and types. Like the BPMN import, it reports what it does not keep; the diagram of a DMN file (its DMNDI part) is not kept, because tok lays out the decision requirements diagram again when it exports. Chapter 9 shows an example. 8.9 Models and sidecars in version control A tok model is a text file, and it belongs in version control (Git or any other) like source code. A few practices make this work well: Keep the canonical form. Run tok fmt -w before every commit, or tok fmt --check in continuous integration (Chapter 15). Then a change of one condition is a change of one line, and a review shows what changed in the process, not in the spacing. Commit the sidecar with the model. FILE.tok.layout is plain text, one line per element, and its changes are readable in a diff. A model and its sidecar are one unit: rename them together, move them together. Rename identifiers with care. The sidecar refers to elements by identifier. If you rename Activity_0assign to assign, the element loses its geometry until you rename it in the sidecar too; a search and replace over both files keeps them in step. Lines for identifiers that no longer exist do no harm: they are ignored. Generated files are projections. BPMN, SVG, DMN and form files can always be produced again from the text and the sidecar. Whether to commit them is a decision of the team: commit them when someone needs them without running tok (a web page with the diagram, a deployment of an executable process), and produce them in a build step otherwise. Never edit them by hand: the next export overwrites the change. Use the history. Because the model is text, git log and git blame tell who changed which step of the process and when, and a commit message can say why. This history of the process is often worth as much as the model itself. Exercises Exercise 8.1 Three projections. Export 08-document-delivery.tok with tok svg, tok bpmn and tok bpmn --no-layout. Compare the sizes of the two BPMN files and open both in bpmn.io. What does the tool show for the file without a diagram? Round trip. Take a model of your own, export it with tok bpmn, import the result with tok import, and compare the text with the original. Explain every difference you find. Import a drawing. Draw a small process with a pool, two lanes, a gateway and a text annotation in bpmn.io or Camunda Modeler, save it, and import it with -o. Read the report of the import, run tok check on the result, and draw it with tok svg. Is the drawing the one you made? Extend an imported model. Download 08-drawn-elsewhere.bpmn, import it with -o, and add a step “Send a reminder the day before” after “Assign a seat”. Draw the model with its sidecar. Which lines of the sidecar do you have to delete to obtain a tidy drawing? Download the drawn file (.bpmn) Rename and keep the drawing. In the imported model, rename the identifiers of the tasks to short readable ones (ask, check, assign, offer). Update the sidecar so that the drawing does not change, and check the result with tok svg. A repository of models. Create a Git repository with two models and their sidecars, a rule that every model is in canonical form, and a short README that says how to produce the BPMN files. Make a change to one model and inspect the diff of the model and of its sidecar.
