Chapter 11 Simulation and process mining In this chapter you will add durations, resources, case variables, branch probabilities and arrivals to a model · run tok sim and read its indicators: end events, cycle time, waiting, processing and utilization · compare scenarios with the same seed and with replications · write the event log as CSV and XES and open it in process-mining tools · simulate from R and Python, run large experiments natively in Julia with Tok.Sim and calibrate a model on an event log with Tok.Fit A process model shows what happens and who does it. It does not show how long the work takes when there are many cases and few people. A head of an archive asks questions of exactly that kind: how long do applicants wait for an answer when requests double, would a third archivist shorten the wait or sit idle, what would change if impossible requests were refused at registration? Trying the answers out in practice is expensive: hiring someone or changing a procedure is a decision for months. Simulation answers such questions on the model. The simulator sends hundreds of invented cases through the process, draws working times and decisions from distributions, makes each case wait while the people it needs are busy, and measures what happens. In tok the simulation is not a separate tool with a separate model: the parameters are written into the same .tok file, and the same file still exports the same BPMN. Simulation does not predict the future. It shows the consequences of assumptions. If you assume that a search in the holdings takes six hours on average and in reality it takes ten, the results will be wrong. Every simulation result is therefore reported together with its assumptions, and the last section of this chapter shows how to estimate the assumptions from data. 11.1 The simulation layer Three statements and six attributes make a model simulable: Statement or attribute Meaning simulate cases=N seed=N arrival="DIST" start="DATETIME" the number of cases (default 100), the seed of the random numbers, the time between consecutive arrivals, and the simulated time of the first arrival (default 2027-01-04T08:00) resource ID "Label" count=N a pool of N interchangeable performers variable NAME "DIST" a case variable, drawn once per case when it starts activity by=ID the activity waits for a free performer of resource ID (first come, first served) activity duration="DIST" the processing time; without it, zero activity assign="NAME=DIST; …" variables set when the activity completes, such as a decision a person takes catch event, receive task or message boundary event delay="DIST" the time until the awaited message or signal arrives flow p=NUMBER the probability of the branch at an xor or or gateway without conditions None of them changes the BPMN export: the diagram in Camunda Modeler looks the same with and without them. In a document of language 0.5 or later resource and by= additionally export BPMN resources and performers (Chapter 6); count= stays a simulation setting. 11.1.1 Distributions Working times are never constant. A search in the holdings takes an hour one day and two days the next. Times are therefore written as distributions, which describe how often short and long cases occur. A distribution is a duration (30m), a number, or a call. Durations use the units s, m (minutes), h and d; inside unif, tri, norm, lnorm and exp the arguments are either all durations or all numbers. Call Meaning When to use it Example fixed(x) or x always x the work always takes the same time fixed(15m), 5m tri(a, mode, b) triangular: minimum, most likely, maximum no data, but the people who do the work can name the shortest, the usual and the longest time tri(5m, 10m, 20m) lnorm(mean, sd) log-normal, given by the mean and standard deviation of the result data from a register: most cases are short, a few are very long lnorm(6h, 3h) norm(mean, sd) normal; a negative duration becomes 0 symmetric variation around a mean norm(1h, 10m) exp(mean) exponential with the given mean the time between independent arrivals exp(4h) unif(a, b) uniform between a and b every value of a range is equally likely unif(20, 300) bern(p) true with probability p an event happens or not bern(0.9) cat(a=p, b=q, …) one of the labels with the given probabilities one of several categories cat(genealogical=0.6, property=0.4) Note the parameters of lnorm: they are the mean and standard deviation of the duration itself, not of its logarithm, so you can take them directly from a register. In cat, the labels true, false and numbers become booleans and numbers. assign= sets several variables at once, separated by semicolons: assign="complete=bern(0.9); urgent=bern(0.1)". 11.1.2 Choosing a branch At a splitting gateway the simulator chooses the branch in one of two ways. If the outgoing flows have conditions (when=), it evaluates them on the variables of the case, exactly as an engine would; the first flow in document order whose condition holds is taken, otherwise the default flow. If the flows have probabilities (p=), it draws one. An or gateway activates every flow whose condition holds or whose probability is drawn, each independently. The check watches over both: S002 reports probabilities of an xor gateway that do not sum to 1, S003 a gateway with several outgoing flows and neither conditions nor probabilities in a document with a simulate statement (the simulator would always take the first flow), and S001 an invalid distribution or probability. 11.2 A simulation model A state archive answers genealogical queries. A registry clerk registers each request. One of two archivists assesses it; one request in ten lacks details, the archivist asks the applicant for them, and the applicant answers after three days on average. Fifteen percent of the requests cannot be answered and are refused; the rest are searched for in the holdings and answered. A request arrives every four hours on average. tok 1.0 "Archive queries: workload simulation" pool archive "State archive" lane registry "Registry" start arrived "Query request received" user register "Register the request" by=clerks duration="tri(5m, 10m, 20m)" send refuse "Send a refusal" by=clerks duration="tri(5m, 10m, 15m)" end refused "Request refused" send answer "Send the answer" by=clerks duration="tri(5m, 10m, 15m)" end answered "Query answered" lane archivist "Archivist" user assess "Assess the request" by=archivists duration="lnorm(30m, 10m)" assign="complete=bern(0.9)" xor is-complete "Is the request complete?" send ask "Ask for missing details" by=archivists duration="5m" catch details "Details received" message="Details" delay="exp(3d)" xor feasible "Is the query feasible?" user search "Search the holdings" by=archivists duration="lnorm(6h, 3h)" user write "Write the answer" by=archivists duration="tri(30m, 1h, 2h)" flow arrived -> register -> assess -> is-complete flow is-complete -> feasible "yes" when="complete = true" flow is-complete -> ask "no" default flow ask -> details -> assess flow feasible -> search "yes" p=0.85 flow feasible -> refuse "no" p=0.15 flow refuse -> refused flow search -> write -> answer -> answered simulate cases=300 seed=7 arrival="exp(4h)" resource archivists "Archivists" count=2 resource clerks "Registry clerks" count=1 Figure 11.1: Archive queries: the model with its simulation parameters. The diagram is the same as without them. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) The model combines both ways of choosing a branch. The assessment sets the variable complete with assign="complete=bern(0.9)", and the gateway is-complete tests it with a condition, as an executable model would. The gateway feasible has no data to decide on, so it draws with p=0.85 and p=0.15. The catch event details waits for the applicant with delay="exp(3d)", and the case then goes back to the assessment, which draws complete again. 11.3 Running tok sim tok sim 11-archive-queries.tok Simulation (seed 7): 300 cases started, 300 finished End events answered 253 84.3% refused 47 15.7% Cycle time: mean 1.2 d, median 19.1 h, 90th percentile 2.3 d Activities (count, mean wait, mean processing) Register the request 300 48 s 11.7 min Assess the request 343 4.5 h 29.7 min Search the holdings 253 4.5 h 5.7 h Write the answer 253 4.4 h 1.2 h Send the answer 253 32 s 9.8 min Send a refusal 47 33 s 9.7 min Ask for missing details 43 3.1 h 5.0 min Resources (utilization) Archivists x2 77.5% Registry clerks x1 8.7% The run uses the 300 cases and the seed 7 of the simulate statement. --cases N and --seed N override them for one run, --lang pl prints the report in Polish and --json prints the indicators as JSON for programs. 11.4 Reading the indicators Indicator What it means In the example end events how many cases ended at each end event 84% answered, 16% refused (the model assumes 15%; the difference is the luck of the draw) cycle time the time from the arrival of a case to its end 1.2 days on average median half of the cases took less, half took more 19.1 hours 90th percentile nine cases in ten ended within this time 2.3 days count completed instances of the activity 343 assessments for 300 requests: 43 were assessed twice mean wait how long a case waited for a free performer before the activity about 4.5 hours before each task of the archivists mean processing how long the work itself took 5.7 hours of search utilization the busy time of a resource divided by its count times the simulated period archivists 77.5%, clerk 8.7% The most important finding is in the waiting column. Before each of the three main tasks of the archivists a case waits about four and a half hours, more than thirteen hours in total, while the work itself takes about seven. The bottleneck of the process is the archivists, not the registry. The clerk, busy less than a tenth of the time, could take on more work. The utilization can be checked by hand, which is a good habit before you trust any simulation. Per request the archivists spend about 0.57 hours on assessments (343 assessments of 29.7 minutes for 300 requests), a little on asking for details, and for the 84% of requests that are answered about 5.7 + 1.2 hours on search and writing: roughly 6.4 hours in total. With a request every four hours and two archivists, they are busy about 6.4 / (2 × 4) ≈ 80% of the time; the simulation gives 77.5%, because its simulated period also includes the time after the last arrival, while the last cases are finished. What the arithmetic cannot tell you is how long the queues are. That is what the simulation adds: at 80% utilization, every cluster of arrivals builds a queue that takes long to clear. The gap between the median (19.1 h) and the mean (1.2 d) has a second cause, which the model makes visible: the requests that wait three days for missing details. They are few, but long, and they pull the mean and the 90th percentile up. For an applicant the predictability of the answer matters as much as its average, which is why reports give percentiles and not only the mean. 11.5 Seeds, cases and replications The simulator draws all its random numbers from one generator seeded with seed=. The same document and the same seed always give the same log and the same indicators, number by number, on the command line, in Python, in R and in the playground, because all of them run the same engine. A result in a report can therefore be checked by anyone who has the file. A seed does not make two scenarios draw the same cases, however. When you change the number of performers, activities finish in another order and the following draws fall to other cases. This is why the share of refusals differs between runs although the model of refusals is the same. Compare scenarios by indicators over hundreds of cases, never by the fate of single cases, and when the differences are small, by several replications: runs with different seeds whose results you average. A short Python script (Chapter 13) does this for two, three and four archivists, with twenty seeds each: from statistics import mean from tok import api text = open("11-archive-queries.tok", encoding="utf-8").read() for n in (2, 3, 4): model = text.replace('count=2', 'count=%d' % n, 1) runs = [api.simulate(model, cases=300, seed=s).kpi() for s in range(1, 21)] cycle = mean(k["cycle_time"]["mean_s"] for k in runs) / 3600 p90 = mean(k["cycle_time"]["p90_s"] for k in runs) / 3600 busy = mean(k["resources"]["archivists"]["utilization"] for k in runs) print("%d archivists: mean cycle %.1f h, p90 %.1f h, utilization %.0f%%" % (n, cycle, p90, 100 * busy)) 2 archivists: mean cycle 26.4 h, p90 47.1 h, utilization 73% 3 archivists: mean cycle 16.3 h, p90 20.9 h, utilization 49% 4 archivists: mean cycle 14.3 h, p90 17.3 h, utilization 38% The third archivist removes most of the queue: the mean cycle time falls by ten hours and the 90th percentile by more than a day. The fourth adds little, because most of the remaining time is the work itself and the applicants’ answers. Utilization falls with every new person. Low utilization is not wasted capacity: it is what lets a team absorb a sudden rush of requests and do work the model does not contain. The simulation gives the head of the archive numbers, not the decision. 11.6 Comparing scenarios A scenario is a copy of the model with one change. The model with three archivists differs in one line: resource archivists "Archivists" count=3 Download the scenario with three archivists (.tok) Simulation (seed 7): 300 cases started, 300 finished End events answered 243 81.0% refused 57 19.0% Cycle time: mean 19.3 h, median 8.8 h, 90th percentile 2.0 d Activities (count, mean wait, mean processing) Register the request 300 43 s 11.4 min Assess the request 346 30.3 min 29.1 min Search the holdings 243 35.2 min 6.2 h Write the answer 243 40.1 min 1.1 h Send the answer 243 31 s 9.9 min Ask for missing details 46 14.0 min 5.0 min Send a refusal 57 0 s 9.5 min Resources (utilization) Archivists x3 54.2% Registry clerks x1 8.9% Indicator 2 archivists 3 archivists mean cycle time 1.2 d 19.3 h median 19.1 h 8.8 h 90th percentile 2.3 d 2.0 d wait before the assessment 4.5 h 30.3 min utilization of the archivists 77.5% 54.2% The median falls to less than half and the waits before the archivists’ tasks almost disappear. The 90th percentile barely moves in this single run, and the replications above tell why: the slowest tenth of the cases are the ones that wait days for missing details, and no archivist shortens that wait. With seed 7 the slowest tenth includes more of them than on average (the twenty seeds gave 20.9 hours for three archivists). An indicator that sits on the edge of such a group varies strongly between runs, which is one more reason to look at replications before drawing conclusions from it. A change that would shorten the tail is a different one: asking for details at registration, before the request waits for an archivist. 11.7 Event logs The report gives averages. For a closer analysis, the simulator writes the individual events on request: tok sim 11-archive-queries.tok --log log.csv --cases-csv cases.csv --xes log.xes The event log (--log) has one row per activity instance: case,activity,label,resource,enqueue,start,end,status 1,register,Register the request,clerks,2027-01-04T08:00:00,2027-01-04T08:00:00,2027-01-04T08:09:55,completed 1,assess,Assess the request,archivists,2027-01-04T08:09:55,2027-01-04T08:09:55,2027-01-04T08:41:05,completed 2,register,Register the request,clerks,2027-01-04T08:39:14,2027-01-04T08:39:14,2027-01-04T08:50:54,completed 2,assess,Assess the request,archivists,2027-01-04T08:50:54,2027-01-04T08:50:54,2027-01-04T09:13:13,completed Column Content case the case number, from 1 activity, label the identifier and the label of the activity resource the resource of by= (empty if none) enqueue when the case reached the activity start when a performer started the work (empty if the activity was interrupted while waiting) end when the activity completed or was interrupted status completed, or interrupted by a boundary timer The waiting time of an instance is start − enqueue, its processing time end − start. The table of cases (--cases-csv) has one row per case: the case number, its start and end, the end event, the cycle time in seconds and the case variables as JSON: case,start,end,end_event,cycle_time_s,variables 1,2027-01-04T08:00:00,2027-01-04T13:31:21,answered,19881.119,"{""complete"": true}" 2,2027-01-04T08:39:14,2027-01-04T17:11:57,answered,30762.674,"{""complete"": true}" 3,2027-01-04T10:28:29,2027-01-04T18:09:43,answered,27674.15,"{""complete"": true}" Simulated time is calendar time counted from start= of simulate, without working-hours calendars: a six-hour task started at 16:00 ends at 22:00. The results therefore describe continuous work; to translate them into working days, divide by the length of a working day and treat the result as an approximation. 11.7.1 XES for process-mining tools --xes writes the same log in XES (IEEE 1849-2016, eXtensible Event Stream), the exchange format of process-mining tools such as ProM, PM4Py, bupaR, Disco and Celonis. They read it without any column mapping. The file declares the standard extensions Concept, Time, Lifecycle and Organizational, three classifiers, and one trace per case: <trace> <string key="concept:name" value="1"/> <date key="start" value="2027-01-04T08:00:00.000"/> <date key="end" value="2027-01-04T13:31:21.119"/> <string key="end_event" value="answered"/> <float key="cycle_time_s" value="19881.119"/> <boolean key="complete" value="true"/> <event> <string key="concept:name" value="Register the request"/> <string key="concept:instance" value="1"/> <string key="lifecycle:transition" value="schedule"/> <date key="time:timestamp" value="2027-01-04T08:00:00.000"/> <string key="org:resource" value="clerks"/> <string key="activity" value="register"/> </event> Each activity instance gives up to three events in the standard lifecycle: schedule when the case reached the activity, start when the work started, and complete when it ended; an instance interrupted by a boundary timer ends with ati_abort while running or withdraw while still waiting. The trace carries the end event, the cycle time and the case variables with their types. Timestamps keep the UTC offset of start=: write start="2027-03-01T09:00+01:00" to get times with +01:00, or leave the offset out to have them read as local time. The same document and seed give the same bytes. 11.8 Process mining on simulated logs Process mining discovers processes from event logs: it draws the process that the log contains, measures the times between activities and finds the variants cases follow. On a simulated log you can try the methods before you have real data, check that a discovered model looks like the one you simulated, and prepare the analysis that will later run on the log of a real system: the columns of tok sim --log have the same structure as event logs exported from workflow and records management systems. In Python, PM4Py reads the XES file directly: import pm4py log = pm4py.read_xes("log.xes") net, initial, final = pm4py.discover_petri_net_inductive(log) pm4py.view_petri_net(net, initial, final) or the CSV log after naming its columns: import pandas as pd import pm4py df = pd.read_csv("log.csv", parse_dates=["enqueue", "start", "end"]) df = pm4py.format_dataframe(df, case_id="case", activity_key="label", timestamp_key="end") pm4py.view_dfg(*pm4py.discover_dfg(df)) ProM, Disco and other desktop tools open the XES file from their import dialogs. In R the package tokr gives the log as a data frame with the column names process-mining packages expect, so bupaR takes it without conversion: library(tokr) s <- tok_sim("11-archive-queries.tok") log <- as.data.frame(s) bupaR::activitylog(log, case_id = "case_id", activity_id = "activity_id", resource_id = "resource_id", timestamps = c("schedule", "start", "complete")) The model you discover from a simulated log is a useful check of the model you wrote: if the discovered process has a path you did not intend, the simulation follows that path too. 11.9 Simulation in R The R package tokr (Chapter 13) runs the same simulator and returns its results as data frames, ready for tables and plots: library(tokr) s <- tok_sim("11-archive-queries.tok") # cases and seed of the model s # the report of tok sim s <- tok_sim("11-archive-queries.tok", cases = 1000, seed = 3) s$kpi$cycle_time$mean_s # mean cycle time in seconds s$kpi$activities # one row per activity s$kpi$resources # one row per resource, utilization as a fraction s$cases # one row per case, one column per variable tok_xes(s, "queries.xes") # the XES log of the same run s$kpi$activities has the columns activity, label, count, mean_wait_s, mean_processing_s, mean_wait and mean_processing; s$kpi$resources has resource, label, count and utilization. The table of cases has the columns case, start, end, end_event and cycle_time_s, then one column per case variable; the event log of as.data.frame(s) has the columns of tok sim --log and, under the names case_id, activity_id, activity_instance_id, resource_id, schedule and complete, the same data for process-mining packages. Times are POSIXct values in UTC. With the two scenario files, a few lines of base R compare their cycle times: cycle_hours <- function(file) tok_sim(file)$cases$cycle_time_s / 3600 two <- cycle_hours("11-archive-queries.tok") three <- cycle_hours("11-archive-queries-3.tok") sapply(list(two = two, three = three), quantile, probs = c(0.5, 0.9)) boxplot(list("2 archivists" = two, "3 archivists" = three), horizontal = TRUE, xlab = "Cycle time (hours)") 11.10 Simulation in Python The module tok.api of the Python package gives the simulation to programs and notebooks: from tok import api text = open("11-archive-queries.tok", encoding="utf-8").read() result = api.simulate(text, cases=1000, seed=3) kpi = result.kpi() # the indicators as a dict, as tok sim --json print(api.format_kpi(kpi)) # the report of tok sim result.log[:3] # the event log: one dict per activity instance result.cases[:3] # one dict per case result.write_csv("log.csv", "cases.csv") # the files of --log and --cases-csv result.write_xes("log.xes") # the file of --xes The indicators have the structure of tok sim --json: kpi["cases"] with started, finished and by_end_event; kpi["cycle_time"] with mean_s, median_s and p90_s in seconds and the same as short texts; kpi["activities"][ID] with count, mean_wait_s and mean_processing_s; kpi["resources"][ID]["utilization"]; kpi["horizon_s"], the simulated period; and kpi["warnings"], conditions or expressions the simulator could not evaluate. With pandas, pd.DataFrame(result.log) turns the log into a data frame. 11.11 Native simulation in Julia Experiments with many scenarios and hundreds of replications are faster in the native simulator of the Julia package, Tok.Sim. It reads the model through the engine, so the document is parsed and checked exactly as tok check does, and it asks the engine to evaluate the conditions of flows, so conditions mean exactly what they mean in tok sim. Everything else runs in compiled Julia, in parallel on the threads you give Julia (julia -t auto). using Tok const S = Tok.Sim text = read("11-archive-queries.tok", String) m = S.model(text) three = S.scenario(m; name="three archivists", resources=Dict("archivists" => 3)) busier = S.scenario(m; name="busier", arrival="exp(3h)") e = S.experiment([m, three, busier]; replications=200, seed=1) for r in S.summarize(e) r.indicator in ("cycle_time_mean_s", "cycle_time_p90_s", "utilization:archivists") || continue println(rpad(r.scenario, 18), rpad(r.indicator, 24), round(r.mean; sigdigits=4), " ± ", round(r.half_width; sigdigits=2)) end model cycle_time_mean_s 96000.0 ± 3000.0 model cycle_time_p90_s 172500.0 ± 6800.0 model utilization:archivists 0.7556 ± 0.0089 three archivists cycle_time_mean_s 59890.0 ± 1100.0 three archivists cycle_time_p90_s 80580.0 ± 3100.0 three archivists utilization:archivists 0.5132 ± 0.0066 busier cycle_time_mean_s 340100.0 ± 17000.0 busier cycle_time_p90_s 580700.0 ± 29000.0 busier utilization:archivists 0.8872 ± 0.011 Each line gives the mean of an indicator over 200 replications and the half-width of its 95% interval; times are in seconds. With 200 replications the comparison is clear: three archivists cut the mean cycle time from about 26.7 to 16.6 hours. The scenario busier, with a request every three hours and two archivists, shows what happens when the work exceeds the capacity: the archivists would need about 6.4 hours per request every 3 hours, more than two people can give, the queue grows for as long as requests keep arriving, and the mean cycle time rises to almost four days. Such a result says less about the exact number than about the fact that the process cannot keep up. S.scenario changes the number of performers (resources=), the durations of activities (durations=Dict("search" => "lnorm(5h, 2h)")), the probabilities and the arrivals. S.summarize(e) gives, per scenario and indicator, the mean, the standard deviation, the half-width of the 95% interval and the number of runs; S.indicators(e) every indicator of every run in long form, for DataFrames. One run on its own is S.simulate(m; seed=7), with S.cycle_time(run) and S.utilization(run, "archivists"). Each replication has its own random stream, derived from the seed and the number of the replication, so the results do not depend on the number of threads, and a single replication can be repeated (S.simulate(m; seed=1, replication=17)). By default all scenarios use the same streams (common random numbers), which makes the differences between scenarios more precise than the scenarios themselves. The native simulator agrees with the engine in distribution, not number by number: it has its own generator. The tests of the package compare the two on 44 models with the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. Some elements are not run natively: decisions of business rule tasks, script expressions, multi-instance activities with a collection, ad-hoc sub-processes, compensation, transactions, complex gateways, standard loops with conditions, multiple events and instantiating elements. S.unsupported(m) lists them before any run; a model that has them runs in the engine instead, with Tok.Engine.simulate(text; cases=…, seed=…). 11.12 Calibration on an event log The parameters of a simulation are assumptions, and the best source of assumptions is a log of the real process. Tok.Fit estimates them from an event log and writes them back into the document, so that the model simulates the process that produced the log: Parameter Statement Observations in the log processing time of an activity duration= end − start of every completed instance; an instance interrupted after it started counts as a censored observation time between arrivals arrival= of simulate the differences between consecutive arrivals of cases branch probabilities p= of the flows of xor and or gateways how often each branch was taken, recognised by the activities that follow it Each duration is fitted in the family the model declares for it (exp, norm, lnorm, unif, tri or a fixed value), or in another family given with families=. The number of performers, the distributions of case variables and the waiting times of events are not fitted, because an event log does not record them. Waiting times are not parameters either: they follow from the arrivals, the durations and the number of performers. The logs are read by F.read_xes (XES from tok sim --xes or from process-mining tools) and F.read_csv_log (the CSV log of tok sim --log, optionally with the table of cases). A test of the method is to fit a log whose true parameters you know. Here the log comes from 3000 simulated cases of the archive model: using Tok const F = Tok.Fit text = read("11-archive-queries.tok", String) log = F.read_xes(Tok.Engine.sim_xes(text; cases=3000, seed=11)) f = F.fit(text, log) for r in F.table(f) println(rpad(r.element, 24), rpad("$(r.family) $(r.name)", 12), round(r.estimate; sigdigits=4), " [", round(r.lower; sigdigits=4), ", ", round(r.upper; sigdigits=4), "]") end register tri a 297.6 [292.5, 304.5] register tri mode 584.1 [568.4, 602.3] register tri b 1204.0 [1194.0, 1212.0] refuse tri a 312.4 [301.1, 333.8] refuse tri mode 602.6 [569.7, 637.4] refuse tri b 908.7 [889.5, 920.8] answer tri a 298.5 [294.1, 306.3] answer tri mode 600.0 [587.0, 613.8] answer tri b 897.0 [890.5, 902.3] assess lnorm mean 1810.0 [1789.0, 1832.0] assess lnorm sd 627.3 [608.5, 646.6] ask fixed x 300.0 [300.0, 300.0] search lnorm mean 21600.0 [21180.0, 22020.0] search lnorm sd 10990.0 [10550.0, 11460.0] write tri a 1832.0 [1797.0, 1890.0] write tri mode 3612.0 [3496.0, 3703.0] write tri b 7210.0 [7134.0, 7254.0] arrival exp mean 14700.0 [14180.0, 15240.0] feasible -> search p p 0.8563 [0.8433, 0.8684] feasible -> refuse p p 0.1437 [0.1316, 0.1567] Durations are in seconds. The estimates recover the parameters of the model: the assessment lnorm(30m, 10m) is 1810 and 627 seconds, the search lnorm(6h, 3h) is 21,600 and 10,990 seconds, the arrivals exp(4h) 14,700 seconds, and the branch to the search 0.856 against the 0.85 of the model. The intervals are maximum-likelihood intervals at 95%: Wald intervals for exp, norm and lnorm, a parametric bootstrap for unif and tri, Wilson score intervals for probabilities. f.notes lists what could not be estimated and why. F.apply(text, f) returns the document with the estimates written in, duration= of the activities, arrival= and p=, rounded to four significant digits by default and in the largest unit that keeps the number at least 1, with comments kept: write("11-archive-queries-fitted.tok", F.apply(text, f)) For a Bayesian estimate, load Turing.jl in the same session: fit_bayes then samples the posterior of every parameter with the No-U-Turn sampler, with weakly informative priors on the scale of the data, and returns posterior means with credible intervals in the same table: using Turing b = F.fit_bayes(text, log; samples=1000) F.table(b) Turing is not a dependency of Tok.jl; the function becomes available when Turing is loaded. With logs of a few hundred cases the posterior means differ from the maximum-likelihood estimates by a fraction of their uncertainty; the Bayesian intervals are worth having when the log is small. The cycle closes here: a model is written from a description, its parameters are estimated from the log of the real process, the calibrated model is simulated in scenarios, and the scenario that is chosen becomes the next version of the model. 11.13 What the simulator does not do Calendars. Time runs without breaks for nights, weekends or holidays. One process. The simulator runs the process of the first pool that has one, or the process of a document without pools. Message flows to other pools are not simulated; a reply from outside is modelled with delay= on the event that waits for it. Throw events and event sub-processes are not simulated. Interchangeable performers. A resource is a group of equal people. Different skills are modelled as separate resources. Loops of activities. Multi-instance collections are simulated from language 0.3 and standard loops with while= or loop-max= from language 0.5; a case that passes more than 10,000 elements is stopped and reported with the end event loop-limit. Exercises Exercise 11.1 Your own parameters. Take a model you wrote in an earlier chapter and add simulate, two resources and duration= on every activity. Ask yourself, or someone who does the work, for the shortest, usual and longest time of each step and use tri. Give every splitting gateway either conditions or probabilities until the check reports no S codes. Reading the report. Run tok sim on 11-archive-queries.tok with --cases 1000 and three different seeds. Which indicators change by less than 5%, and which change more? Explain the difference with what you know about the requests that wait for details. Earlier refusal. Change the model so that the clerk checks feasibility at registration (tri(10m, 20m, 30m)) and refuses impossible requests with p=0.15 there; the archivist’s assessment then takes tri(10m, 15m, 30m) and refuses nothing. Compare the scenario with the original by replications in Python or Julia. Does the registry become a new bottleneck? More requests. Set arrival="exp(3h)" with two and with three archivists and run both. What happens to the waiting times with two archivists as you increase --cases from 300 to 1000? What does that tell you about the process? Process mining. Write the XES log of the model and open it in a process-mining tool (PM4Py, bupaR, ProM or Disco). Discover the process from the log and compare it with the diagram. Where does the loop through the missing details appear, and how often is it taken? Calibration. In Julia, simulate 500 cases of the model, fit the log with Tok.Fit.fit and compare the intervals with those of 3000 cases. Then change the model to duration="exp(6h)" for the search, fit the same log again, and compare the estimates of the two families. Which family does the log support, and how can you tell?

Chapter 12 Editors and the playground 12.1 The VS Code extension 12.2 The language server for other editors 12.3 The playground in the browser 12.4 Choosing a tool Exercises

Chapter 12 Editors and the playground In this chapter you will install the VS Code extension of tok and work with its diagnostics, formatting, navigation, rename, outline and live diagram · set up the language server tok-lsp in Neovim, Helix, Emacs or another editor with an LSP client · write, check, simulate and share models in the browser playground, which runs the engine as WebAssembly without a server A tok model is a text file, so any text editor can open it. The tools in this chapter make editing comfortable: they show the diagnostics of tok check while you type, format the text on request, take you from a name to its declaration, rename an element everywhere at once and draw the diagram next to the text. All of them run the tok engine itself, so they give exactly the results of the command line. There are three ways to work: Tool For whom What you need the VS Code extension most users: one installation and everything works VS Code, VSCodium or another editor that installs extensions from Open VSX tok-lsp in another editor users of Neovim, Helix, Emacs, Sublime Text, Kate, Zed and other editors with an LSP client the program tok-lsp and a few lines of configuration the playground trying tok without installing anything, teaching, sharing a model by a link a web browser 12.1 The VS Code extension 12.1.1 Installing The extension is called tok, published by tok-lang-bpm. Install it in VS Code from the Extensions view (search for tok and check the publisher) or from the Visual Studio Marketplace. VSCodium, Eclipse Theia and other editors that use the Open VSX registry install the same extension from Open VSX. From a terminal: code --install-extension tok-lang-bpm.tok The packages for Windows, Linux and macOS carry the language server tok-lsp for their platform, so nothing else is needed: you do not have to install the tok command or Python for the editor to work. Open any .tok file and the extension starts. 12.1.2 What you see while editing Open 12-reading-room.tok, a small model of a reading room order: tok 1.0 "Reading room order" pool library "University library" lane reader "Reader" start wish "Reader needs a volume" user order "Order the volume to the reading room" lane stacks "Stacks" user fetch "Fetch the volume from the stacks" xor found "Volume found?" user deliver "Deliver to the reading room" end delivered "Volume ready in the reading room" user notify "Notify the reader" end missing "Volume reported missing" flow wish -> order -> fetch -> found flow found -> deliver "yes" flow found -> notify "no" flow deliver -> delivered flow notify -> missing Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) Syntax highlighting colours statements, identifiers, labels, attributes, flags, flows, comments and the rows of decision tables, so the structure of each line is visible at a glance. Diagnostics appear as you type: every check of tok check, from the structure of the document through the BPMN 2.0 rules to the Camunda profile of executable models, decisions, FEEL and simulation parameters. They are underlined in the text and listed in the Problems panel with their codes. Make a typo in the first flow, flow wish -> ordr -> fetch -> found, and the line is marked at once with the message the command line would give: reading-room.tok:15: error R002: unknown flow node 'ordr' reading-room.tok:15: error R002: unknown flow node 'ordr' reading-room.tok: 2 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) The error appears twice because the chain on line 15 is two flows, wish -> ordr and ordr -> fetch, and both name the unknown node. In the editor both are attached to the identifier ordr itself. Formatting (Format Document, or format on save) rewrites the document in the canonical form of tok fmt. A document with syntax errors is not formatted, because the canonical form of a text that does not parse would lose part of it; the editor shows the first error instead. Hover over an identifier shows the kind of the element, its label, the BPMN or DMN element it exports and the line of its declaration; over a keyword, what the statement declares; over a diagnostic or a diagnostic code, the explanation of the code in English and Polish. Completion offers the keywords at the start of a line, the attribute keys and flags of a statement, the identifiers of the right kind after keys that name elements (activities after on=, forms after form=, decisions after decision=, resources after by=), the nodes after -> on a flow line, the hit policies after hit= and the field types after type= on a form field. 12.1.3 Navigation and rename Every identifier of a model is declared once and used in many places: in flows, in on= of boundary events, in form= and decision=, in reads and writes, in requires= of decisions, and in the FEEL expressions of a decision model. The extension knows all of them: Action How What it does Go to definition F12, or Ctrl+click jumps from any use of an identifier to its declaration Find all references Shift+F12 lists every use of the identifier Highlight place the cursor on a name marks the declaration and every use in the document Rename F2 renames the identifier everywhere Outline the Outline view, or Ctrl+Shift+O pools with their lanes and nodes, sub-processes, decisions, forms with their fields and the other blocks Rename is more than search and replace. It checks that the new name is a valid identifier ([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_-]*, ASCII, because identifiers become XML id attributes) and that no other element uses it, and refuses otherwise with the reason. Rename fetch to retrieve in the reading room model, and the declaration and the chain order -> fetch -> found change together. The derived identifiers of flows (f-SOURCE-TARGET) follow the names of their ends, also where another statement refers to them. In a decision model, FEEL names in expressions follow the rename too, while a word that only begins a longer name, a key of a context and a name inside a string literal are left alone. 12.1.4 The diagram beside the text tok: Show diagram (also the preview button in the title bar of a .tok editor) opens the diagram of the model in a panel beside the editor. It is the picture tok svg draws, made from the text in the editor whether it is saved or not, and it is redrawn as you type. While the document has errors, the panel lists them instead. When a layout sidecar FILE.tok.layout lies next to the file (Chapter 8), the diagram keeps the drawing of the imported model. Working with the diagram open is the fastest way to learn the language. Add a boundary event, and a moment later it sits on the border of its task; join two branches with the wrong kind of gateway, and you see the problem in the picture and in the Problems panel at the same time. 12.1.5 Commands and settings Command What it does tok: Show diagram the live diagram beside the editor tok: Export BPMN writes NAME.bpmn (BPMN 2.0 XML with the diagram layout) next to the document tok: Export all files writes every file of tok export (BPMN, SVG, DMN and forms) into a folder you choose tok: Check summarises the diagnostics of the document tok: Restart language server restarts tok-lsp Setting Default Meaning tok.lang auto language of the diagnostics: en, pl, or auto (Polish when VS Code runs in Polish) tok.level full teaching level, the elements a document may use: basic, analytic, full, as tok check --level tok.class none the BPMN 2.0.2 conformance class to check against: descriptive, analytic, common-executable, full, as tok check --class tok.server.path empty the path of tok-lsp; empty means the server of the extension, or else tok-lsp on the PATH Changes of tok.lang, tok.level and tok.class apply at once to every open document. A teacher can set tok.level to basic in the workspace settings of a course, so that students see an error as soon as they use an element the first lessons do not cover. A change of tok.server.path restarts the server. 12.2 The language server for other editors tok-lsp is the language server of tok: a program that an editor starts and talks to over its standard input and output with the Language Server Protocol (LSP 3.17). The VS Code extension uses it, and so can every editor with an LSP client. The features are those described above: diagnostics on opening and after every change, formatting, go to definition, references, highlight, rename, outline, hover and completion. Positions are counted in UTF-16 code units, as every LSP client expects, so labels with accented letters or other non-ASCII characters do not shift what follows them. 12.2.1 Installing the server Install it from crates.io with Rust, or take the program from the release archives of the repository, and put it on the PATH: cargo install tok-lsp tok-lsp --version Without arguments, or with --stdio, which editors often add, the server serves one editor on its standard streams. 12.2.2 What an editor needs Every editor needs three things: the command: tok-lsp; the file type: files ending in .tok; comments start with #, indentation is two spaces and never tabs; optionally, the settings as initialization options: {"lang": "en", "level": "full", "class": null}, the same three settings as in VS Code (class set to one of the conformance classes, or null for none). The editor may change the settings later with workspace/didChangeConfiguration, either as {"settings": {"tok": {…}}} or directly as {"settings": {…}}; every open document is checked again. Messages are in Polish when the editor runs in Polish or lang is pl. 12.2.3 Neovim Neovim 0.11 and later configure language servers without plugins. In init.lua: vim.filetype.add({ extension = { tok = "tok" } }) vim.lsp.config("tok", { cmd = { "tok-lsp" }, filetypes = { "tok" }, root_markers = { ".git" }, init_options = { lang = "en", level = "full" }, }) vim.lsp.enable("tok") vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd("FileType", { pattern = "tok", callback = function() vim.bo.commentstring = "# %s" vim.bo.expandtab = true vim.bo.shiftwidth = 2 end, }) Diagnostics appear as the file is edited; vim.lsp.buf.format() formats, CTRL-] goes to the definition, grr lists the references, grn renames, gO shows the outline and K the hover text. 12.2.4 Helix In languages.toml, in the configuration folder of Helix or as .helix/languages.toml of a project: [language-server.tok-lsp] command = "tok-lsp" config = { lang = "en", level = "full" } [[language]] name = "tok" scope = "source.tok" file-types = ["tok"] comment-token = "#" indent = { tab-width = 2, unit = " " } language-servers = ["tok-lsp"] Helix sends config as the initialization options. :format formats, gd goes to the definition, gr lists the references, <space>r renames and <space>s opens the outline; hx --health tok shows whether Helix finds the server. 12.2.5 Emacs Emacs 29 and later include the LSP client eglot. A small major mode gives .tok files their comments and indentation, and eglot starts the server for it: (define-derived-mode tok-mode prog-mode "tok" "Major mode for process models in the tok language." (modify-syntax-entry ?# "<" tok-mode-syntax-table) (modify-syntax-entry ?\n ">" tok-mode-syntax-table) (modify-syntax-entry ?- "_" tok-mode-syntax-table) (setq-local comment-start "# ") (setq-local indent-tabs-mode nil) (setq-local tab-width 2)) (add-to-list 'auto-mode-alist '("\\.tok\\'" . tok-mode)) (with-eval-after-load 'eglot (add-to-list 'eglot-server-programs '(tok-mode . ("tok-lsp" :initializationOptions (:lang "en" :level "full"))))) (add-hook 'tok-mode-hook #'eglot-ensure) M-x eglot-format-buffer formats, M-. goes to the definition, M-? lists the references, M-x eglot-rename renames and M-x imenu uses the outline; Flymake shows the diagnostics. 12.2.6 Other editors Sublime Text (with its LSP package), Kate, Zed and other editors with an LSP client take the same three things: the command tok-lsp, the extension .tok and, if you want them, the initialization options. Highlighting in these editors comes from the editor’s own configuration; the language server supplies everything else. 12.2.7 Requests for editor extensions Besides the standard methods, the server answers four requests that let an editor extension show and export a model without running the tok command: tok/check (the numbers of errors, warnings and notes and the BPMN conformance class), tok/svg (the picture), tok/bpmn (the BPMN XML) and tok/export (every file of tok export). They take {"textDocument": {"uri": URI}} of an open document and use the text the editor holds, not the file on disk. The diagram panel of the VS Code extension is built on tok/svg; an extension for another editor can do the same. 12.2.8 Limits The server analyses each document on its own, as tok check does. Identifiers are not resolved across files, so a process= of a call activity that names a process in another file is left alone, and rename works within one document. The server never writes files: export goes through the commands of the extension or the tok command. 12.3 The playground in the browser The playground at https://tok-lang-bpm.github.io/playground/ is a web page where you write and check a tok model in the browser. The engine runs inside the page, compiled to WebAssembly from the same Rust code as the tok command, so the diagnostics, the canonical form, the diagram, the BPMN file, the simulation and the decisions are exactly those of tok. Nothing is sent to a server: the page is a set of static files. 12.3.1 The page Editor with line numbers. Every change is checked after a short pause. The diagnostics appear below the editor with their line, severity, code and message, in English or Polish (Messages), and a click on one selects its line. The summary gives the numbers of errors, warnings and notes and the smallest BPMN conformance class of the document. Diagram: the SVG picture of the model, redrawn whenever the document has no errors. While it has errors, the last picture stays, dimmed, so you do not lose sight of the model while you fix a line. bpmn-js: the BPMN 2.0 XML of the model in the bpmn-js viewer of bpmn.io, which you can zoom and move. This is how the file will look in bpmn.io and in Camunda Modeler. Simulation: runs tok sim with the cases and seed of the model, or with the ones you give, and shows the report. Decisions: evaluates a decision of the document for input values written as a JSON object, as tok eval does, for example {"kind": "print", "price": 120}. Files: every file tok export writes (BPMN, SVG, DMN with its pictures, Camunda forms), each one a download. Above the editor, Format replaces the text with its canonical form; Download .tok and Download BPMN save the document and its BPMN file; Open… loads a .tok file, or imports a BPMN or DMN file into tok; Example loads one of the example models. 12.3.2 Sharing a model by a link Copy link puts the whole document into the address of the page, as #doc=… with the text encoded in base64url, and copies the link. Whoever opens the link sees the same model, checked and drawn, without any server storing it. The parameter ?tab= opens a tab directly: ?tab=viewer (bpmn-js), diagram, simulation, decisions or files. A teacher can put a link with ?tab=diagram into an assignment, and a student can send a link to a model with a question about one line of it. Long models make long links; for anything you want to keep, download the .tok file. 12.3.3 Offline and privacy Once the page is loaded, everything works without a network connection, except the bpmn-js tab: the viewer is loaded from unpkg.com, with integrity hashes so the browser refuses any other file, and without access to it the tab says that the viewer could not be loaded. The text of your model never leaves the browser, which makes the playground suitable for models of internal procedures. The page can also be served from your own web server or from a local folder over HTTP (browsers load WebAssembly only over HTTP, not from file: addresses), for example a classroom without internet access. The same WebAssembly module can be used in your own web pages; Chapter 13 shows how. 12.3.4 Limits of the browser WebAssembly runs here without threads, so the simulator runs on a smaller stack than in the tok command. A model whose cases pass through very long chains of gateways and events without time in between could exhaust it. FEEL now() and today() read the clock of the page, in UTC. If the engine stops on an internal error, the page reports it, writes the message to the console of the browser and loads a fresh module. The page has no layout sidecar: imported BPMN files are drawn with the automatic layout. 12.4 Choosing a tool Task Best tool your first model, a quick test of a construct the playground a model to share with someone who has nothing installed the playground, with Copy link daily work on models in a repository the VS Code extension, or tok-lsp in your editor renaming elements in a large model the extension or tok-lsp (rename) teaching with a restricted subset of BPMN the extension with tok.level, or tok check --level export for Camunda, simulation runs with files, automation the tok command (Chapter 2, the command reference) All of them read and write the same text, so you can move between them at any time: draft in the playground, download the .tok file, continue in the editor, and check it in continuous integration (Chapter 15). Chapter 13 Programming interfaces In this chapter you will see how one engine in Rust reaches every host language · call tok from Python with tok.api · work with models as data frames in R with tokr, draw them with tok_plot() and write them in R Markdown and Quarto chunks · use Tok.jl and Tok.Engine in Julia · run the engine in a web page through WebAssembly · link the C library tokengine with tok.h · use the Rust crates from crates.io · choose the interface that fits your program Everything tok does, from checking a document to simulating it, is written once, in Rust. The command tok, the language server, the MCP server and the playground are programs around that engine, and so are the packages for Python, R and Julia. This chapter is about using the engine from your own code: a script that checks every model of a repository, a notebook that draws a model next to its analysis, a web service that converts text to BPMN, a Julia experiment that simulates thousands of scenarios. 13.1 One engine, many bindings The engine consists of a few Rust crates. The bindings are thin layers that pass text in and results out: tok-core (parser, checker, printer, BPMN and DMN export and import, FEEL) tok-bpmn (BPMN rules, layout, SVG) tok-sim (simulator) │ │ │ tok-cli: the module tok_cli::api │ ┌───────────┬───────────┬──────────────┼────────────┬──────────────┐ R tokr tok (CLI) tok-lsp tok-mcp tokengine tok-wasm Python tok-lang (editors) (agents) (C, tok.h) (browser) (tok.api, tok mcp) │ Julia Tok.jl The functions in tok_cli::api take the text of a document and options as JSON and return a JSON result. The C library, the language server, the MCP server and the WebAssembly module call exactly these functions, so they accept the same options and give the same results; the Python package builds on the same crates, and the R package compiles the core crates into itself. The consequence for you is simple: every interface gives the same diagnostics, the same canonical text, the same files and the same simulation results, number by number for the same seed. A model checked in a notebook is checked exactly as in continuous integration, and a simulation in R can be reproduced in the playground. Interface Package Install Best for command line tok pip install tok-lang or cargo install tok-cli shells, scripts, continuous integration Python tok-lang, module tok.api pip install tok-lang scripts, notebooks, services R tokr install.packages("tokr") data analysis, R Markdown and Quarto documents Julia Tok.jl Pkg.add("Tok") large simulation experiments, calibration JavaScript tok-wasm the WebAssembly module of the playground web pages, browser tools C and any language with a C interface tokengine, header tok.h release archives, or a build from source C, C++, Go, Zig, Fortran, … Rust tok-core, tok-bpmn, tok-sim, tok-cli crates.io Rust programs The examples of this chapter use one small model: a loan renewal decided by a decision table, with simulation parameters. tok 1.0 "Loan renewal" start asked "Reader asks for a renewal" rule decide "Decide on the renewal" decision=renewal result=renewal by=desk duration="tri(1m, 2m, 4m)" xor allowed "Is the renewal allowed?" task extend "Extend the loan period" by=desk duration="tri(1m, 3m, 6m)" task explain "Explain the refusal" by=desk duration="tri(3m, 5m, 10m)" end extended "Loan extended" end refused "Renewal refused" flow asked -> decide -> allowed flow allowed -> extend "yes" when="renewal = \"allowed\"" flow allowed -> explain "no" default flow extend -> extended flow explain -> refused inputdata renewals "Renewals so far" type=number inputdata reserved "Reserved by another reader" type=boolean decision renewal "Renewal" type=string requires="renewals reserved" hit=first | reserved: boolean | renewals: number || renewal: string | | true | - || "refused" | | - | >= 3 || "refused" | | - | - || "allowed" | simulate cases=200 seed=3 arrival="exp(10m)" resource desk "Loan desk" count=1 variable renewals "cat(0=0.5, 1=0.3, 2=0.15, 3=0.05)" variable reserved "bern(0.1)" Figure 13.1: The loan renewal used in the examples of this chapter. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) 13.2 Python The package tok-lang on PyPI gives both the tok command and the module tok.api. It installs a wheel with the Rust engine compiled in, for every Python from 3.8: Windows x64, Linux x86_64 and aarch64, and macOS for Intel and Apple silicon. On another platform pip builds the engine from the source archive, which needs Rust. pip install tok-lang Every function of tok.api takes the text of a document (or of a BPMN file): Function Command Result check(text, lang="en", level="full", bpmn=True) tok check the diagnostics: a list of dicts with code, severity, line, id and message, sorted by line and code fmt(text) tok fmt the canonical text bpmn(text) tok bpmn BPMN 2.0 XML with the diagram layout svg(text, title=None) tok svg the SVG picture export(text, name="model") tok export every file of tok export as a dict file name → content import_bpmn(xml, keep_ids=True) tok import (text, warnings) eval_decision(text, decision, values=None) tok eval the value of a decision for a dict of inputs simulate(text, cases=None, seed=None) tok sim the result of the simulation format_kpi(kpi, lang="en") tok sim the text report for simulate(...).kpi() engine(), version() tok --version "rust" for the engine, and its version The functions that need a valid document raise ValueError with the error diagnostics, one per line, as tok check prints them; check returns them as data instead. A session with the renewal model: from tok import api text = open("13-loan-renewal.tok", encoding="utf-8").read() print(api.engine()) print(api.check(text)) print(api.eval_decision(text, "renewal", {"renewals": 3, "reserved": False})) files = api.export(text, name="loan-renewal") print(sorted(files)) result = api.simulate(text, cases=500, seed=1) kpi = result.kpi() print(kpi["cycle_time"]["mean"], kpi["resources"]["desk"]["utilization"]) print(result.log[0]) rust [] refused ['loan-renewal.bpmn', 'loan-renewal.svg', 'renewal.dmn', 'renewal.drd.svg'] 11.7 min 0.6138 {'case': 1, 'activity': 'decide', 'label': 'Decide on the renewal', 'resource': 'desk', 'enqueue': '2027-01-04T08:00:00', 'start': '2027-01-04T08:00:00', 'end': '2027-01-04T08:02:48', 'status': 'completed'} export returns the contents of the files instead of writing them, which suits a web service or a test; writing them is a loop over the dict. A document with an error, here a misspelt decision: broken = text.replace("decision=renewal", "decision=renewl") for d in api.check(broken): print(d) try: api.bpmn(broken) except ValueError as e: print("ValueError:", e) {'code': 'R002', 'severity': 'error', 'line': 4, 'id': 'renewl', 'message': "unknown decision 'renewl'"} ValueError: line 4: error R002: unknown decision 'renewl' The result of simulate has kpi() (the indicators as a dict, as tok sim --json), log (one dict per activity instance), cases (one dict per case), warnings, seed, horizon, to_json(include_log=False), write_csv(path_log, path_cases=None), to_xes() and write_xes(path). Chapter 11 uses them for replications and process mining. In a Jupyter notebook a model can be drawn in a cell with IPython.display.SVG(api.svg(text)), which Chapter 15 uses for documents. The package also contains a pure-Python implementation of the language, frozen at language 0.3, which serves as the reference of the parity tests of the engine. The environment variable TOK_ENGINE=python selects it, and api.engine() then returns "python"; it reads only documents of languages 0.1 and 0.3. For everything else, and by default, the functions run on the engine. 13.3 R The R package tokr runs the same engine, compiled into the package, and gives its results as R objects: diagnostics and simulation results as data frames, diagrams in the viewer, models in R Markdown and Quarto chunks. install.packages("tokr") Installing from source compiles the engine and needs Rust; on Windows also Rtools for your version of R. Function What it does tok_read(path) reads a .tok file into a tok_model (a list with text, path and name) tok_check(x, lang, level, bpmn = TRUE) the diagnostics as a data frame with the columns line, code, severity, id and message, no rows when the model is clean tok_fmt(x, write = FALSE, lang) the canonical text; write = TRUE rewrites the file tok_bpmn(x, file = NULL, lang), tok_svg(x, file = NULL, title = NULL, lang) BPMN XML and SVG, written to file when given tok_plot(x, title = NULL, lang) the diagram in the viewer of RStudio or Positron, or in the browser tok_export(x, dir = ".", name = NULL, lang) every file of tok export into a folder; returns their paths tok_import(file, keep_ids = TRUE) a BPMN file as a tok_model; what was not kept is signalled as warnings tok_eval(x, decision, inputs = list(), lang) the value of a decision for a named list of inputs tok_sim(x, cases = NULL, seed = NULL, lang) the simulation, with indicators, the event log and the table of cases as data frames tok_xes(x, file = NULL, cases = NULL, seed = NULL, lang) the XES log of a simulation tok_version() the version of the engine Every function takes a model read with tok_read(), the path of a .tok file, or the text of a model. options(tok.lang = "pl") switches all messages to Polish. library(tokr) m <- tok_read("13-loan-renewal.tok") d <- tok_check(m) # a data frame, printed like tok check nrow(d) # 0: no problems tok_plot(m) # the diagram in the viewer tok_eval(m, "renewal", list(renewals = 3, reserved = FALSE)) tok_export(m, dir = "out") # BPMN, SVG, DMN and forms s <- tok_sim(m, cases = 500, seed = 1) s$kpi$activities # one row per activity head(as.data.frame(s)) # the event log Because diagnostics are a data frame, they combine with the rest of R. A course can check all submitted models in one call and tabulate the codes: files <- list.files("submissions", pattern = "\\.tok$", full.names = TRUE) all <- do.call(rbind, lapply(files, function(f) cbind(file = basename(f), tok_check(f)))) table(all$code[all$severity == "error"]) 13.3.1 The knitr engine Loading tokr registers a knitr engine called tok. A chunk written as ```{tok, fig.cap = "Loan renewal"} tok 1.0 "Loan renewal" start asked "Reader asks for a renewal" task extend "Extend the loan period" end extended "Loan extended" flow asked -> extend -> extended ``` draws the diagram of the model in the chunk, as a figure with its caption. Chunk options choose another output: Option Effect tok.output = "svg" the diagram (default) tok.output = "check" the diagnostics, as tok check prints them tok.output = "fmt" the canonical text tok.output = "bpmn" the BPMN XML tok.title = "…" a title drawn above the diagram tok.lang = "pl" the language of the messages tok.export = "dir" also writes every exported file into dir The diagram is written as an SVG file, which suits HTML output; for PDF output use tok.output = "check" or include an exported picture. Chapter 15 shows the engine in reports and course materials. 13.4 Julia Tok.jl brings tok to Julia in three layers: Tok.Engine gives the whole language through the C interface of the engine; the module Tok itself contains a second, independent implementation of the core of the specification; and Tok.Sim and Tok.Fit are a native simulator and the calibration of simulation parameters (Chapter 11). using Pkg Pkg.add("Tok") The package needs Julia 1.10 or newer. It looks for the engine library in this order: at the path in the environment variable TOK_LIBTOK (tokengine.dll, libtokengine.so or libtokengine.dylib), in the binary package tok_jll when it is installed in the active environment, and in the build folder of a checkout of the repository. Tok.Engine.available() tells whether it was found and Tok.Engine.library() where. Without it the independent core still works. The functions of Tok.Engine mirror those of Python and R: Julia Python R check(text; lang, level, class) check tok_check fmt(text) fmt tok_fmt bpmn(text), svg(text; title) bpmn, svg tok_bpmn, tok_plot export_files(text; name) export tok_export import_bpmn(xml), import_dmn(xml), import_file(xml) import_bpmn tok_import eval_decision(text, decision, values) eval_decision tok_eval simulate(text; cases, seed, xes), sim_xes(text) simulate, SimResult.to_xes tok_sim, tok_xes bpmn_class(text) cli(args) export, import and eval are reserved words or functions of Julia, hence the longer names. using Tok const E = Tok.Engine text = read("13-loan-renewal.tok", String) println(E.check(text)) println(E.bpmn_class(text)) println(E.eval_decision(text, "renewal", Dict("renewals" => 3, "reserved" => false))) println(sort(collect(keys(E.export_files(text; name="loan-renewal"))))) r = E.simulate(text; cases=500, seed=1) println(r) println(r.kpi["cycle_time"]["mean"]) Any[] full refused ["loan-renewal.bpmn", "loan-renewal.svg", "renewal.dmn", "renewal.drd.svg"] SimResult(500 cases, seed 1) 11.7 min The mean cycle time is the one Python gave for the same cases and seed, because both ran the same engine. The class full is the smallest BPMN 2.0.2 conformance class the document fits (Chapter 7). Errors of the engine are thrown as Tok.Engine.TokError with a kind, a message and, for a document with errors, its diagnostics: try E.bpmn(replace(text, "decision=renewal" => "decision=renewl")) catch err println(err.kind, ": ", err.message) end document: line 4: error R002: unknown decision 'renewl' The functions may be called from several threads at once. The independent core is a second implementation of the lexer, the parser, the canonical printer and the semantic BPMN export, written in Julia without the engine. It exists because two implementations of one specification are the strongest test that the specification is unambiguous, and it passes the core level of the conformance corpus for every case: doc, diags = Tok.parse_tok(text) print(Tok.fmt(doc)) # the canonical text print(Tok.semantic_xml(doc)) # the semantic BPMN XML of the conformance corpus 13.5 JavaScript and WebAssembly The crate tok-wasm compiles the engine to WebAssembly. The result is an ES module, tok_wasm.js, with the WebAssembly file tok_wasm_bg.wasm next to it. The playground (Chapter 12) is built on it, and its folder pkg/ holds both files; you can also build them from the repository with the Rust target wasm32-unknown-unknown and the wasm-bindgen command (the playground documentation of the repository gives the commands). The module’s default export loads the WebAssembly code. Its other exports are the functions of the engine. Each takes the text of a document (or of an XML file) and the options as a JSON string, and returns a JSON string: {"ok": VALUE} on success, {"error": {"kind", "message"}} on failure, with the options and results of the C interface (below). The functions are check, fmt, bpmn, svg, sim, version and cheatsheet, and, because export, import and eval are reserved words of JavaScript, _export, _import and _eval. A page imports the module as a namespace: import init, * as tok from "./pkg/tok_wasm.js"; await init(); const text = document.querySelector("#model").value; const checked = JSON.parse(tok.check(text, JSON.stringify({ lang: "en" }))); console.log(checked.ok.errors, checked.ok.bpmn_class); const decided = JSON.parse(tok._eval(text, JSON.stringify({ decision: "renewal", values: { renewals: 3, reserved: false } }))); console.log(decided.ok); const files = JSON.parse(tok._export(text, JSON.stringify({ name: "loan-renewal" }))); console.log(Object.keys(files.ok)); const run = JSON.parse(tok.sim(text, JSON.stringify({ seed: 1, log: false, cases_table: false }))); console.log(run.ok.kpi.cycle_time.mean, run.ok.kpi.resources.desk.utilization); const picture = JSON.parse(tok.svg(text, "{}")).ok; // an SVG string to put into the page With the renewal model the calls print: 0 full refused [ 'loan-renewal.bpmn', 'loan-renewal.svg', 'renewal.dmn', 'renewal.drd.svg' ] 11.5 min 0.662 (The simulation uses the 200 cases of the model’s simulate statement here, so its mean differs from the 500 cases above.) A document with errors gives an error object; for svg of a document whose flow names unknown nodes: document line 2: error R002: unknown flow node 'a' where document is the kind and the rest the message. Browsers load WebAssembly only over HTTP, so serve the page from a web server, even a local one, not from a file: address. In Node.js the default export takes the bytes of the WebAssembly file: await init({ module_or_path: await readFile("./pkg/tok_wasm_bg.wasm") }). The module has no threads: the simulator runs on the module’s stack, and FEEL now() and today() read the clock of the page in UTC. 13.6 The C interface The engine is also a C library, tokengine, with the declarations in the header tok.h. Any language that can call C can use it: C and C++ directly, Go through cgo, Zig, Fortran, and Julia, whose Tok.Engine is built on it. The library comes as a shared library (tokengine.dll on Windows, libtokengine.so on Linux, libtokengine.dylib on macOS) and as a static library. Every function has the same shape: char *tok_check(const char *text, const char *options); Arguments are NUL-terminated UTF-8 strings: the text of a document (or of an XML file, an expression, a list of command-line arguments) and the options, a JSON object such as {"lang": "pl"}; NULL or an empty string means no options. An unknown option is an error, so that a misspelt option does not go unnoticed. The result is a newly allocated string with one JSON object, {"ok": VALUE} or {"error": {"kind": KIND, "message": TEXT}}. The caller frees it with tok_free, exactly once. No function returns NULL. Errors have a kind: invalid_argument, document (with the diagnostics of the document), render, import, unknown_decision, decision, feel, distribution, simulation, io or internal. Threads. The functions keep no state, are reentrant and can be called from several threads at once. A panic in the engine never unwinds into the caller; it is returned as an error of kind internal. Function Options Result tok_check lang, level, bpmn, class {"errors", "bpmn_class", "diagnostics"}, as tok check --json tok_fmt lang the canonical text tok_bpmn lang, layout, sidecar (the text of a layout sidecar) BPMN 2.0 XML tok_svg lang, title, sidecar the SVG picture tok_export lang, name, sidecar an object file name → content tok_import format (auto, bpmn, dmn), flow_ids, layout {"format", "text", "warnings", "layout"} tok_eval decision, values, lang the value of the decision tok_sim cases, seed, lang, log, cases_table, csv, xes {"kpi", "report", …} tok_sim_model, tok_sim_dist, tok_sim_eval the simulation model, a parsed distribution, an evaluated expression: the building blocks of external simulators such as Tok.Sim tok_cli the tok command line with the arguments of a JSON array tok_version(), tok_abi_version(), tok_free(s) the version of the engine (a static string, not freed), the version of the C interface, freeing a result A small program: #include <stdio.h> #include "tok.h" int main(void) { const char *doc = "tok 1.0 \"Example\"\n" "start s\n" "task a \"Work\" duration=\"exp(1h)\"\n" "end e\n" "flow s -> a -> e\n" "simulate cases=10 seed=1\n"; printf("engine %s, interface %u\n", tok_version(), tok_abi_version()); char *r = tok_check(doc, "{\"lang\": \"en\"}"); printf("%s\n", r); tok_free(r); r = tok_fmt("tok 1.0 \"Broken\"\nstart s \"unterminated\n", NULL); printf("%s\n", r); tok_free(r); return 0; } Compiled against the library (on Linux cc app.c -I include -L lib -ltokengine -o app, with the folders of tok.h and of the library), it prints: engine 1.0.3, interface 1 {"ok": {"errors": 0, "bpmn_class": "descriptive", "diagnostics": []}} {"error": {"kind": "document", "message": "line 2: error T001: invalid token: unterminated string", "diagnostics": [{"code": "T001", "severity": "error", "line": 2, "id": null, "message": "invalid token: unterminated string"}]}} tok_abi_version() changes only when a function is removed or changes its parameters, or when a member of a result changes its meaning. New functions, options and members keep the version, so a program should ignore members it does not know; it can compare tok_abi_version() with the constant TOK_ABI_VERSION of the header it was built with. The library comes with the release archives of the repository. To build it yourself, run cargo build --release -p tok-capi in the folder rust/ of a checkout; the files appear in rust/target/release. 13.7 The Rust crates The engine is published on crates.io as six crates: Crate Contents tok-core the parser, the checker, the canonical printer, BPMN 2.0 and DMN 1.5 export and import, and FEEL tok-bpmn the BPMN 2.0 rules, the automatic layout and the SVG rendering tok-sim the discrete-event simulator tok-cli the tok command (the program is called tok; the crate name tok was taken) and the library tok_cli with the module api tok-lsp the language server (Chapter 12) tok-mcp the MCP server for AI agents (Chapter 14) The programs install with cargo: cargo install tok-cli # the program tok cargo install tok-lsp tok-mcp # the language server and the MCP server In a Rust program, the simplest entry point is tok_cli::api: the functions of the C interface as Rust functions, fn check(text: &str, options: &str) -> Result<Json, ApiError> and the others (fmt, bpmn, svg, export_files, import_file, eval, sim, sim_model, sim_dist, sim_eval, cli), with the same options and results. api::respond turns a result into the JSON text the C functions return. The crate tok-core gives the lower levels, such as tok_core::parse, which returns the document and its parser diagnostics, and tok_core::fmt, which prints a document in canonical form: [dependencies] tok-cli = "1.0.3" tok-core = "1.0.3" use tok_cli::api; fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let text = std::fs::read_to_string("13-loan-renewal.tok")?; // the functions of the C interface, with options and results as JSON let checked = api::check(&text, r#"{"lang": "en"}"#); println!("{}", api::respond(&checked)); let value = api::eval(&text, r#"{"decision": "renewal", "values": {"renewals": 3, "reserved": false}}"#); println!("{}", api::respond(&value)); // the core: parse and print the canonical form let (doc, diags) = tok_core::parse(&text); for d in &diags { println!("{}", tok_core::diagnostics::format_diag(d, "en", None)); } print!("{}", &tok_core::fmt(&doc)[..40]); println!(); Ok(()) } {"ok": {"errors": 0, "bpmn_class": "full", "diagnostics": []}} {"ok": "refused"} tok 1.0 "Loan renewal" start asked "Rea The JSON interface of tok_cli::api is the stable one: it is the interface of the C library, documented option by option. The internal modules of tok-core follow the structure of the implementation and are the place for programs that need to work on the document model itself. 13.8 Which interface to choose Situation Interface a script in a shell or a CI job the tok command, with --json where a program reads the output a Python script, notebook or web service tok.api an analysis or a report in R, a course with R Markdown tokr and its knitr engine simulation experiments with many scenarios and replications Tok.Sim in Julia a web page that checks or draws models in the browser the WebAssembly module a program in C, C++, Go or another language with a C interface tokengine with tok.h a Rust program tok_cli::api, or tok-core for the document model an editor tok-lsp (Chapter 12) an AI agent tok-mcp or tok mcp (Chapter 14) Whatever you choose, the text of the model stays the source. Programs read and write .tok files, the engine does the work, and the results are the same in every host language. The sources of the engine and of every binding are in the repository https://github.com/tok-lang-bpm/tok, where questions and bug reports go to its issues. Exercises Exercise 13.1 A checker for a folder. Write a Python script that checks every .tok file in a folder with api.check, prints one line per file with the numbers of errors and warnings, and exits with status 1 when any file has errors. Run it on the examples/ folder of this book: which files have errors, and why? Decisions as a table. In R, evaluate the decision renewal of 13-loan-renewal.tok for every combination of renewals from 0 to 4 and reserved TRUE and FALSE with tok_eval, and arrange the results in a data frame with one row per combination. Compare the table with the rules of the decision. Two implementations. In Julia, parse the examples of this book with the independent core (Tok.parse_tok) and print them with Tok.fmt. Compare the text with Tok.Engine.fmt for each file. Are there differences? A page. Build a minimal web page with a text area and a picture: on every change it calls check of the WebAssembly module and shows the number of errors, and when there are none, puts the result of svg into the page. Serve it with python -m http.server. The same result everywhere. Simulate 13-loan-renewal.tok with 300 cases and seed 5 from the command line (tok sim --cases 300 --seed 5), from Python and from R or Julia. Compare the mean cycle times and the utilization. What do you conclude about reproducing results reported by someone else?
