Chapter 14 Working with AI agents 14.1 Why a text language suits agents 14.2 The skill tok-modelling 14.3 The MCP server 14.4 Configuring clients 14.5 Working without MCP 14.6 A session: from a table of steps to a BPMN file 14.7 Reviewing what an agent produces Exercises

Chapter 14 Working with AI agents In this chapter you will see why a short text language suits AI agents that write process models · learn what the skill tok-modelling teaches an agent and which files it contains · start the MCP server with tok mcp or tok-mcp and know its tools · configure MCP clients, VS Code and Claude Code, and point other agents to the skill · work without MCP with tok cheatsheet and tok check --json · follow a session from a table of process steps to a checked model and a BPMN file · review what an agent produces, because a clean check is not proof that the model matches reality An AI agent is a language model that does not only answer but acts: it reads and writes files, runs commands, looks at their output and plans its next step from it. Agents are good at turning a description of a process into a structured model, and they are increasingly used for it. This chapter shows how to give an agent the tok language and the tok tools, and how to check what it produces. 14.1 Why a text language suits agents An agent asked to produce a BPMN diagram directly has to write XML: hundreds of lines with namespaces, generated identifiers, references between elements and, in the diagram interchange part, coordinates of every shape and every bend of every arrow. Each of these is a place for a mistake that is hard to see and hard to locate, and coordinates are something a language model has no good way to compute. With tok the work is divided differently. The agent writes a short text that describes only the meaning of the process. The engine checks it, reports each problem with a code and a line number, prints the canonical form and produces the BPMN file with a computed layout. The agent never writes XML and never places a shape. The same features that make tok easy to review for people make it easy to write for agents: Feature of tok What it gives the agent What it gives you one statement per line, one keyword per statement a mistake concerns one line, and a fix changes one line you review the model line by line, like text explicit identifiers references cannot dangle silently: an unknown name is the error R002 with its line you refer to elements by name in reviews and in requests for corrections the whole language on one page the cheat sheet fits into the context of the agent the same cheat sheet is the appendix of this book diagnostics with stable codes, line numbers and --json the agent reads the result of a check without guessing you can follow what the agent fixed and why one canonical form (tok fmt) the text has one layout, whoever wrote it the differences between versions are small and readable no coordinates nothing to draw the diagram is always drawn the same way The division of work is worth keeping in mind through the whole chapter: the agent is responsible for the meaning, the engine for the mechanics, and you for the judgement. The engine can tell the agent that a message flow connects two lanes of one pool; it cannot tell either of you that a step the description calls “automatic” was modelled as a user task. 14.2 The skill tok-modelling A skill is a folder of instructions and reference material that an agent loads when a task matches its description. The skill tok-modelling teaches an agent to model processes in tok. Its files are: File Content SKILL.md the instructions: when the skill applies, which tools to use, the workflow, the rules models most often break, and a summary of every layer of the language references/cheatsheet.md the language on one page, read before writing the first line references/spec.md the specification, for the sections the cheat sheet does not cover references/feel.md FEEL in tok references/diagnostics.md every diagnostic code with its explanation, in English and Polish SKILL.md begins with a front matter that names the skill and describes when to use it: for .tok files, for turning a process description such as a table of steps into a model, for decision models, and for executable or simulated processes. Agent tools that support skills read this description and load the skill when a task matches it. The workflow the skill prescribes is the one an experienced modeller follows: Read the process description completely: the participants, the roles, the steps, the decisions, the deadlines, the messages to other organisations and the documents. Write a mapping first: a file mapping.md with one row per step, giving the tok element (kind and identifier), the lane, the words of the description that justify the choice, and any doubts. The person the agent works for reviews the model through this table. Write the .tok file: one statement per line, short ASCII identifiers, labels in the language of the description, the header tok 1.0 for a new model. Check the model and fix every error, then check again until there are none; fix or justify the warnings. Format it into canonical form. Export what the task asks for: the BPMN file, the picture, the files for Camunda. Report briefly: the files created, the number of elements, the decisions that were ambiguous. The skill ends its workflow with the sentence that matters most for the person who uses it: no errors means the model follows the rules of the notation, not that it matches the description; the mapping is there for that. It then lists the rules models most often break: a message flow connects different pools, a splitting gateway is labelled with a question and its flows with the answers, branches are joined with the same kind of gateway they were split with, deadlines during a task are boundary events and not extra gateways, an event sub-process has no incoming or outgoing flows, and a flow line with a label has exactly one arrow. A skill is plain text. You can read it before you let an agent use it, and you can extend it: an institution can add its own naming rules, its own roles or its own patterns. Writing a good skill is a way of handing an agent the knowledge of your organisation. 14.3 The MCP server The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard way for an agent application to call tools of local programs. The MCP server of tok gives an agent the engine as tools: it checks a model and returns the diagnostics, prints the canonical form, exports BPMN, SVG, DMN and form files, imports BPMN and DMN, simulates and evaluates decisions, checks BPMN XML files from any tool (check_bpmn), and returns the language reference. The skill uses the server when the agent has it, and the tok command otherwise. 14.3.1 Starting the server There are two ways to run it. Both speak MCP over standard input and output (the stdio transport) and serve one client until it closes the connection: tok mcp from the Python package. If you have installed tok with pip install tok-lang, you already have the server: the command tok mcp starts it. This is the simplest way on any computer with Python. tok-mcp, a separate program, from crates.io (cargo install tok-mcp) or from the release archives of the repository. It is useful where you do not want Python, for example in a container. tok mcp --version and tok-mcp --version print the version of the server. You do not normally start the server yourself: the agent application starts it when it needs it, using the configuration below. 14.3.2 Tools Every tool that reads a document takes it either as text (the tok text) or as path (a .tok file the server reads), never both. lang (en or pl) chooses the language of the diagnostics and reports. Tool Arguments Result check text or path, lang, level (basic, analytic, full), class (descriptive, analytic, common-executable, full), bpmn (default true: also the BPMN 2.0 rules) {"errors", "bpmn_class", "diagnostics"}, as tok check --json fmt text or path, lang {"text"}: the canonical form export text or path, formats (a list of bpmn, svg, dmn, forms; all when left out), name, sidecar, lang {"files": {NAME: CONTENT}}: the files tok export writes import xml or path, format (auto, bpmn, dmn), flow_ids, layout {"format", "text", "warnings", "layout"}: the tok document, what was not kept, and for BPMN the layout sidecar sim text or path, cases, seed, and the booleans log, cases_table, csv, xes {"kpi", "report"} and, on request, the event log and the table of cases eval text or path, decision, values (an object input name → value), lang {"value"}: the value of the decision reference topic: cheatsheet (default), spec, diagnostics, feel, cli {"text"}: the reference document The same reference documents are also available as resources, for clients that attach resources to the context: tok://reference/cheatsheet, tok://reference/spec, tok://reference/diagnostics, tok://reference/feel and tok://reference/cli. Three properties of the server are worth knowing: It writes nothing. fmt and export return the text and the files; the agent writes them with its own file tools. This keeps every change to your files visible in the agent’s normal workflow. Two kinds of errors. A problem the agent can fix (a document with errors, an unknown decision, an argument of the wrong type) is a tool error with an explanation; a malformed request is a protocol error. check is the exception: a document with errors is its normal result, with errors greater than 0. No network, the rights of its user. The server opens no network connection and runs with the rights of the user who starts it; it reads the files named by path and the layout sidecars next to them. A client that lets an agent call tools should still show you the calls, as MCP recommends. To try the server by hand, the MCP Inspector of the protocol project starts it and lists its tools: npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector tok mcp. 14.4 Configuring clients 14.4.1 Clients with an mcpServers configuration Many agent applications read a JSON configuration with an object mcpServers. The server needs no environment and, with the Python package, one argument: { "mcpServers": { "tok": { "command": "tok", "args": ["mcp"] } } } With the separate program, the command is "tok-mcp" without arguments. When the program is not on the PATH, give its full path; on Windows, for example, "command": "C:\\tools\\tok\\tok-mcp.exe". Paths given to the tools are read relative to the working directory of the server, which is the folder the client starts it in; give the agent absolute paths when in doubt. 14.4.2 VS Code VS Code reads the MCP servers of a workspace from .vscode/mcp.json, with the key servers and the type of the transport: { "servers": { "tok": { "type": "stdio", "command": "tok", "args": ["mcp"] } } } Commit the file with the project, and everyone who opens the folder gets the server for the agent of VS Code. The VS Code extension of tok (Chapter 12) is independent of it: the extension serves you while you edit, the MCP server serves the agent. 14.4.3 Claude Code For Claude Code, the repository tok-agent (https://github.com/tok-lang-bpm/tok-agent) is a plugin marketplace with a plugin that brings both the skill and the MCP server. In Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add tok-lang-bpm/tok-agent /plugin install tok@tok-lang-bpm The first command adds the marketplace (named tok-lang-bpm), the second installs the plugin tok from it; the skill is then available as tok:tok-modelling, with its companion tok:bpmn-modelling for agents that write BPMN 2.0 XML directly, and the plugin starts the MCP server with tok mcp. Install the engine on the computer first (pip install tok-lang), so that the tools of the server and the commands of the skill can run. To add only the MCP server to Claude Code, without the plugin, the command line of Claude Code takes the command of the server after --: claude mcp add tok -- tok mcp. 14.4.4 Other agents Agents that read skills in the format of a folder with SKILL.md can use the skill folder of the tok-agent repository, plugins/tok/skills/tok-modelling, directly: copy it to the place where your agent looks for skills, or point the agent to it. The README of tok-agent gives the MCP configuration for other clients (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI), and its file templates/AGENTS.md is a ready section for the AGENTS.md of a project. Agents that read an AGENTS.md file at the root of a project (a file of standing instructions read at the start of each session) need only a few lines there that point to the skill files and state the rules of the project, for example: ## Process models Process models in this repository are tok files (`models/*.tok`). Before writing or changing one, read `skills/tok-modelling/SKILL.md` and `skills/tok-modelling/references/cheatsheet.md`, and follow their workflow. Check every model with `tok check FILE --json` until it has no errors, format it with `tok fmt FILE -w`, and never edit the `.bpmn` files by hand: export them with `tok bpmn FILE`. Most agents can also use an MCP server; configure it as above where the agent supports it. 14.5 Working without MCP An agent that can run commands in a shell needs no MCP server. Two commands give it everything: tok cheatsheet prints the one-page summary of the language. Put it into the context of the agent, or tell the agent to run it before writing the first line. It begins like this: # tok 1.0 — cheat sheet One statement per line. Blocks by indentation (spaces). `#` starts a comment. Every statement starts with a keyword. Identifiers: `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_-]*`, unique. Labels: "quoted text". tok check FILE --json prints the diagnostics in a form a program reads without parsing text. The agent reads the code, the line and the identifier of each diagnostic, fixes the line and runs the check again: { "file": "complaint.tok", "errors": 0, "bpmn_class": "analytic", "diagnostics": [ { "code": "W054", "severity": "warning", "line": 9, "id": "remind", "message": "message task or event without a message flow in a model with several pools (remind)" } ] } With tok fmt FILE -w, tok bpmn FILE, tok svg FILE, tok export FILE -o DIR, tok sim FILE --seed N and tok eval FILE DECISION name=value … the agent has every operation of the MCP server. If the agent can run neither the server nor the command, it can still write a model by the cheat sheet, and it should then say clearly that the model has not been checked. 14.6 A session: from a table of steps to a BPMN file The following session shows the workflow on a small but realistic task. A university repository receives complaints about publications that may infringe copyright. The person in charge writes the procedure as a table and asks an agent, which has the skill and the MCP server, to model it. # Step Who 1 A complainant sends a complaint about a publication by e-mail. complainant 2 The repository officer registers the complaint in the repository system. repository officer 3 The system hides the publication automatically until the complaint is resolved. repository system 4 The officer assesses whether the complaint is justified. If the assessment is not finished within 10 days, the officer reminds the head of the repository; the assessment continues. repository officer 5 If the complaint is justified, the officer informs the author that the publication will be removed, and the system removes it. repository officer, system 6 If the complaint is not justified, the system restores the publication. repository system 7 In both cases the officer replies to the complainant, and the complaint is closed. repository officer The mapping. The agent reads the table and first writes mapping.md. Its rows record decisions such as these: the complainant and the author are outside the university, so they are pools without a block, black boxes that only exchange messages; the officer and the system are lanes of the repository’s pool; step 1 is a message start event, because the process begins when the e-mail arrives; step 3 says “automatically”, so it is a service task in the lane of the system; the 10-day reminder of step 4 happens while the assessment continues, so it is a non-interrupting boundary timer; steps 5 and 6 are the two answers of an exclusive gateway, joined again before step 7. One row records a doubt: the table does not say how the officer reminds the head of the repository. The first check. The agent writes complaint.tok and calls check. The answer contains one error (the diagnostics are shown here as tok check prints them; the tool returns the same as JSON): complaint.tok:35: error R022: message flow register -> hide must connect two different pools complaint.tok: 1 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) The agent had written a message flow from the registration to the hiding of the publication, as if the officer sent a message to the system. Both lanes belong to one pool, and within a pool the order of work is a sequence flow. The agent removes the message flow; the sequence flow register -> hide is already in the chain of flows. The second check. Now the BPMN rules run, and they find a warning: complaint.tok:9: warning W054: message task or event without a message flow in a model with several pools (remind) complaint.tok: 0 error(s), 1 warning(s), 0 note(s) The agent had made the reminder a send task with a message, but the head of the repository is not a participant of the model, so the message goes nowhere. This is the doubt from the mapping, and the warning makes it visible. Two readings are possible: the head is a separate participant (a third black-box pool with a message flow), or the reminder is internal work of the officer. The agent chooses the second, changes the line to a user task user remind "Remind the head of the repository", and writes the choice and its reason into the mapping, so that the person reviewing it can disagree. The third check is clean: complaint.tok: 0 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) The agent then formats the file and exports the diagram: tok fmt complaint.tok -w tok bpmn complaint.tok BPMN: complaint.bpmn tok svg complaint.tok SVG: complaint.svg The result is the model below. It is the file 14-copyright-complaint.tok of this book. tok 1.0 "Copyright complaint in the university repository" pool repository "University repository" lane officer "Repository officer" start received "Complaint received" message="Complaint" user register "Register the complaint" user assess "Assess the complaint" boundary reminder "10 days passed" noninterrupting on=assess timer=P10D user remind "Remind the head of the repository" end reminded "Head reminded" xor justified "Is the complaint justified?" send inform "Inform the author" message="Notice of removal" xor merge send reply "Reply to the complainant" message="Reply" end closed "Complaint closed" lane system "Repository system" service hide "Hide the publication" service remove "Remove the publication" service restore "Restore the publication" pool complainant "Complainant" pool author "Author" flow received -> register -> hide -> assess -> justified flow justified -> inform "yes" flow justified -> restore "no" flow inform -> remove -> merge flow restore -> merge -> reply -> closed flow reminder -> remind -> reminded message complainant -> received "Complaint" message inform -> author "Notice of removal" message reply -> complainant "Reply" Figure 14.1: The copyright complaint, modelled from the table of steps and checked by the engine. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) Its report to the person is short: the files mapping.md, complaint.tok, complaint.bpmn and complaint.svg; three pools, two lanes, fourteen flow nodes in the repository’s process; one ambiguous point, the reminder, modelled as internal work of the officer. Notice what the engine contributed. It found the message flow between lanes, which a reader of the XML might have missed, and it turned an unstated assumption about the reminder into a warning with a line number. Notice also what it could not contribute. Whether the hiding of the publication really happens before the assessment, whether the author is informed before or after the removal, whether “the system removes it” might rather be a decision of a person: these are questions about the procedure, and only someone who knows it can answer them. 14.7 Reviewing what an agent produces An agent can be wrong in a convincing way. A model without errors and with a clean diagram can still have the wrong kinds of tasks, the wrong kind of boundary event or a missing branch. A clean check is not a proof that the model matches reality. It proves that the model follows the rules of BPMN and of tok; whether it says what the description says is for you to judge. A review in four passes covers most of what goes wrong: Participants and roles. Do the pools and lanes correspond to the description? Are outside parties black-box pools? Is every element in the lane of the role that performs the step? Kinds of elements. For each step, compare the keyword (user, service, manual, rule, send, …) with the words of the description: “in the system” points to a user task, “automatically” to a service task, “face to face” or “on paper” to a manual task, “strictly by a table of rules” to a business rule task. The flow. Walk the flow lines from the start to every end. Are splits and joins of the same kind? Does every loop return to the right place? Exceptions and messages. Are boundary events on the right activities, and are they interrupting or non-interrupting as the description says? Does every message of the description have a message flow? The mapping makes this review fast, because every choice is written next to the words that justify it. When you find a mistake, ask for a correction precisely: name the step, what is wrong, what it should be and why, quoting the description. “Step 4: the reminder must not stop the assessment, because the description says the assessment continues; make the boundary event non-interrupting” leads to the fix you want. “Fix the model” leads to the fixes the agent thinks of. A few further habits help: Keep the model in version control. Each change by the agent is then a small diff of text that you can read and revert. The canonical form keeps the diffs small. Keep a record of the requests. What you asked the agent to do is part of the documentation of the model, and some institutions require you to disclose generated content. Do not put personal data into requests. Process models describe roles, not people. Check the executable layer and the simulation separately. An executable model is tested by running it (Chapter 10); a simulation by checking its assumptions and its arithmetic (Chapter 11). Neither is established by a clean check. Exercises Exercise 14.1 Read the skill. Read SKILL.md of the skill tok-modelling before using it. Which three rules in its list of frequent mistakes would you have broken yourself when you started with BPMN? Add one rule of your own organisation to a copy of the skill. Configure a client. Configure the MCP server in an agent application you use, with tok mcp or tok-mcp. Ask the agent to call the tool reference and to summarise the header line of a tok document. Then ask it to check 14-copyright-complaint.tok with the tool check and report the BPMN conformance class. A session of your own. Write a table of six to ten steps for a procedure you know, with at least one decision, one deadline and one message to an outside party. Let an agent model it with the skill, following the workflow of this chapter. Note every diagnostic the agent met on the way, and classify each as a mistake of notation or a mistake of understanding. Review. Review the model of exercise 3 in the four passes. Write at least two precise requests for corrections, quoting your table, and check the result again. Without MCP. Repeat a short session with an agent that has only a shell: give it the output of tok cheatsheet and tell it to use tok check --json. Compare the number of steps and the result with the session that used the MCP server. Find what the check cannot. Take the final model of the copyright complaint and change it so that it still checks without errors but no longer matches the table of steps (for example, make the reminder interrupting). Give the changed model to a colleague, or to an agent, with the table, and ask for a review. Is the change found?

Chapter 15 Integrations In this chapter you will check models in continuous integration with the GitHub Action tok-lang-bpm/setup-tok@v1, and with the same commands in Forgejo, Codeberg or any other CI · keep models canonical with a pre-commit hook · put models into R Markdown, Quarto and Jupyter documents · move models between tok and Camunda Modeler, Camunda Web Modeler, bpmn.io and other BPMN tools, with the MIWG round-trip results as evidence of what survives · hand logs to process-mining tools and decisions to other DMN engines · organise a version-control workflow around text, diffs, reviews and the layout sidecar A model is useful when it is where people work: in the repository with the code of the system that runs the process, in the report that analyses it, in the modelling tool a colleague prefers, in the engine that executes it. Because a tok model is a text file and the engine produces standard files, it fits into all of these places without special infrastructure. This chapter goes through them one by one. The examples use a small model of a thesis deposit: tok 1.0 "Thesis deposit" pool university "University" lane student "Student" start ready "Thesis ready" user upload "Upload the thesis to the repository" lane office "Dean's office" user verify "Verify the metadata" xor complete "Are the metadata complete?" user correct "Ask for corrections" lane system "Repository system" service plagiarism "Run the similarity check" service archive "Archive the thesis" end deposited "Thesis deposited" flow ready -> upload -> verify -> complete flow complete -> plagiarism "yes" flow complete -> correct "no" flow correct -> upload flow plagiarism -> archive -> deposited Figure 15.1: The thesis deposit, the model of the examples in this chapter. Download the model (.tok) Download the BPMN export (.bpmn) 15.1 Continuous integration on GitHub Continuous integration (CI) runs checks on every change pushed to a repository and on every pull request. For a repository of process models the checks are the obvious ones: every model passes tok check, and every model is in canonical form. The GitHub Action tok-lang-bpm/setup-tok@v1 does the first of them in one step. It installs tok from PyPI, puts the tok command on the PATH for the later steps of the job, checks the models, and shows their diagnostics as annotations on the lines of the files, so that a reviewer of a pull request sees an error next to the line that causes it. Input Meaning version the version of tok-lang to install from PyPI; by default the latest check a glob of the models to check, by default **/*.tok; an empty string installs tok without checking anything lang the language of the diagnostics: en (the default) or pl fail-on the severity that fails the step: error (the default), or warning to fail on warnings too A workflow that checks the models, verifies their canonical form and keeps their BPMN exports as an artifact of the run, saved as .github/workflows/models.yml: name: models on: push: pull_request: jobs: models: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Install tok and check the models uses: tok-lang-bpm/setup-tok@v1 with: check: "models/**/*.tok" fail-on: warning - name: Canonical form run: | status=0 for f in $(git ls-files 'models/*.tok'); do tok fmt --check "$f" || status=1 done exit $status - name: Export BPMN and pictures run: | mkdir -p out for f in $(git ls-files 'models/*.tok'); do name=$(basename "$f" .tok) tok bpmn "$f" -o "out/$name.bpmn" tok svg "$f" -o "out/$name.svg" done - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4 with: name: diagrams path: out/ The second and third steps use the tok command that the action installed. Each command of tok takes one file, so the steps loop over the files that Git tracks. With fail-on: warning a model with a warning fails the run; use error while a repository still has warnings you have decided to accept. To pin the version of tok for reproducible runs, add version: with a version number; the outputs of a release 1.x do not change except for documented bug fixes, so a newer 1.x gives the same results for valid documents. To install tok without checking anything, for example in a job that only exports, set check: "" and run the commands yourself in later steps. 15.2 Other CI systems Nothing in the checks depends on GitHub. Every CI system that can run a shell with Python can do the same with three commands: pip install tok-lang, tok check and tok fmt --check. A script that checks every model and its canonical form, and fails when any of them fails: #!/bin/sh # check every model and its canonical form; exit 1 when any of them fails status=0 for f in $(find models -name '*.tok' | sort); do tok check "$f" || status=1 tok fmt --check "$f" || status=1 done exit $status On a folder with three models, one of them not formatted: models/complaint.tok: 0 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) models/complaint.tok: not in canonical form models/reading-room.tok: 0 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) models/thesis-deposit.tok: 0 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 note(s) The script ends with the exit status 1, which fails the job. tok check exits with 1 when a document has errors, and tok fmt --check when the file is not canonical; both exit with 0 otherwise. The fix is tok fmt -w models/complaint.tok. Forgejo and Codeberg Actions read workflows from .forgejo/workflows/ in a syntax close to that of GitHub. The label in runs-on depends on the runners available to your repository: on: [push, pull_request] jobs: models: runs-on: docker container: python:3.12 steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: pip install tok-lang - run: sh check-models.sh GitLab CI and other systems take the same commands: models: image: python:3.12 script: - pip install tok-lang - sh check-models.sh Where a program reads the result, tok check FILE --json prints the diagnostics as JSON, with the smallest BPMN conformance class of the document: { "file": "models/thesis-deposit.tok", "errors": 0, "bpmn_class": "descriptive", "diagnostics": [] } A repository can use it to enforce a conformance class, for example to require that published models stay in the descriptive class, or check them with tok check FILE --class descriptive, which reports every element outside the class as R075. 15.3 A pre-commit hook CI finds problems after they are pushed. A Git hook finds them before the commit is made. The hook below checks every .tok file staged for the commit, and refuses the commit when one has errors or is not canonical. Save it as .git/hooks/pre-commit and make it executable: #!/bin/sh # refuse a commit with a model that has errors or is not in canonical form status=0 for f in $(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM -- '*.tok'); do tok fmt --check "$f" || status=1 tok check "$f" > /dev/null || { tok check "$f"; status=1; } done if [ $status -ne 0 ]; then echo "fix the models above (tok fmt -w FILE formats a file) and commit again" fi exit $status The hook prints the diagnostics only for files with errors, to keep the output of a normal commit quiet. With the pre-commit framework, the same check is a local hook in .pre-commit-config.yaml; because each tok command takes one file, the entry loops over the files the framework passes: repos: - repo: local hooks: - id: tok name: tok check and fmt --check language: system files: \.tok$ entry: sh -c 'status=0; for f in "$@"; do tok check "$f" >/dev/null || { tok check "$f"; status=1; }; tok fmt --check "$f" || status=1; done; exit $status' -- A hook that formats the files instead of only checking them (tok fmt -w "$f" followed by git add "$f") is possible too. Checking is the safer default: it never changes a file behind the author’s back. 15.4 Models in documents 15.4.1 R Markdown and Quarto The R package tokr registers a knitr engine called tok (Chapter 13). In an R Markdown document, load the package in a setup chunk, then write models in chunks of the engine: ```{r setup, include=FALSE} library(tokr) ``` ```{tok, fig.cap = "Thesis deposit"} tok 1.0 "Thesis deposit" start ready "Thesis ready" user upload "Upload the thesis to the repository" user verify "Verify the metadata" end deposited "Thesis deposited" flow ready -> upload -> verify -> deposited ``` The chunk is drawn as a figure with its caption. The chunk option tok.output chooses what the chunk shows instead: "check" the diagnostics, "fmt" the canonical text, "bpmn" the BPMN XML; tok.export = "dir" also writes every exported file into a folder, so a report can link to the BPMN file of the model it shows. Quarto documents run R chunks through knitr, so the same chunks work in a .qmd file with engine: knitr. A report that analyses a process can keep the model, its diagram, its simulation and the analysis in one document. A chunk with tok.output = "check" documents that the model was valid when the report was rendered; R chunks with tok_sim() produce the tables and plots of Chapter 11. For PDF output, which does not take the SVG pictures of the engine directly, use tok.output = "check" or include a picture exported in another format. 15.4.2 Jupyter In a Jupyter notebook the Python package draws a model in a cell. api.svg returns the SVG text, and IPython displays it: from IPython.display import SVG, display from tok import api text = open("15-thesis-deposit.tok", encoding="utf-8").read() display(SVG(api.svg(text))) A small helper shows either the diagnostics or the diagram, which makes a notebook a convenient place to develop a model step by step: def show(text): problems = api.check(text) for d in problems: print("%s %s line %s: %s" % (d["severity"], d["code"], d["line"], d["message"])) if not any(d["severity"] == "error" for d in problems): display(SVG(api.svg(text))) The same helper works in JupyterLab, VS Code notebooks and other front ends that display SVG. 15.5 BPMN tools The BPMN file that tok bpmn writes is standard BPMN 2.0 XML with diagram interchange, so every tool that reads BPMN reads it. Tool How the model gets there What you see Camunda Modeler (desktop) open the .bpmn file; for an executable model also the .dmn and .form files of tok export the diagram with every property; an executable model opens as a Camunda 8 diagram with the extensions in the properties panel, the decisions in the DMN editor, the forms in the form editor Camunda Web Modeler upload the files to a project the same diagrams, shared with a team in the browser, and deployment to a Camunda 8 cluster bpmn.io open or drop the file in the viewer or the online modeler the diagram as it looks in the bpmn-js toolkit, which the playground also uses (Chapter 12) other BPMN tools import BPMN 2.0 XML the semantics of the model with the layout computed by tok The way back is tok import. A diagram drawn or edited in any of these tools converts to tok text, with what tok cannot express reported on standard error; with -o FILE.tok the drawing of the file is kept in a layout sidecar FILE.tok.layout next to the model, so that tok bpmn and tok svg draw the model as it was drawn (Chapter 8). A colleague can therefore keep working in Camunda Modeler while the repository keeps the text: import the changed file, review the diff of the text, and commit it. 15.5.1 How much survives a round trip The evidence for exchange with other tools is the test suite of the BPMN Model Interchange Working Group (MIWG): 22 reference models written by different tools, from simple processes to collaborations with data and Camunda extensions. Each model is imported into tok, printed as text, read again and exported, and the semantic content of the export is compared with the reference fact by fact: structure, nodes, events, activities, gateways, flows, data, declarations, documentation, artifacts and Camunda extensions. Result models 22 facts kept 3533 of 3770 (93.7 %) models kept completely A.1.0, A.2.0, A.3.0, A.4.0, C.2.0, C.5.0, C.6.0 facts not kept 237, each one reported by the import facts added by design 52, for example a participant for a process that no participant references facts of vendor extensions (in 15 models) 1019, not kept by design What is lost is listed with its reason, and none of it is lost silently. The largest groups are the isImmediate attribute of sequence flows, which most tools write as a default, the technology attribute implementation of tasks, imports of other files, transformations of data associations, embedded forms and forms referenced by a key, and extensions of other vendors. A second round trip, export, import and export again, does not change the semantic BPMN. The appendix on conformance gives the table per model. The layout of the reference models is not compared: tok has no coordinates and lays every diagram out itself, or keeps the drawing in the sidecar. 15.6 Camunda 8 For an executable model, tok export writes everything Camunda 8 needs (the BPMN file with the Camunda extensions, the DMN files and the forms), and the files deploy through Camunda Modeler, Web Modeler or the REST API. Chapter 10 describes the executable layer, the deployment to Camunda 8 Run step by step, a Python script that drives an instance, and the conformance runs that verify the translation on Camunda. 15.7 Process-mining tools tok sim --xes writes the simulated event log in XES (IEEE 1849-2016), which ProM, PM4Py, bupaR, Disco, Celonis and other process-mining tools read without any mapping; --log writes the same log as CSV, with the columns case, label, start and end that these tools map to case, activity and timestamps. In R, the event log of tok_sim() has the column names bupaR expects. Chapter 11 shows the code. The direction from logs to models exists too: Tok.Fit in Julia estimates the durations, arrivals and branch probabilities of a model from an XES or CSV log of a real system and writes them into the document. 15.8 Decisions in other DMN engines The decisions of a document of language 0.7 or 1.0 are exported by tok export as DMN 1.5 files, one per connected decision requirements graph, with a DMNDI diagram, so they open in DMN editors and run in DMN engines other than Camunda. Two details matter: Names in FEEL. In an executable document for Camunda the exporter writes FEEL names with spaces or symbols in backticks, which Camunda’s FEEL needs and standard FEEL does not have. For another engine, export the decisions from a document without the flag executable, which writes standard FEEL. Evaluation. tok eval evaluates a decision with everything it requires, with FEEL at DMN conformance level 3. Its results are tested against the DMN Technology Compatibility Kit: at compliance level 2 all 126 results of 28 models pass, at level 3 3313 of 3331 results of 114 models (99.5 %), with every failing result listed with its reason. The same tests make tok eval a reference to compare another engine against. tok import FILE.dmn reads DMN 1.1 to 1.5 files from other tools into a document of language 0.7, so decision tables written elsewhere can be kept, reviewed and tested as text (Chapter 9). 15.9 A version-control workflow Process models change: a regulation is amended, a step is automated, a role is merged into another. In tok the history of the model is the history of a text file, and the tools of software development apply to it unchanged. Diffs. A change to a process is a change of a few lines. Adding a notification of the supervisor to the thesis deposit gives this diff: @@ -11,10 +11,11 @@ pool university "University" lane system "Repository system" service plagiarism "Run the similarity check" service archive "Archive the thesis" + service notify "Notify the supervisor" end deposited "Thesis deposited" flow ready -> upload -> verify -> complete flow complete -> plagiarism "yes" flow complete -> correct "no" flow correct -> upload -flow plagiarism -> archive -> deposited +flow plagiarism -> archive -> notify -> deposited The same change in BPMN XML touches the process, two sequence flows and the diagram interchange, with new coordinates for every shape that moved. The canonical form keeps diffs like this one small: whoever writes the model, and whatever editor they use, tok fmt prints it in one way, so the diff shows only what changed in the meaning. Reviews. A pull request with a model change can be reviewed like a change of code: the reviewer reads the diff, CI shows the diagnostics as annotations, and the BPMN and SVG exports of the run show the new diagram. Comments refer to lines and identifiers. Combined with a mapping table for larger changes (Chapter 14), this is also the natural way to review models written by AI agents. What to commit. Commit the .tok files, and their layout sidecars .tok.layout when the models were imported from a drawing tool and the drawing should be kept. The BPMN files, pictures, DMN files and forms are projections of the text; you can generate them in CI, as in the workflow above, or commit them as well for readers who do not have tok, but never edit them by hand: an edited export is overwritten by the next one. If they are committed, a CI step that exports and then runs git diff --exit-code checks that they are up to date. The layout sidecar. The sidecar is a plain text file with one line per shape or edge, so it diffs and merges like the model. When an element is renamed or removed in the model, the line of the old identifier is ignored; new elements are placed next to their neighbours. A sidecar never changes the meaning of the model, so a conflict in it can always be resolved by taking either side, or by deleting the file to return to the automatic layout. Tags and versions. A version of a procedure that is approved or published can be marked with a Git tag; for executable models the same version can be given to the process definition with version-tag= (Chapter 10), so that an instance in Camunda can be traced to the commit of the text it was deployed from. Where does the diagnostic appear, and what does the reviewer see? Warnings as failures. B Language on one page The whole language of tok 1.0 on one page, as tok cheatsheet prints it and as the skill for AI agents carries it. The normative description is the specification, docs/spec.md. One statement per line. Blocks by indentation (spaces). # starts a comment. Every statement starts with a keyword. Identifiers: [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_-]*, unique. Labels: “quoted text”. Attributes: key=value (value: word, number or “text”) and bare flags. A key or flag is written once per line, the triggers of multiple events aside (in 1.0 a repeated one is the deprecation warning R090). tok 1.0 "Title" [executable] # header, first line (0.1–0.7 documents stay valid) [process-name="Name"] (process of a document without pools) doc="Text" on any statement: documentation start ID "Label" [message="M" | timer=P3D | signal="S" | condition="feel"] [form=F] end ID "Label" [message="M" | error="E" | escalation="X" | signal="S" | terminate] # error/escalation: [code="E1"] catch ID "Label" message="M" | timer=PT2H | signal="S" | condition="feel" | link="L" throw ID "Label" [message="M" | escalation="X" | signal="S" | link="L" | compensate] boundary ID "Label" on=ACTIVITY timer=P7D [noninterrupting] # also message/error/escalation/signal several triggers = multiple event: message="A" message="B" signal="C"; Compensation and catch-all events (any document): service a … compensate=h + service h … compensation · throw c … compensate [activity=a] · boundary b on=a error (any error) · boundary b on=a escalation (any escalation) Executable layer (only with executable; values computed at run time start with =): user t … assignee="kierownik" candidate-groups="a, b" due="=now() + duration(\"P3D\")" priority=70 user t … candidate-users="ola, jan" follow-up="2027-01-20T09:00:00Z" user t … parallel collection="items" item=x output=results output-item="x.result" until="numberOfCompletedInstances >= 2" adhoc a … active="chosen" until="done = true" wait call c … process=child binding=deployment|latest|version-tag version="v2" child-vars=none parent-vars=none business-id="=numer" service s … type="job" retries=5 headers="key: value; …" inputs="target = expr; …" outputs="target = expr; …" service r … connector=rest method=GET url="https://…" result=response [body= query= headers-in=] end e … message="M" type="job" catch|boundary … condition="x > 1" events="create, update" any … listeners="start: job-type; end: job-type (5)" (user tasks also: creating, assigning, updating, completing, canceling) tok 0.3 "T" executable version-tag="v1" pool p … version-tag="v1" Language 0.5 elements (transaction, cancel, complex, loop conditions, multiple events, instantiate, process data, global tasks, operations, keys) and 0.6 elements (conversations, choreographies, min/max) are BPMN only: --level basic|analytic rejects them, and in executable documents for Camunda they are reported as C100–C123. Decisions of 0.7 are level full; Camunda codes C130 (bkm with invoke=), C131 (non-literal function body), C132 (decision without logic). In 0.5 documents resource and by= also export BPMN performers. commands.html
C Command reference

C Command reference The commands of the tok program, their options, their output for programs (--json) and their exit codes. The Python package adds one command of its own, tok mcp, which runs the MCP server for AI agents (Chapter 14): tok mcp # serve one MCP client on standard input and output tok mcp --version # print the version of the server tok check FILE [--level basic|analytic|full] [--class descriptive|analytic|common-executable|full] [--lang en|pl] [--json] tok check FILE.bpmn [--steps] [--steps-from DESCRIPTION.md] [--camunda] [--lang en|pl] [--json] tok fmt FILE [-w|--write] [--check] [--lang en|pl] [--json] tok bpmn FILE [-o|--output OUT.bpmn] [--no-layout] [--no-sidecar] [--lang en|pl] [--json] tok bpmn FILE.bpmn [-o|--output OUT.bpmn] tok svg FILE [-o|--output OUT.svg] [--no-sidecar] [--lang en|pl] [--json] tok svg FILE.bpmn [-o|--output OUT.svg] tok export FILE [-o|--output FOLDER] [--no-sidecar] [--lang en|pl] [--json] tok import FILE.bpmn|FILE.dmn [-o|--output OUT.tok] [--no-flow-ids] [--no-layout] [--lang en|pl] tok sim FILE [--cases N] [--seed N] [--log LOG.csv] [--cases-csv CASES.csv] [--xes LOG.xes] [--lang en|pl] [--json] tok eval FILE DECISION name=value … [--lang en|pl] tok cheatsheet tok --version tok [COMMAND] -h|--help Command What it does check parses the document and lists diagnostics (codes in diagnostics.md). Exit code 1 if there are errors. --level restricts the accepted elements to a teaching level. --class checks the document against a conformance class of BPMN 2.0.2 and reports every element outside it (R075); --json also gives the smallest class the document fits ("bpmn_class"; see bpmn-rules.md). check FILE.bpmn checks a BPMN 2.0 XML file, from tok or from any modelling tool, with the BPMN rules that tok check applies to the export of a document (bpmn-rules.md), and lists the findings with the line of each element; exit code 1 if there are errors. --steps requires every element name to start with the step number of a process description (K01); --steps-from DESCRIPTION.md reads the steps from the table of that file and reports steps without an element and elements without a step (K02, K03); --camunda adds the Camunda 8 profile of executable models (C…; the forms and decisions it refers to are looked for in the file’s folder). The codes are in diagnostics.md (BPMN 2.0 rules; BPMN files). fmt prints the canonical form. -w rewrites the file, --check only reports whether the file is already canonical. bpmn writes BPMN 2.0 XML with an automatic diagram layout. The file opens in Camunda Modeler and bpmn.io. When the layout sidecar FILE.layout exists next to the document (written by tok import), the shapes and edges it names keep their geometry and new elements are placed around them; --no-sidecar ignores it. svg writes a picture of the diagram (with the layout sidecar, as bpmn). bpmn FILE.bpmn, svg FILE.bpmn lay out a BPMN 2.0 XML file (a new diagram written into the file, or into -o) and draw the picture of its diagram. export writes the BPMN file, the SVG picture, the decision files and one .form file per form: everything Camunda 8 needs for an executable document (with the layout sidecar, as bpmn). The decision files are one DMN 1.3 file per decision table in documents of languages 0.1–0.6, and in a document of language 0.7 or 1.0 one DMN 1.5 file per decision requirements graph (NAME.dmn, named after its first decision, with a DMNDI diagram) and its picture (NAME.drd.svg); a 0.7 or 1.0 document without a process writes only the decision files and forms. In an executable document for Camunda the FEEL names with spaces or symbols are written in backticks (spec §9.5). import converts a BPMN 2.0 XML file (for example drawn in Camunda Modeler) to tok, or a DMN 1.1–1.5 file (.dmn, or any file whose root is a DMN definitions) to a document of language 0.7 (import.md). Elements tok does not cover are reported on standard error. With -o OUT.tok the diagram of the file is written to the layout sidecar OUT.tok.layout next to it, so that tok bpmn OUT.tok draws the model as it was drawn (--no-layout: no sidecar). --no-flow-ids drops the identifiers of sequence flows so they print as compact chains. sim runs the simulation described by simulate, resource, variable and the simulation attributes; prints indicators, optionally writes the event log and the per-case table as CSV (--log, --cases-csv) and the event log as XES, IEEE 1849-2016, for process-mining tools (--xes; see simulation.md). eval evaluates a decision for the given input values: tok eval proposal.tok tryb-akceptacji rodzaj=e-book cena=120. A value is true/false, a number, or else text. The result is printed as JSON. In documents of languages 0.1–0.6 the decision table alone is evaluated, and the result is an object of outputs, null when no rule matches, a list of objects for hit policy collect. In a document of language 0.7 or 1.0 the decision is evaluated with the decisions, input data and business knowledge models it requires; name is the FEEL name of input data ("Zaległe opłaty=60"), a value may also be a JSON object or list (czytelnik='{"wiek": 20}'), and text for input data of a temporal type is read as that type (termin=2027-01-15); the result is the value of the decision (spec §9.3), with dates, times and durations as their FEEL text. Exit code 1 when the document has errors or a hit policy is violated (several rules under unique, different outputs under any), in the decision or in a decision it requires; 2 for an unknown decision or an argument that is not name=value. cheatsheet prints the one-page language summary; useful as context for an AI agent. --lang pl (or the environment variable TOK_LANG=pl) switches messages to Polish. --json prints machine-readable output for programs: the diagnostics of check, the indicators of sim, and for fmt, bpmn, svg and export the diagnostics of a document with errors ({"file", "errors", "diagnostics"}) instead of the text report. -h or --help after a command prints its options. The exit code is 0 on success, 1 when the document has errors or the command fails, 2 for a usage error. The layout sidecar is plain text and can be kept in version control next to the model; its format is described in spec §16: tok import diagram.bpmn -o model.tok # writes model.tok and model.tok.layout # … edit model.tok … tok bpmn model.tok # model.bpmn with the drawing of diagram.bpmn, new elements placed around it Without installation the same commands run as python -m tok … with PYTHONPATH pointing to python/src. That pure-Python implementation is frozen at language 0.3 and has no tok sim --xes, no tok check --class and no layout sidecar; they need the Rust engine (the native tok program, or the tok-lang package with the engine).

E Conformance with Camunda 8

E Conformance with Camunda 8 What tok expresses of the BPMN, DMN and FEEL that Camunda 8 executes, the conformance case that fixes each translation, and the case of the executable conformance run that deploys it to Camunda 8 Run and drives it to its end. The same kind of table for every element of the BPMN 2.0.2 and DMN 1.5 metamodels, with the results of the round trip of the BPMN Model Interchange Working Group models and of the DMN Technology Compatibility Kit, is docs/conformance-bpmn.md. This table lists every element of BPMN, DMN and FEEL that Camunda 8.10 lists as supported in its published coverage (the BPMN coverage and DMN coverage pages of the Camunda 8 documentation), with the construct of tok that expresses it, the conformance case whose expected BPMN or DMN export fixes the translation (conformance/cases, compared byte for byte by every implementation, spec §15), and the case of the executable conformance run that deploys it to Camunda 8 Run and drives an instance to its expected end (conformance/camunda/run.py, below). Elements Camunda does not execute are listed at the end, with the codes tok check reports for them in executable documents. Executable means: the header or a pool has the flag executable, and target= is camunda (the default). Without it, every element below is still modelled and exported, but the attributes of the executable layer are ignored (R055).  The run on Camunda 8 Run 8.10.7: the executable cases of conformance/camunda (documents of language 0.3, exported by the Python implementation of that language; the constructs are those of conformance cases 19–30, whose expected BPMN both the Python implementation and the engine produce) the process of case 63, a document of language 1.0 exported by the native tok program, and the decisions of cases 61 and 63 (exported by the native program, evaluated by Camunda and compared with tok eval and the expected values): Case Result multi-instance, adhoc, call-activity, mappings, user-task, message-job, compensation, errors, conditional, listeners, connector, version-tag passed: deployed, started and run to completion, with the user tasks, jobs, messages, errors, variables and headers each case checks 63-executable-10 (language 1.0: the process with its forms and decisions deployed together) passed: a script in FEEL of conformance level 3 (sum(for d in dni return d * 0.5)), the condition of an exclusive gateway, a job with its retries, header and variables, a user task with its assignee and priority, the expected end event, the version tag 1.0 of the process definition 61-executable-decisions (9 evaluations of 6 decisions) passed: deployed, evaluated by Camunda, equal to tok eval and to the expected values 63-executable-10, decisions (3 evaluations of 2 decisions, one input named with two words) passed, as for case 61 All 15 runs passed (PYTHONPATH=python/src python conformance/camunda/run.py, with TOK set to the native program of release 1.0.0), on a fresh data folder of Camunda 8 Run; the process cases ran first and the decision cases last. The run evaluates the decisions last, for a reason that lies in Camunda 8 Run 8.10.7, not in the models: after decisions have been evaluated through the REST API, the exporter to its local secondary storage (H2) can stop on a primary key violation of a decision instance, and from then on searches no longer see new instances, so process cases run afterwards end with a timeout. When that happens, the cases pass again after Camunda 8 Run is stopped and its folders camunda-data and camunda-zeebe-8.10.7/data are emptied. F Glossary

F Glossary Term Meaning activity Work done in a process: a task, a sub-process or a call activity. Drawn as a rounded rectangle. ad-hoc sub-process A sub-process whose activities run in any order, as the performers decide (adhoc). association A dotted line that links an annotation or data to an element. attribute A key=value pair on a statement, such as message="Order" or timer=P3D. black-box pool A pool without a process inside, standing for a participant whose work is not modelled (pool ID "Label" without a block). boundary event An event attached to the border of an activity: it catches something that happens while the activity runs (boundary ID on=ACTIVITY …). It interrupts the activity unless it is noninterrupting. BPMN Business Process Model and Notation, the OMG standard (version 2.0.2, ISO/IEC 19510) for process diagrams and their XML files. BPMN conformance class One of the subsets of BPMN the standard defines: descriptive, analytic, common executable, full. tok check --class checks a document against one. business knowledge model A reusable piece of decision logic, a function that decisions invoke (bkm). business rule task A task whose result comes from a decision (rule … decision=). call activity An activity that runs another process or a global task (call … process= or task=). canonical form The one way tok fmt prints a model: indentation, order of attributes, quoting. Two models with the same meaning print identically. catching event An event that waits for something to happen (outline icon). choreography A model of the messages exchanged between participants, without their internal processes (choreography). collaboration Several pools that exchange messages. compensation Undoing the effect of work already done, by a handler activity bound to the activity it undoes. conformance case A document of the tok repository with its expected outputs (BPMN, SVG, DMN, diagnostics), which every implementation must reproduce byte for byte. conversation A group of message exchanges between pools about one subject, drawn as a hexagon. data object Information that exists while a case of the process runs, such as a request or a decision letter (data). data store Information that outlives the process, such as a catalogue or a register (store). decision requirements graph The decisions of a model with the input data, knowledge sources and business knowledge models they require (DMN). decision table A table of rules that maps input values to outputs, with a hit policy. default flow The flow a gateway takes when no condition of its other flows is true (default). diagnostic A message of tok check: a code, a severity (error, warning, note), a line and a text. DMN Decision Model and Notation, the OMG standard for decisions (version 1.5). engine The program that does the work of tok: the Rust library that parses, checks, prints, exports, imports, evaluates and simulates. The command line, the Python, R and Julia packages, the language server, the MCP server and the playground all call it. event Something that happens during a process: a message arrives, a time passes, an error occurs. Drawn as a circle. event sub-process A sub-process started by an event at any moment while its process runs (eventsub). event-based gateway A gateway after which the first of several events to happen decides the path (eventgw). executable document A document with the flag executable, whose processes carry what Camunda 8 needs to run them. export Writing a model in another format: BPMN, SVG, DMN, Camunda forms. FEEL Friendly Enough Expression Language, the expression language of DMN, used in conditions, decisions and mappings. flag An attribute without a value, such as noninterrupting or parallel. form A Camunda form shown to the person who works on a user task or starts a process (form). gateway A point where paths split or join. Drawn as a diamond. header The first line of a document: tok 1.0 "Title". hit policy The rule that says what a decision table returns when several rules match (unique, first, any, priority, collect, rule-order, output-order). identifier The name of an element for programs: ASCII letters, digits, _ and -, unique in the document. import Reading a BPMN or DMN file into a tok model (tok import). job Work that Camunda 8 hands to a program (a worker): service tasks, message throw events. label The name of an element for people, in quotes, in any language. lane A partition of a pool, usually a role or a department (lane). language level A subset of the language for teaching (basic, analytic, full); tok check --level rejects what is outside it. layout sidecar The file MODEL.tok.layout that keeps the drawing of an imported diagram, so exports keep its geometry. LSP Language Server Protocol: the protocol editors use to get diagnostics, formatting and navigation from a language server (tok-lsp). MCP Model Context Protocol: the protocol AI agents use to call tools; the tok MCP server is tok mcp. message flow A dashed line between pools: one participant sends something to another (message A -> B). multi-instance An activity done once for every item of a collection, in parallel or in sequence (parallel, sequential). pool A participant of a collaboration, with the process it performs (pool). process The order of work of one participant: events, activities, gateways and flows. sequence flow A solid arrow: what comes next in one process (flow A -> B). simulation Running many cases of a process with random durations, arrivals and choices to estimate times and workloads (tok sim). skill A folder of instructions and references that teaches an AI agent a task; the tok skill is tok-modelling. sub-process An activity with its own inner process (sub). throwing event An event that makes something happen, such as sending a message (filled icon). transaction A sub-process whose work is completed together or undone together (transaction). trigger What starts or is caught by an event: message, timer, signal, error, escalation, condition, link, compensation, cancel. user task Work a person does in a system, for example by filling in a form (user). XES eXtensible Event Stream, the IEEE standard format of event logs for process mining (IEEE 1849-2016).
